abstract: We describe a method of constructing higher-order neural networks that respond invariantly under geometric transformations on the input space. By requiring each unit to satisfy a set of constraints on the interconnection weights, a particular structure is imposed on the network. A network built using such an architecture maintains its invariant performance independent of the values the weights assume, of the learning rules used, and of the form of the nonlinearities in the network. The invariance exhibited by a first(cid:173) order network is usually of a trivial sort, e.g., responding only to the average input in the case of translation invariance, whereas higher-order networks can perform useful functions and still exhibit the invariance. We derive the weight constraints for translation, rotation, scale, and several combinations of these transformations, and report results of simulation studies.

paragraphs: The paper constructs neural networks whose responses remain unchanged under specified geometric transformations of the input. It derives constraints on connection weights for translation, rotation, scaling, and several combinations. The aim is to make invariance a property of the network's structure rather than something dependent on a particular learned solution.

Each unit must satisfy the relevant weight constraints. Within the resulting architecture, invariant behavior is maintained regardless of the particular permitted weight values, the learning rule, or the form of the network's nonlinearities. This separates the guarantee of geometric invariance from the choice of how the network is trained.

The authors explain why higher-order networks matter for this construction. A first-order network may achieve only a trivial invariant response, such as using the average input for translation invariance. Higher-order networks can retain useful functionality while satisfying the invariance requirements. Alongside the derivations, the paper reports simulation studies. The central contribution is an architectural route to preserving geometric consistency without restricting the network to such simple invariant summaries.
summary.tldr: Weight constraints build geometric invariance into higher-order networks independently of the learning rule and permitted weight values.

title: Encoding Geometric Invariances in Higher-Order Neural Networks

paragraphs: This paper studies the perceptron's learning speed under explicit assumptions about how examples are distributed. Within Valiant's learning framework, it proves fast learning of an arbitrary half-space when examples are sampled uniformly from the unit sphere. A half-space is a classification region defined by a linear boundary, the kind of decision a perceptron represents.

The paper also proposes a revised learning protocol. Adversaries may choose both the example distribution and the target function, but the two adversaries cannot communicate. This restriction changes how the difficult aspects of a learning problem can be coordinated. Under the revised definition, the author establishes a distribution-independent learning result for the perceptron.

The contribution highlights how learning guarantees depend on the relationship between the target and the sampling distribution. An appendix further shows that, under uniform distributions, certain classes with infinite VC dimension are learnable, including convex sets and a class of nested differences of convex sets. These results make the distributional assumptions central to interpreting what can be learned efficiently.
summary.tldr: The perceptron learns quickly under uniform sampling and gains a distribution-independent guarantee in a protocol restricting coordination between adversaries.

title: The Perceptron Algorithm Is Fast for Non-Malicious Distributions

abstract: The classical computational model for stereo vision incorporates a uniqueness inhibition constraint to enforce a one-to-one feature match, thereby sacrificing the ability to handle transparency. Crit(cid:173) ics of the model disregard the uniqueness constraint and argue that the smoothness constraint can provide the excitation support required for transparency computation. However, this modifica(cid:173) tion fails in neighborhoods with sparse features. We propose a Bayesian approach to stereo vision with priors favoring cohesive over transparent surfaces. The disparity and its segmentation into a multi-layer "depth planes" representation are simultaneously com(cid:173) puted. The smoothness constraint propagates support within each layer, providing mutual excitation for non-neighboring transparent or partially occluded regions. Test results for various random-dot and other stereograms are presented.

paragraphs: The paper addresses stereo vision when a scene includes transparent or partially occluded surfaces. A classical one-to-one feature-matching constraint prevents the model from handling transparency. Simply removing that constraint and relying on local smoothness also creates difficulties, particularly in image neighborhoods with few features.

The authors propose a Bayesian method with prior preferences for cohesive surfaces over transparent ones. It estimates stereo disparity and simultaneously organizes the result into multiple depth planes. This joint representation allows the method to consider layered surfaces while still expressing a preference for coherent interpretations.

Smoothness supplies support within each depth layer. As a result, transparent or partly hidden regions can reinforce one another even when they are not immediate neighbors. This addresses the weakness of support based only on sparse local features. The paper presents tests on random-dot and other stereograms. Its central contribution is to combine layered depth organization with probabilistic preferences and within-layer support for interpreting both opaque and transparent scenes.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian stereo model jointly estimates disparity and depth layers so separated transparent or occluded regions can support one another.

title: The Computation of Stereo Disparity for Transparent and for Opaque Surfaces

paragraphs: The paper presents a neural architecture that learns structure within sequences of symbols. Its target is hierarchical and recursive organization: a smaller unit can sit inside a larger unit, and the same kind of organization can occur at several levels. Recognizing this structure requires more than identifying which symbols appear.

The architecture builds compact descriptions by replacing a substring with a single symbol. That replacement can then participate in a higher-level reduction, allowing the system to work through multiple layers of structure. An external stack provides memory alongside the neural network. Together, these components let the architecture learn to parse strings belonging to LR(0) context-free grammars.

Training uses both accepted and rejected examples, and the authors report learning to recognize many different grammars. Only one layer contains adjustable weights, which makes the learned behavior relatively straightforward to interpret. The contribution is a concrete way to combine learned neural processing, symbolic reduction, and explicit memory to discover nested sequence structure.
summary.tldr: A neural architecture uses symbol reduction and stack memory to learn hierarchical structure in LR(0) context-free languages.

title: A Connectionist Symbol Manipulator That Discovers the Structure of Context-Free Languages

abstract: We address the problem of learning an unknown function by pu tting together several pieces of information (hints) that we know about the function. We introduce a method that generalizes learn(cid:173) ing from examples to learning from hints. A canonical representa(cid:173) tion of hints is defined and illustrated for new types of hints. All the hints are represented to the learning process by examples, and examples of the function are treated on equal footing with the rest of the hints. During learning, examples from different hints are selected for processing according to a given schedule. We present two types of schedules; fixed schedules that specify the relative em(cid:173) phasis of each hint, and adaptive schedules that are based on how well each hint has been learned so far. Our learning method is compatible with any descent technique that we may choose to use.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a learner can combine several pieces of knowledge about an unknown function. Ordinary input-output examples are one source of information, but the authors also consider other hints about that function. Their method brings these sources into a common learning process instead of requiring examples to carry all the available knowledge.

The key is a canonical representation that presents every hint to the learner through examples. Direct observations of the function receive the same status as examples expressing other hints. This common representation makes the choice of what to process next an explicit part of training: the learner draws examples from different hints according to a schedule.

The paper offers fixed schedules, which set each hint's relative emphasis, and adaptive schedules, which respond to how well each hint has been learned. The method can work with any chosen descent technique. Its contribution is therefore a way to organize knowledge and allocate learning effort across it, while leaving the underlying descent procedure flexible.
summary.tldr: The method turns different kinds of prior knowledge into training examples and schedules learning across them.

title: A Method for Learning From Hints

paragraphs: This paper introduces Holographic Recurrent Networks, a recurrent architecture that incorporates associative memory techniques to store sequential structure. The task is sequence generation: the network must produce outputs in an appropriate progression. The design brings a memory mechanism into the recurrent network specifically to support the representation of that progression.

The authors describe training these networks with gradient descent and report that training can be easy and fast. They consider two forms of output: sequences of discrete items and trajectories through continuous space. These settings place the same broad demand on the model—generating an ordered development over time—while differing in whether the outputs are separate symbols or continuously varying values.

Holographic Recurrent Networks outperform ordinary recurrent networks on the sequence generation tasks studied. The finding supports incorporating associative memory into recurrent models for these tasks. The contribution is an architectural approach in which storing sequential structure is part of the design, together with evidence that this design benefits generation of both discrete sequences and continuous trajectories.
summary.tldr: Holographic Recurrent Networks combine recurrence with associative memory and outperform ordinary recurrent networks on the studied sequence-generation tasks.

title: Holographic Recurrent Networks

The present paper clarifies asymptotic properties and their relation of t.wo learning curves, one concerning the predictive loss or generalization loss and the other the training loss. The result gives a natural definition of the complexity of a neural network. Moreover, it provides a new criterion of model selection.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural-network performance changes as the number of training examples grows. It distinguishes two learning curves: training loss, measured on the examples used for fitting, and predictive or generalization loss, which concerns predictions beyond those examples. Comparing these curves connects learning from a finite sample with the network's complexity.

The analysis clarifies their asymptotic properties and their relationship. Asymptotic behavior concerns what happens as the amount of training data becomes large. Examining both curves together gives a way to understand how the network's fit to its training examples relates to its predictive performance as more evidence becomes available.

The resulting theory provides a natural definition of neural-network complexity and a new model-selection criterion. The significance is that complexity is linked to learning behavior, giving the choice of a model a basis in the relationship between fitting and prediction. The contribution is therefore a theoretical connection among sample size, the two kinds of loss, and the selection of a suitable network.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic analysis of training and predictive learning curves yields a definition of network complexity and a model-selection criterion.

title: Learning Curves, Model Selection and Complexity of Neural Networks

paragraphs: When collecting observations is expensive, a learner benefits from choosing its next observation carefully. This paper develops a sequential query-selection method for neural-network models within Bayesian decision theory. Its distinguishing feature is that the value of a candidate observation depends explicitly on how the model's predictions will be used.

This connects data collection to the eventual prediction task. An observation is assessed through a criterion that incorporates the intended use of predictions, giving the selection process a purpose beyond simply accumulating more data. The quantities needed by the criterion are approximated using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, with the approximation carried out to a desired precision.

The framework also changes model complexity as the dataset grows, using Bayesian model selection. Data acquisition and model capacity are therefore both addressed within the learning process. Numerical experiments demonstrate properties of two versions of the query criterion. The contribution is a decision-based method for selecting informative observations while allowing the model's complexity to evolve with the available evidence.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian query strategy chooses new observations according to the intended use of predictions and adapts model complexity as data accumulates.

title: Bayesian Query Construction for Neural Network Models

abstract: One of the current challenges to understanding neural information processing in biological systems is to decipher the "code" carried by large populations of neurons acting in parallel. We present an algorithm for automated discovery of stochastic firing patterns in large ensembles of neurons. The algorithm, from the "Helmholtz Machine" family, attempts to predict the observed spike patterns in the data. The model consists of an observable layer which is directly activated by the input spike patterns, and hidden units that are ac(cid:173) tivated through ascending connections from the input layer. The hidden unit activity can be propagated down to the observable layer to create a prediction of the data pattern that produced it. Hidden units are added incrementally and their weights are adjusted to im(cid:173) prove the fit between the predictions and data, that is, to increase a bound on the probability of the data given the model. This greedy strategy is not globally optimal but is computationally tractable for large populations of neurons. We show benchmark data on artifi(cid:173) cially constructed spike trains and promising early results on neuro(cid:173) physiological data collected from our chronic multi-electrode cortical implant.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for discovering stochastic firing patterns in recordings from many neurons. The objective is to help describe information carried by populations acting in parallel. A model from the Helmholtz-machine family learns to predict observed spike patterns through a layer of hidden units.

Recorded spikes activate the observable layer, and ascending connections produce hidden-unit activity. That activity is then passed downward to predict the input pattern. The algorithm adds hidden units incrementally and adjusts their weights to improve the match between predictions and recordings, specifically by increasing a bound on the data's probability under the model.

This incremental strategy is greedy and does not guarantee a globally optimal solution, but the authors state that it is computationally tractable for large neuronal populations. They report benchmarks on artificial spike trains and promising early results from chronic multi-electrode cortical recordings. The work offers a practical route to learning population-level firing patterns while explicitly accepting a tradeoff in optimization.
summary.tldr: An incrementally trained Helmholtz machine discovers neuronal firing patterns by learning to reconstruct multichannel spike recordings.

title: Using Helmholtz Machines to Analyze Multi-channel Neuronal Recordings

abstract: Principal curves have been defined as "self consistent" smooth curves which pass through the "middle" of a d-dimensional probability distri(cid:173) bution or data cloud. Recently, we [1] have offered a new approach by defining principal curves as continuous curves of a given length which minimize the expected squared distance between the curve and points of the space randomly chosen according to a given distribution. The new definition made it possible to carry out a theoretical analysis of learning principal curves from training data. In this paper we propose a practical construction based on the new definition. Simulation results demonstrate that the new algorithm compares favorably with previous methods both in terms of performance and computational complexity.

paragraphs: A principal curve describes the central shape of a cloud of points using a curve rather than a single straight direction. The paper builds on a definition in which a continuous curve has a specified length and is chosen to minimize the average squared distance from randomly sampled points to the curve. This gives a precise objective for what passing through the data should mean.

The authors had previously used that definition to analyze how principal curves can be learned from training data. Here they turn the definition into a practical construction using a polygonal line. The contribution connects a mathematically specified fitting problem with an algorithm for constructing a curve from observations.

Simulations show favorable comparisons with earlier methods in both performance and computational complexity. These results support the practical usefulness of the construction alongside its theoretical motivation. The evidence is a simulation-based comparison: it indicates that the proposed formulation can lead to an effective algorithm, without establishing that it outperforms every alternative on every distribution.
summary.tldr: A polygonal-line algorithm turns a length-constrained definition of principal curves into a practical method with favorable simulation results.

title: A Polygonal Line Algorithm for Constructing Principal Curves

abstract: In this paper we give necessary and sufficient conditions under which kernels of dot product type k(x, y) = k(x . y) satisfy Mer(cid:173) cer's condition and thus may be used in Support Vector Ma(cid:173) chines (SVM), Regularization Networks (RN) or Gaussian Pro(cid:173) cesses (GP). In particular, we show that if the kernel is analytic (i.e. can be expanded in a Taylor series), all expansion coefficients have to be nonnegative. We give an explicit functional form for the feature map by calculating its eigenfunctions and eigenvalues.

In particular, we show that if the kernel is analytic (i.e. can be expanded in a Taylor series), all expansion coefficients have to be nonnegative. paragraphs: The paper studies kernel functions whose value depends on the dot product of their two inputs. Its central question is when such a function satisfies Mercer's condition, making it suitable for use in support vector machines, regularization networks, or Gaussian processes. The authors provide necessary and sufficient conditions for this class of kernels.

For an analytic kernel, which can be expressed as a Taylor series, the paper identifies nonnegativity of every expansion coefficient as a requirement. This translates the validity question into a condition on the coefficients defining the function. It gives a concrete mathematical restriction on candidate dot-product kernels.

The authors also calculate eigenfunctions and eigenvalues to obtain an explicit form of the feature map. This connects the kernel's numerical similarity calculation with the feature representation it implies. The contribution therefore goes beyond deciding whether a kernel is admissible: it also describes the representation underlying it, linking kernel design, spectral structure, and the learning methods that can use it.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes valid dot-product kernels and derives explicit feature maps from their eigenfunctions and eigenvalues.

title: Regularization with Dot-Product Kernels

abstract: We present a novel, ﬂexible statistical approach for modelling music and text jointly. The approach is based on multi-modal mixture models and maximum a posteriori estimation using EM. The learned models can be used to browse databases with documents containing music and text, to search for music using queries consisting of music and text (lyrics and other contextual information), to annotate text documents with music, and to automatically recommend or identify similar songs.

The approach is based on multi-modal mixture models and maximum a posteriori estimation using EM. The learned models can be used to browse databases with documents containing music and text, to search for music using queries consisting of music and text (lyrics and other contextual information), to annotate text documents with music, and to automatically recommend or identify similar songs.

paragraphs: Music collections can contain both musical content and associated text, such as lyrics or contextual descriptions. This paper proposes a statistical approach that models the two together. The goal is to make their relationship useful for searching and browsing collections, including situations where a query contains both music and words.

The approach uses multimodal mixture models, with parameters learned through maximum a posteriori estimation using EM. Music and text are treated as parts of a shared statistical modeling problem. This gives the learned model a basis for connecting the two forms of content across documents and queries, rather than requiring a search request to use only one form.

The authors describe several uses for the learned models: browsing documents containing music and text, searching with mixed queries, adding music to text documents, and recommending or identifying similar songs. These capabilities give the joint model a broader role than song identification alone. Its contribution is a flexible probabilistic framework connecting musical and textual information across these retrieval and annotation tasks.
summary.tldr: Joint probabilistic models of music and text support mixed queries, browsing, music annotation, and song recommendation.

title: "Name That Song!" A Probabilistic Approach to Querying on Music and Text

paragraphs: The paper addresses novelty detection by seeking a small region of input space containing a specified fraction of the underlying probability mass. Observations outside that region can then be treated as departures from the modeled data. The proposed single-class minimax probability machine frames this region-finding task through worst-case probabilistic reasoning.

Its distribution-free method uses only a distribution's mean and covariance matrix, without assuming a further distributional form. Given that information, it minimizes the worst-case probability that a point lies outside a convex set. This makes the available moment information central to the guarantee, while allowing the rest of the distribution's shape to remain unspecified.

The authors also develop a robust approach for estimating the mean and covariance in the general two-class MPM setting and explain how it specializes to the single-class case. This connects robust parameter estimation to the novelty-detection construction. Empirical comparisons include a single-class SVM and a two-class SVM method. The abstract states that these comparisons are provided, without asserting a particular winning method or performance margin.
summary.tldr: Single-class MPM uses mean and covariance information to find a novelty-detection region through distribution-free worst-case probability reasoning.

title: Robust Novelty Detection with Single-Class MPM

abstract: We present an algorithm that uses multiple cues to recover shading and reﬂectance intrinsic images from a single image. Using both color in- formation and a classiﬁer trained to recognize gray-scale patterns, each image derivative is classiﬁed as being caused by shading or a change in the surface’s reﬂectance. Generalized Belief Propagation is then used to propagate information from areas where the correct classiﬁcation is clear to areas where it is ambiguous. We also show results on real images.

Generalized Belief Propagation is then used to propagate information from areas where the correct classiﬁcation is clear to areas where it is ambiguous. We also show results on real images.

The algorithm approaches this separation by deciding which of these two causes accounts for local changes in the observed image.

It combines color information with a classifier trained to recognize grayscale patterns. These cues are used to classify each image derivative as arising from shading or a reflectance change. Working with derivatives focuses the decision on changes across the image, providing local evidence for how the two underlying components should be separated.

Some locations offer clearer evidence than others. Generalized belief propagation carries information from confident areas into ambiguous ones, allowing the decomposition to use relationships beyond each isolated local decision. The authors show results on real images. The contribution is a combination of complementary visual cues and information propagation for recovering intrinsic images from one observation, with the reported demonstrations establishing application to real imagery.
summary.tldr: The algorithm combines color, learned grayscale cues, and generalized belief propagation to separate shading from reflectance in a single image.

title: Recovering Intrinsic Images from a Single Image

abstract: Go is an ancient oriental game whose complexity has defeated attempts to automate it. We suggest using probability in a Bayesian sense to model the uncertainty arising from the vast complexity of the game tree. We present a simple conditional Markov random field model for predicting the pointwise territory outcome of a game. The topology of the model reflects the spatial structure of the Go board. We describe a version of the Swendsen-Wang process for sampling from the model during learning and apply loopy belief propagation for rapid inference and prediction. The model is trained on several hundred records of professional games. Our experimental results indicate that the model successfully learns to predict territory despite its simplicity.

paragraphs: The paper treats the complexity of Go's game tree as a source of uncertainty that can be represented probabilistically. Its prediction target is the eventual territory outcome at individual board locations. This focuses the modeling task on a spatial description of how a game will end, using Bayesian probability to express uncertainty about that outcome.

The authors construct a simple conditional Markov random field whose connections reflect the board's spatial organization. This allows territory predictions to be modeled through relationships across board locations. They describe a version of the Swendsen-Wang sampling process for learning and use loopy belief propagation to obtain rapid inference and predictions.

The contribution is therefore a probabilistic approach to one important Go prediction task, showing that a spatially organized model can extract useful territory information from recorded play without representing the entire game tree explicitly.
summary.tldr: A spatial probabilistic model trained on professional Go records learns to predict territory outcomes while representing uncertainty.

title: Modelling Uncertainty in the Game of Go

abstract: Spiking activity from neurophysiological experiments often exhibits dy- namics beyond that driven by external stimulation, presumably reﬂect- ing the extensive recurrence of neural circuitry. Characterizing these dynamics may reveal important features of neural computation, par- ticularly during internally-driven cognitive operations. For example, the activity of premotor cortex (PMd) neurons during an instructed de- lay period separating movement-target speciﬁcation and a movement- initiation cue is believed to be involved in motor planning. We show that the dynamics underlying this activity can be captured by a low- dimensional non-linear dynamical systems model, with underlying re- current structure and stochastic point-process output. We present and validate latent variable methods that simultaneously estimate the system parameters and the trial-by-trial dynamical trajectories. These meth- ods are applied to characterize the dynamics in PMd data recorded from a chronically-implanted 96-electrode array while monkeys perform delayed-reach tasks.

Such dynamics may reflect recurrent circuitry and could reveal how the brain carries out internally driven operations. This paper examines premotor cortex activity during the delay between learning a movement target and receiving the cue to begin moving, a period believed to involve motor planning.

The authors represent the underlying activity with a low-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system. Its recurrent structure describes how an internal state evolves, while a stochastic point-process output connects that state to observed spikes. This separates the proposed underlying dynamics from the individual firing events used to infer them.

The methods are applied to recordings from a chronically implanted 96-electrode array in monkeys performing delayed reaches. The reported ability to capture these dynamics supports studying coordinated neural activity through a compact evolving state, while preserving differences between trials.
summary.tldr: A latent dynamical model captures trial-specific structure in premotor neural activity during delayed reaching.

title: Extracting Dynamical Structure Embedded in Neural Activity

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel exemplar-based approach to extract dynamic foreground regions from a changing background within a collection of images or a video sequence. By using image segmentation as a pre-processing step, we convert this traditional pixel-wise labeling problem into a lower-dimensional supervised, binary labeling procedure on image segments. Our approach consists of three steps. First, a set of random image patches are spatially and adaptively sampled within each segment. Second, these sets of extracted samples are formed into two "bags of patches" to model the foreground/background appearance, respectively. We perform a novel bidirectional consistency check between new patches from incoming frames and current "bags of patches" to reject outliers, control model rigidity and make the model adaptive to new observations. Within each bag, image patches are further partitioned and resampled to create an evolving appearance model. Finally, the foreground/background decision over segments in an image is formulated using an aggregation function defined on the similarity measurements of sampled patches relative to the foreground and background models. The essence of the algorithm is conceptually simple and can be easily implemented within a few hundred lines of Matlab code. We evaluate and validate the proposed approach by extensive real examples of the object-level image mapping and tracking within a variety of challenging environments. We also show that it is straightforward to apply our problem formulation on non-rigid object tracking with difficult surveillance videos.

It first divides images into segments, turning a decision for every pixel into a supervised foreground-or-background decision for each segment. The method samples random patches adaptively inside each segment and maintains two collections of examples, one for foreground and one for background. New patches undergo a bidirectional consistency check against these collections. This check rejects outliers and controls how readily the appearance models adapt. Partitioning and resampling patches further updates the models as new observations arrive.

To label a segment, the system combines patch similarities to the two appearance models into a final decision. The authors validate the approach through real examples of object-level image mapping and tracking in challenging environments, including non-rigid objects in surveillance videos. The approach's value lies in pairing a simple segment-level decision with appearance models that evolve as the scene changes.
summary.tldr: Adaptive collections of random image patches support segment-level foreground extraction and tracking as object and background appearances change.

title: Dynamic Foreground/Background Extraction from Images and Videos using Random Patches

abstract: We address the problem of adaptive sensor control in dynamic resource-constrained sensor networks. We focus on a meteorological sensing network comprising radars that can perform sector scanning rather than always scanning 360 degrees. We compare three sector scanning strategies. The sit-and-spin strategy always scans 360 degrees. The limited lookahead strategy additionally uses the expected environmental state K decision epochs in the future, as predicted from Kalman filters, in its decision-making. The full lookahead strategy uses all expected future states by casting the problem as a Markov decision process and using reinforcement learning to estimate the optimal scan strategy. We show that the main benefits of using a lookahead strategy are when there are multiple meteorological phenomena in the environment, and when the maximum radius of any phenomenon is sufficiently smaller than the radius of the radars. We also show that there is a trade-off between the average quality with which a phenomenon is scanned and the number of decision epochs before which a phenomenon is rescanned.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a resource-constrained radar network should adapt its scanning as weather phenomena evolve. The radars can scan selected sectors, creating a decision about where to direct sensing effort. The authors compare three strategies that differ in how much predicted future information they use.

The sit-and-spin strategy repeatedly scans the full circle. Limited lookahead also considers the environmental state predicted a specified number of decision steps ahead using Kalman filters. Full lookahead represents the problem as a Markov decision process and uses reinforcement learning to estimate an optimal scanning strategy based on expected future states.

The results identify circumstances in which lookahead is most beneficial: multiple weather phenomena are present, and their maximum radius is sufficiently smaller than the radars’ radius. The authors also find a tradeoff between average scanning quality and the delay before a phenomenon is scanned again. This means scan planning must balance the quality of observations against revisit frequency; the reported benefits of prediction depend on the environment’s structure.
summary.tldr: Predictive radar scanning is most beneficial for multiple sufficiently small weather phenomena, with a tradeoff between observation quality and revisit delay.

title: Scan Strategies for Meteorological Radars

abstract: Electrical power management in large-scale IT systems such as commercial data- centers is an application area of rapidly growing interest from both an economic and ecological perspective, with billions of dollars and millions of metric tons of CO2 emissions at stake annually. Businesses want to save power without sac- riﬁcing performance. This paper presents a reinforcement learning approach to simultaneous online management of both performance and power consumption. We apply RL in a realistic laboratory testbed using a Blade cluster and dynam- ically varying HTTP workload running on a commercial web applications mid- dleware platform. We embed a CPU frequency controller in the Blade servers’ ﬁrmware, and we train policies for this controller using a multi-criteria reward signal depending on both application performance and CPU power consumption. Our testbed scenario posed a number of challenges to successful use of RL, in- cluding multiple disparate reward functions, limited decision sampling rates, and pathologies arising when using multiple sensor readings as state variables. We describe innovative practical solutions to these challenges, and demonstrate clear performance improvements over both hand-designed policies as well as obvious “cookbook” RL implementations.

paragraphs: Managing server power is useful only when application performance is also considered. This paper applies reinforcement learning to manage both objectives online. The authors test the approach on a laboratory Blade cluster running commercial web application middleware under a changing HTTP workload, giving the controller a realistic setting with varying demand.

A CPU frequency controller is embedded in the servers’ firmware. Its policies are trained using a reward signal that depends on both application performance and CPU power consumption. This makes the learning objective explicitly responsive to the tradeoff the system is meant to manage, rather than judging the controller on power use alone.

The authors describe solutions and demonstrate clear improvements over hand-designed policies and straightforward reinforcement learning implementations. The findings show the importance of adapting the learning setup to operational constraints when applying reinforcement learning to joint performance and power management.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning CPU controller jointly manages power and application performance, outperforming hand-designed and straightforward RL policies in a laboratory server cluster.

title: Managing Power Consumption and Performance of Computing Systems Using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The principles by which spiking neurons contribute to the astounding computational power of generic cortical microcircuits, and how spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) of synaptic weights could generate and maintain this computational function, are unknown. We show here that STDP, in conjunction with a stochastic soft winner-take-all (WTA) circuit, induces spiking neurons to generate through their synaptic weights implicit internal models for subclasses (or causes") of the high-dimensional spike patterns of hundreds of pre-synaptic neurons. Hence these neurons will fire after learning whenever the current input best matches their internal model. The resulting computational function of soft WTA circuits, a common network motif of cortical microcircuits, could therefore be a drastic dimensionality reduction of information streams, together with the autonomous creation of internal models for the probability distributions of their input patterns. We show that the autonomous generation and maintenance of this computational function can be explained on the basis of rigorous mathematical principles. In particular, we show that STDP is able to approximate a stochastic online Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for modeling the input data. A corresponding result is shown for Hebbian learning in artificial neural networks."

paragraphs: The paper investigates how spike-timing-dependent plasticity, or STDP, could give spiking neural circuits a useful computational function. The proposed setting combines STDP with a stochastic soft winner-take-all circuit. Within that combination, neurons develop synaptic weights that implicitly model subclasses, described as hidden causes, of high-dimensional input spike patterns.

After learning, a neuron fires when the current input best matches its internal model. The authors suggest that such circuits could reduce the dimensionality of incoming information while autonomously constructing models of the probability distributions behind their inputs. This interpretation links the behavior of individual neurons to a statistical description of patterns across hundreds of presynaptic neurons.

The authors provide a mathematical account of how this function can arise and be maintained. In particular, they show that STDP can approximate a stochastic online expectation-maximization algorithm for modeling the input data. They also establish a corresponding result for Hebbian learning in artificial neural networks. The work offers a principled computational interpretation of the specified learning-and-circuit combination.
summary.tldr: STDP in stochastic soft winner-take-all circuits approximates online expectation-maximization, enabling neurons to learn implicit models of input-pattern subclasses.

title: STDP enables spiking neurons to detect hidden causes of their inputs

abstract: Most current image categorization methods require large collections of manually annotated training examples to learn accurate visual recognition models. The time-consuming human labeling effort effectively limits these approaches to recognition problems involving a small number of different object classes. In order to address this shortcoming, in recent years several authors have proposed to learn object classifiers from weakly-labeled Internet images, such as photos retrieved by keyword-based image search engines. While this strategy eliminates the need for human supervision, the recognition accuracies of these methods are considerably lower than those obtained with fully-supervised approaches, because of the noisy nature of the labels associated to Web data. In this paper we investigate and compare methods that learn image classifiers by combining very few manually annotated examples (e.g., 1-10 images per class) and a large number of weakly-labeled Web photos retrieved using keyword-based image search. We cast this as a domain adaptation problem: given a few strongly-labeled examples in a target domain (the manually annotated examples) and many source domain examples (the weakly-labeled Web photos), learn classifiers yielding small generalization error on the target domain. Our experiments demonstrate that, for the same number of strongly-labeled examples, our domain adaptation approach produces significant recognition rate improvements over the best published results (e.g., 65% better when using 5 labeled training examples per class) and that our classifiers are one order of magnitude faster to learn and to evaluate than the best competing method, despite our use of large weakly-labeled data sets.

These findings show that abundant weak supervision can be useful when incorporated through an appropriate adaptation approach.
summary.tldr: Domain adaptation combines a few carefully labeled images with many noisy web images to improve recognition and computational efficiency.

title: Exploiting weakly-labeled Web images to improve object classification: a domain adaptation approach

abstract: We propose a discriminative latent model for annotating images with unaligned object-level textual annotations. Instead of using the bag-of-words image representation currently popular in the computer vision community, our model explicitly captures more intricate relationships underlying visual and textual information. In particular, we model the mapping that translates image regions to annotations. This mapping allows us to relate image regions to their corresponding annotation terms. We also model the overall scene label as latent information. This allows us to cluster test images. Our training data consist of images and their associated annotations. But we do not have access to the ground-truth region-to-annotation mapping or the overall scene label. We develop a novel variant of the latent SVM framework to model them as latent variables. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model compared with other baseline methods.

paragraphs: An image may come with object names without indicating which region each name describes. This paper learns from that incomplete supervision: training examples provide images and associated annotations, but neither region-to-word correspondences nor overall scene labels. The task is to recover useful relationships between visual content and language while learning to annotate images.

The proposed discriminative model explicitly represents a mapping between image regions and annotation terms. It also treats the overall scene category as hidden information. A new variant of the latent support vector machine framework learns with both kinds of unknown variables, allowing local object correspondences and broader scene information to participate in the model.

Experiments show that the model is effective compared with the tested baseline methods. The hidden scene representation also allows test images to be clustered. The contribution is a way to learn richer visual-textual relationships from image-level annotations, without requiring the training data to identify every object's location or supply scene categories.
summary.tldr: A latent discriminative model learns image-region-to-word correspondences and hidden scene categories from images with unaligned object annotations.

title: A Discriminative Latent Model of Image Region and Object Tag Correspondence

abstract: Extensive evidence suggests that items are not encoded independently in visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, previous research has not quantitatively considered how the encoding of an item influences the encoding of other items. Here, we model the dependencies among VSTM representations using a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a stimulus-dependent mean and covariance matrix. We report the results of an experiment designed to determine the specific form of the stimulus-dependence of the mean and the covariance matrix. We find that the magnitude of the covariance between the representations of two items is a monotonically decreasing function of the difference between the items' feature values, similar to a Gaussian process with a distance-dependent, stationary kernel function. We further show that this type of covariance function can be explained as a natural consequence of encoding multiple stimuli in a population of neurons with correlated responses.

paragraphs: Items held in visual short-term memory need not be encoded independently. This paper asks how to describe the dependence between their representations quantitatively. It models the collection of remembered items with a multivariate Gaussian distribution whose mean and covariance depend on the stimuli being presented.

The authors report an experiment designed to determine how those distribution parameters vary with stimulus properties. They find that the magnitude of covariance between two item representations decreases monotonically as the difference between their feature values increases. In this account, items closer in feature value have more strongly coupled representations.

That pattern resembles a Gaussian process with a stationary kernel based on distance. The authors further show how such covariance can arise when several stimuli are encoded by a population of neurons with correlated responses. This links a statistical description of memory dependencies to a possible neural explanation, without requiring the interpretation that this is the only mechanism capable of producing the pattern.
summary.tldr: Visual memory representations show stronger covariance for similar items, a pattern that can arise from correlated neural population responses.

title: Probabilistic Modeling of Dependencies Among Visual Short-Term Memory Representations

abstract: In this paper, we consider the 'Precis' problem of sampling K representative yet diverse data points from a large dataset. This problem arises frequently in applications such as video and document summarization, exploratory data analysis, and pre-filtering. We formulate a general theory which encompasses not just traditional techniques devised for vector spaces, but also non-Euclidean manifolds, thereby enabling these techniques to shapes, human activities, textures and many other image and video based datasets. We propose intrinsic manifold measures for measuring the quality of a selection of points with respect to their representative power, and their diversity. We then propose efficient algorithms to optimize the cost function using a novel annealing-based iterative alternation algorithm. The proposed formulation is applicable to manifolds of known geometry as well as to manifolds whose geometry needs to be estimated from samples. Experimental results show the strength and generality of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: The Precis problem asks for a fixed number of data points that summarize a large dataset while remaining diverse. Representativeness and diversity serve different purposes: the selection should reflect the dataset without spending its limited size on redundant examples. The paper considers this problem for applications including video and document summarization, exploration, and pre-filtering.

The authors develop a formulation covering both ordinary vector spaces and non-Euclidean manifolds. They introduce measures of selection quality that use the manifold's own geometry to assess representativeness and diversity. This extends the selection problem to data such as shapes, human activities, and textures, where the relevant geometry may differ from ordinary vector-space distance.

An annealing-based iterative alternation algorithm optimizes the resulting cost function. The formulation can use known manifold geometry or geometry estimated from samples, making it applicable under both circumstances. Experimental results support its strength and generality. The central contribution is a common framework for selecting compact, varied summaries while taking the geometry of the data into account.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware selection framework uses annealing to choose representative, diverse subsets from vector spaces and non-Euclidean manifolds.

title: Manifold Precis: An Annealing Technique for Diverse Sampling of Manifolds

abstract: In many applications, one has information, e.g., labels that are provided in a semi-supervised manner, about a specific target region of a large data set, and one wants to perform machine learning and data analysis tasks nearby that pre-specified target region. Locally-biased problems of this sort are particularly challenging for popular eigenvector-based machine learning and data analysis tools. At root, the reason is that eigenvectors are inherently global quantities. In this paper, we address this issue by providing a methodology to construct semi-supervised eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian, and we illustrate how these locally-biased eigenvectors can be used to perform locally-biased machine learning. These semi-supervised eigenvectors capture successively-orthogonalized directions of maximum variance, conditioned on being well-correlated with an input seed set of nodes that is assumed to be provided in a semi-supervised manner. We also provide several empirical examples demonstrating how these semi-supervised eigenvectors can be used to perform locally-biased learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses data analysis focused on a particular region of a large dataset. A user may have labels or other information identifying that region and want learning to concentrate nearby. Standard eigenvector-based methods are challenging to use for this purpose because eigenvectors describe global structure.

The authors construct semi-supervised eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian using a supplied seed set of nodes. These vectors capture directions of maximum variance while being constrained to correlate well with the seeds. Successive directions are orthogonalized, providing distinct directions that retain the intended local emphasis. The seed set is therefore an essential input linking the mathematical representation to the region of interest.

Several empirical examples demonstrate how the resulting vectors support locally biased learning. The contribution is a way to incorporate partial supervision into eigenvector construction itself, so that the representation reflects the target region. This connects a global analysis tool to tasks in which the relevant structure is defined partly by what the user already knows.
summary.tldr: Semi-supervised graph eigenvectors use seed nodes to focus variance-based representations on a chosen region of a dataset.

title: Semi-supervised Eigenvectors for Locally-biased Learning

abstract: By making personalized suggestions, a recommender system is playing a crucial role in improving the engagement of users in modern web-services. However, most recommendation algorithms do not explicitly take into account the temporal behavior and the recurrent activities of users. Two central but less explored questions are how to recommend the most desirable item \emph{at the right moment}, and how to predict \emph{the next returning time} of a user to a service. To address these questions, we propose a novel framework which connects self-exciting point processes and low-rank models to capture the recurrent temporal patterns in a large collection of user-item consumption pairs. We show that the parameters of the model can be estimated via a convex optimization, and furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm that maintains $O(1 / \epsilon)$ convergence rate, scales up to problems with millions of user-item pairs and thousands of millions of temporal events. Compared to other state-of-the-arts in both synthetic and real datasets, our model achieves superb predictive performance in the two time-sensitive recommendation questions. Finally, we point out that our formulation can incorporate other extra context information of users, such as profile, textual and spatial features.

title: Time-Sensitive Recommendation From Recurrent User Activities

abstract: We consider a sequential learning problem with Gaussian payoffs and side information: after selecting an action $i$, the learner receives information about the payoff of every action $j$ in the form of Gaussian observations whose mean is the same as the mean payoff, but the variance depends on the pair $(i,j)$ (and may be infinite). The setup allows a more refined information transfer from one action to another than previous partial monitoring setups, including the recently introduced graph-structured feedback case. For the first time in the literature, we provide non-asymptotic problem-dependent lower bounds on the regret of any algorithm, which recover existing asymptotic problem-dependent lower bounds and finite-time minimax lower bounds available in the literature. We also provide algorithms that achieve the problem-dependent lower bound (up to some universal constant factor) or the minimax lower bounds (up to logarithmic factors).

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions where choosing an action also supplies information about other actions' payoffs. Every observation is Gaussian with the corresponding action's mean payoff, but its variance depends on both the chosen action and the action being observed. Variance may be infinite, allowing the model to represent missing useful information.

This setup describes information transfer more finely than feedback models that only specify which actions reveal which others. Two observations about the same action can have different usefulness because they have different variances. The authors derive problem-dependent lower bounds on regret that apply at finite time to every algorithm, while recovering known asymptotic and finite-time minimax bounds.

They also provide algorithms approaching these limits: one achieves the problem-dependent lower bound within a universal constant factor, while another reaches minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. The contribution pairs a richer model of side observations with guarantees about both unavoidable learning cost and achievable performance, making observation quality part of the theoretical account.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian side-observation model captures varying information quality and admits finite-time regret lower bounds with algorithms that nearly match them.

title: Online Learning with Gaussian Payoffs and Side Observations

abstract: We consider the following detection problem: given a realization of asymmetric matrix $X$ of dimension $n$, distinguish between the hypothesisthat all upper triangular variables are i.i.d. Gaussians variableswith mean 0 and variance $1$ and the hypothesis that there is aplanted principal submatrix $B$ of dimension $L$ for which all upper triangularvariables are i.i.d. Gaussians with mean $1$ and variance $1$, whereasall other upper triangular elements of $X$ not in $B$ are i.i.d.Gaussians variables with mean 0 and variance $1$. We refer to this asthe `Gaussian hidden clique problem'. When $L=( 1 + \epsilon) \sqrt{n}$ ($\epsilon > 0$), it is possible to solve thisdetection problem with probability $1 - o_n(1)$ by computing thespectrum of $X$ and considering the largest eigenvalue of $X$.We prove that when$L < (1-\epsilon)\sqrt{n}$ no algorithm that examines only theeigenvalues of $X$can detect the existence of a hiddenGaussian clique, with error probability vanishing as $n \to \infty$.The result above is an immediate consequence of a more general result on rank-oneperturbations of $k$-dimensional Gaussian tensors.In this context we establish a lower bound on the criticalsignal-to-noise ratio below which a rank-one signal cannot be detected.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a hidden signal can be detected in a matrix of Gaussian noise. Under the signal hypothesis, a principal submatrix of size L has entries whose mean is shifted from zero to one, while their variance remains one. The task is to distinguish this case from pure noise.

For fixed positive ε, a hidden block of size (1 + ε)√n can be detected with probability approaching one by examining the largest eigenvalue. The authors prove that below (1 − ε)√n, no algorithm using only the matrix's eigenvalues can achieve error probability tending to zero. The restriction to eigenvalue information is essential to the scope of this impossibility result.

This boundary follows from a broader result about rank-one signals added to Gaussian tensors. There, the authors establish a lower bound on the critical signal-to-noise ratio needed for detection. The work therefore identifies a precise information bottleneck for spectral detection and connects it to a more general family of noisy signal problems.
summary.tldr: Below a hidden-block size of roughly √n, eigenvalue-only methods cannot detect a Gaussian hidden clique with vanishing error.

title: On the Limitation of Spectral Methods: From the Gaussian Hidden Clique Problem to Rank-One Perturbations of Gaussian Tensors

abstract: Many information systems use tags and keywords to describe and annotate content. These allow for efficient organization and categorization of items, as well as facilitate relevant search queries. As such, the selected set of tags for an item can have a considerable effect on the volume of traffic that eventually reaches an item. In tagging systems where tags are exclusively chosen by an item's owner, who in turn is interested in maximizing traffic, a principled approach for assigning tags can prove valuable. In this paper we introduce the problem of optimal tagging, where the task is to choose a subset of tags for a new item such that the probability of browsing users reaching that item is maximized. We formulate the problem by modeling traffic using a Markov chain, and asking how transitions in this chain should be modified to maximize traffic into a certain state of interest. The resulting optimization problem involves maximizing a certain function over subsets, under a cardinality constraint. We show that the optimization problem is NP-hard, but has a (1-1/e)-approximation via a simple greedy algorithm due to monotonicity and submodularity. Furthermore, the structure of the problem allows for an efficient computation of the greedy step. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we perform experiments on three tagging datasets, and show that the greedy algorithm outperforms other baselines.

The theoretical guarantee applies to the modeled traffic objective, while the experiments provide evidence for the practical effectiveness of that approach.
summary.tldr: A Markov-chain model turns traffic-maximizing tag selection into a problem with an efficient greedy algorithm and a 1−1/e approximation guarantee.

title: Optimal Tagging with Markov Chain Optimization

abstract: We present a novel technique for learning the mass matrices in samplers obtained from discretized dynamics that preserve some energy function. Existing adaptive samplers use Riemannian preconditioning techniques, where the mass matrices are functions of the parameters being sampled. This leads to significant complexities in the energy reformulations and resultant dynamics, often leading to implicit systems of equations and requiring inversion of high-dimensional matrices in the leapfrog steps. Our approach provides a simpler alternative, by using existing dynamics in the sampling step of a Monte Carlo EM framework, and learning the mass matrices in the M step with a novel online technique. We also propose a way to adaptively set the number of samples gathered in the E step, using sampling error estimates from the leapfrog dynamics. Along with a novel stochastic sampler based on Nos\'{e}-Poincar\'{e} dynamics, we use this framework with standard Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) as well as newer stochastic algorithms such as SGHMC and SGNHT, and show strong performance on synthetic and real high-dimensional sampling scenarios; we achieve sampling accuracies comparable to Riemannian samplers while being significantly faster.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to learn mass matrices for Bayesian samplers based on discretized, energy-preserving dynamics. Existing adaptive approaches can make those matrices depend on the sampled parameters, introducing complicated dynamics, implicit equations, and costly matrix inversions. The authors seek a simpler way to adapt the matrices while retaining existing sampling dynamics.

Their solution uses a Monte Carlo expectation-maximization framework. The sampling step runs the existing dynamics, and the maximization step learns mass matrices through a new online procedure. They also adapt how many samples the expectation step collects, using estimates of sampling error from the leapfrog dynamics. This addresses both the sampler’s matrix settings and the amount of sampling used during adaptation.

The framework is applied to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, SGHMC, SGNHT, and a new stochastic sampler based on Nosé-Poincaré dynamics. Experiments cover synthetic and real high-dimensional sampling problems. The authors report accuracy comparable to Riemannian samplers with substantially greater speed, supporting the practical value of separating matrix learning from more complicated parameter-dependent dynamics.
summary.tldr: A Monte Carlo EM framework learns sampler mass matrices and adapts sample counts, achieving accuracy comparable to Riemannian samplers substantially faster in experiments.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Sampling with Monte Carlo EM

abstract: Calcium imaging permits optical measurement of neural activity. Since intracellular calcium concentration is an indirect measurement of neural activity, computational tools are necessary to infer the true underlying spiking activity from fluorescence measurements. Bayesian model inversion can be used to solve this problem, but typically requires either computationally expensive MCMC sampling, or faster but approximate maximum-a-posteriori optimization. Here, we introduce a flexible algorithmic framework for fast, efficient and accurate extraction of neural spikes from imaging data. Using the framework of variational autoencoders, we propose to amortize inference by training a deep neural network to perform model inversion efficiently. The recognition network is trained to produce samples from the posterior distribution over spike trains. Once trained, performing inference amounts to a fast single forward pass through the network, without the need for iterative optimization or sampling. We show that amortization can be applied flexibly to a wide range of nonlinear generative models and significantly improves upon the state of the art in computation time, while achieving competitive accuracy. Our framework is also able to represent posterior distributions over spike-trains. We demonstrate the generality of our method by proposing the first probabilistic approach for separating backpropagating action potentials from putative synaptic inputs in calcium imaging of dendritic spines.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging measures fluorescence that indirectly reflects neural activity, so recovering spike trains requires computational inference. Bayesian model inversion can address this problem, but repeated sampling is expensive, while maximum-a-posteriori optimization supplies a faster approximation. This paper trains a neural network to perform the inversion efficiently using a variational-autoencoder framework.

The approach amortizes inference by learning the computational work in advance. Its recognition network is trained to generate samples from the posterior over spike trains. After training, inference requires a single forward pass, avoiding a new iterative optimization or sampling procedure for each input. The framework can therefore represent uncertainty over possible spike trains while providing fast inference.

The authors show that the approach works with a range of nonlinear generative models and substantially improves computation time while maintaining competitive accuracy. They also demonstrate its flexibility with a probabilistic method for separating backpropagating action potentials from putative synaptic inputs in dendritic-spine imaging. This application extends the framework beyond extracting a single undifferentiated activity signal.
summary.tldr: A variational-autoencoder framework learns fast posterior inference for neural spike trains from calcium imaging, achieving competitive accuracy.

title: Fast amortized inference of neural activity from calcium imaging data with variational autoencoders

abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) is ubiquitous in machine learning and underlies most supervised learning methods. While there is a large body of work on algorithms for various ERM problems, the exact computational complexity of ERM is still not understood. We address this issue for multiple popular ERM problems including kernel SVMs, kernel ridge regression, and training the final layer of a neural network. In particular, we give conditional hardness results for these problems based on complexity-theoretic assumptions such as the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. Under these assumptions, we show that there are no algorithms that solve the aforementioned ERM problems to high accuracy in sub-quadratic time. We also give similar hardness results for computing the gradient of the empirical loss, which is the main computational burden in many non-convex learning tasks.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization fits a model by reducing its loss on observed data. Although many algorithms implement this principle, the computational effort fundamentally required is less well understood. This paper studies that question for kernel support-vector machines, kernel ridge regression, and training the final layer of a neural network.

The authors establish conditional hardness results based on complexity-theoretic assumptions, including the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. Under those assumptions, the studied problems cannot be solved to high accuracy in subquadratic time. The accuracy requirement and the underlying complexity assumptions are both essential parts of the stated result.

The paper also derives related hardness results for computing empirical-loss gradients, an operation that accounts for much of the work in many nonconvex learning tasks. This extends the analysis from completing optimization to performing a central computational step within it. The contribution provides conditional boundaries on possible algorithmic speedups, helping distinguish improvements in implementation from improvements that would conflict with the assumed complexity foundations.
summary.tldr: Under stated complexity assumptions, several learning problems and gradient computations cannot achieve high accuracy in subquadratic time.

title: On the Fine-Grained Complexity of Empirical Risk Minimization: Kernel Methods and Neural Networks

abstract: Neural networks have a smooth initial inductive bias, such that small changes in input do not lead to large changes in output. However, in reinforcement learning domains with sparse rewards, value functions have non-smooth structure with a characteristic asymmetric discontinuity whenever rewards arrive. We propose a mechanism that learns an interpolation between a direct value estimate and a projected value estimate computed from the encountered reward and the previous estimate. This reduces the need to learn about discontinuities, and thus improves the value function approximation. Furthermore, as the interpolation is learned and state-dependent, our method can deal with heterogeneous observability. We demonstrate that this one change leads to significant improvements on multiple Atari games, when applied to the state-of-the-art A3C algorithm.

paragraphs: Neural networks initially tend to produce similar outputs for nearby inputs. The paper identifies a mismatch between this smooth bias and value functions in reinforcement learning with sparse rewards. When rewards arrive, the relevant value structure can have an asymmetric discontinuity, making a purely smooth approximation harder to learn.

The proposed mechanism learns how to interpolate between two estimates. One is a direct estimate of value. The other projects value using the encountered reward and the previous estimate. Combining them reduces how much discontinuous structure the model must learn directly, using information already available from the transition in experience.

The interpolation depends on the state and is itself learned, allowing the method to adjust how much it trusts the projected estimate. The authors state that this also accommodates heterogeneous observability, where the available information varies across situations. Adding this mechanism to A3C produces significant improvements on multiple Atari games. The results support adapting value estimation to reward-driven discontinuities through a learned use of past estimates.
summary.tldr: Learning when to combine direct values with reward-adjusted past estimates improves value approximation and reported A3C performance on multiple Atari games.

title: Natural Value Approximators: Learning when to Trust Past Estimates

abstract: We propose a Bayesian decision making framework for control of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with unknown dynamics and large, possibly continuous, state, action, and parameter spaces in data-poor environments. Most of the existing adaptive controllers for MDPs with unknown dynamics are based on the reinforcement learning framework and rely on large data sets acquired by sustained direct interaction with the system or via a simulator. This is not feasible in many applications, due to ethical, economic, and physical constraints. The proposed framework addresses the data poverty issue by decomposing the problem into an offline planning stage that does not rely on sustained direct interaction with the system or simulator and an online execution stage. In the offline process, parallel Gaussian process temporal difference (GPTD) learning techniques are employed for near-optimal Bayesian approximation of the expected discounted reward over a sample drawn from the prior distribution of unknown parameters. In the online stage, the action with the maximum expected return with respect to the posterior distribution of the parameters is selected. This is achieved by an approximation of the posterior distribution using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, followed by constructing multiple Gaussian processes over the parameter space for efficient prediction of the means of the expected return at the MCMC sample. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated using a simple dynamical system model with continuous state and action spaces, as well as a more complex model for a metastatic melanoma gene regulatory network observed through noisy synthetic gene expression data.

paragraphs: Controlling a system with unknown dynamics is difficult when collecting experience is expensive, physically constrained, or ethically problematic. This paper addresses Markov decision processes with large, potentially continuous state, action, and parameter spaces. Its Bayesian framework separates preparation from execution so that planning does not require sustained interaction with either the system or a simulator.

During offline planning, the method samples unknown parameters from a prior distribution. Parallel Gaussian process temporal difference learning then provides near-optimal Bayesian approximations of expected discounted rewards for those samples. The online calculation uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to approximate the posterior distribution and multiple Gaussian processes to predict expected returns efficiently at the sampled parameters. Demonstrations include a continuous dynamical system and a metastatic melanoma gene regulatory network model observed through noisy synthetic expression data. These examples support the framework's effectiveness in the studied settings, including control under substantial uncertainty with limited data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian controller combines offline reward approximation with online posterior-based action selection to handle large systems with limited interaction data.

title: Bayesian Control of Large MDPs with Unknown Dynamics in Data-Poor Environments

abstract: We consider the problem of generating automatic code given sample input-output pairs. We train a neural network to map from the current state and the outputs to the program's next statement. The neural network optimizes multiple tasks concurrently: the next operation out of a set of high level commands, the operands of the next statement, and which variables can be dropped from memory. Using our method we are able to create programs that are more than twice as long as existing state-of-the-art solutions, while improving the success rate for comparable lengths, and cutting the run-time by two orders of magnitude. Our code, including an implementation of various literature baselines, is publicly available at https://github.com/amitz25/PCCoder

paragraphs: The paper studies how to generate a program from examples of its inputs and desired outputs. Its neural network predicts the next statement from the current program state and the target outputs. This makes synthesis a sequence of decisions about how to extend a partially constructed program toward the demonstrated behavior.

The network learns several related tasks together. It chooses the next high-level operation, identifies the operands that operation should use, and decides which variables can be removed from memory. That last decision supplies the learned garbage collector in the title. Managing intermediate variables becomes part of the synthesis process itself, alongside deciding what computation to perform next.

The authors report generating programs more than twice as long as those produced by existing leading approaches. They also report better success rates at comparable program lengths and a runtime reduction of two orders of magnitude. These findings connect the combined prediction and memory-management approach to improvements in program length, synthesis reliability, and speed within the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: A neural program synthesizer jointly predicts statements and disposable variables, enabling longer programs with higher success rates and much shorter runtimes.

title: Automatic Program Synthesis of Long Programs with a Learned Garbage Collector

abstract: It is well known that the problems of stochastic planning and probabilistic inference are closely related. This paper makes two contributions in this context. The first is to provide an analysis of the recently developed SOGBOFA heuristic planning algorithm that was shown to be effective for problems with large factored state and action spaces. It is shown that SOGBOFA can be seen as a specialized inference algorithm that computes its solutions through a combination of a symbolic variant of belief propagation and gradient ascent. The second contribution is a new solver for Marginal MAP (MMAP) inference. We introduce a new reduction from MMAP to maximum expected utility problems which are suitable for the symbolic computation in SOGBOFA. This yields a novel algebraic gradient-based solver (AGS) for MMAP. An experimental evaluation illustrates the potential of AGS in solving difficult MMAP problems.
