paragraphs: This paper develops the connection between planning under uncertainty and inference in probabilistic models. Its starting point is SOGBOFA, a heuristic planning algorithm previously shown to work well with large, factored state and action spaces. The authors analyze its computation to explain how a successful planning procedure can also be understood through an inference framework.

They show that SOGBOFA acts as a specialized inference algorithm combining a symbolic form of belief propagation with gradient ascent. This interpretation identifies the computational ingredients behind its solutions. It also provides a route for using the same style of symbolic computation in a different problem: Marginal MAP inference.

The second contribution is a reduction from Marginal MAP to maximum expected utility problems suited to SOGBOFA's symbolic machinery. This leads to AGS, an algebraic solver that uses gradients. Experiments illustrate its potential on difficult Marginal MAP problems. The paper thus contributes both an explanation of an existing planner and a new inference solver derived from that connection.
summary.tldr: An inference interpretation of SOGBOFA leads to a new algebraic gradient-based solver for Marginal MAP problems.

title: From Stochastic Planning to Marginal MAP

abstract: Accurately answering a question about a given image requires combining observations with general knowledge. While this is effortless for humans, reasoning with general knowledge remains an algorithmic challenge. To advance research in this direction a novel fact-based' visual question answering (FVQA) task has been introduced recently along with a large set of curated facts which link two entities, i.e., two possible answers, via a relation. Given a question-image pair, deep network techniques have been employed to successively reduce the large set of facts until one of the two entities of the final remaining fact is predicted as the answer. We observe that a successive process which considers one fact at a time to form a local decision is sub-optimal. Instead, we develop an entity graph and use a graph convolutional network to reason' about the correct answer by jointly considering all entities. We show on the challenging FVQA dataset that this leads to an improvement in accuracy of around 7% compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Answering a factual question about an image can require general knowledge beyond what is directly visible. The factual visual question answering task supplies curated facts that connect pairs of entities through relations. A system must combine this knowledge with the image and question to choose an entity as its answer.

Earlier approaches described in the paper progressively narrow the fact collection until an entity from a remaining fact is selected. The authors argue that making local decisions one fact at a time is suboptimal. Their alternative builds an entity graph and applies a graph convolutional network so that the answer is determined while jointly considering the entities.

This changes the reasoning process from successive local filtering to a graph-based treatment of the candidate answers and their relationships. On the FVQA dataset, the authors report an accuracy improvement of around 7% over the state of the art. The result supports the usefulness of considering connected knowledge jointly for this benchmark, where an image alone does not supply all the information needed to answer.
summary.tldr: An entity graph and graph convolutional network improve factual visual question answering by jointly considering possible answers.

title: Out of the Box: Reasoning with Graph Convolution Nets for Factual Visual Question Answering

abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layers are general, and that they learn generalized coordinates over the input domain. Deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we also apply our method to networks trained on MNIST, and show it is consistent with, and complimentary to, another study of intrinsic dimensionality.

paragraphs: This paper asks how general a neural network's layers are across a family of related tasks. It introduces a measurement technique based on singular vector canonical correlation analysis, or SVCCA, for tasks that vary continuously with parameters. The aim is to identify representations shared across problems and distinguish them from representations specific to individual tasks.

The authors study networks solving parameterized boundary-value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. They find that early hidden layers learn general representations resembling generalized coordinates over the input domain. Later layers become progressively more task-specific. This gives a concrete account of how shared and specialized representations appear within the networks studied.

To validate the measurement, the authors compare it with an existing approach based on transfer-learning experiments. The two methods agree closely, while the proposed technique is much faster, especially for continuously parameterized problems. An additional MNIST application is consistent with and complements another study of intrinsic dimensionality. The contribution therefore includes both a tool for measuring generality and evidence about where general representations arise.
summary.tldr: An SVCCA-based measure finds general early-layer representations and increasingly specialized deeper layers in networks solving parameterized differential equations.

title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations

abstract: Hypothesis testing for graphs has been an important tool in applied research fields for more than two decades, and still remains a challenging problem as one often needs to draw inference from few replicates of large graphs. Recent studies in statistics and learning theory have provided some theoretical insights about such high-dimensional graph testing problems, but the practicality of the developed theoretical methods remains an open question. In this paper, we consider the problem of two-sample testing of large graphs. We demonstrate the practical merits and limitations of existing theoretical tests and their bootstrapped variants. We also propose two new tests based on asymptotic distributions. We show that these tests are computationally less expensive and, in some cases, more reliable than the existing methods.

We also propose two new tests based on asymptotic distributions. We show that these tests are computationally less expensive and, in some cases, more reliable than the existing methods.

paragraphs: Two-sample testing for graphs asks whether two collections of networks differ statistically. The setting is difficult when each graph is large but only a few graph replicates are available. This paper focuses on whether theoretically developed testing methods are practically useful under that combination of high-dimensional observations and limited replication.

The authors examine existing theoretical tests and versions that use bootstrap resampling. Their analysis identifies practical merits as well as limitations, bringing computational and reliability considerations into the assessment. They also introduce two new tests based on asymptotic distributions, using distributional approximations to construct alternative procedures for the same testing problem.

The proposed tests are computationally less expensive than the existing methods considered and are more reliable in some cases. The qualification matters: the reported reliability advantage is conditional on the cases studied, rather than a universal ranking of all graph tests. The paper's contribution is to connect statistical theory with practical use, offering additional testing options where large graphs and few observations make method selection consequential.
summary.tldr: Two new graph two-sample tests reduce computation and, in some cases, improve reliability over existing methods.

title: Practical Methods for Graph Two-Sample Testing

abstract: This paper studies a recent proposal to use randomized value functions to drive exploration in reinforcement learning. These randomized value functions are generated by injecting random noise into the training data, making the approach compatible with many popular methods for estimating parameterized value functions. By providing a worst-case regret bound for tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes, we show that planning with respect to these randomized value functions can induce provably efficient exploration.
originalAbstract: This paper studies a recent proposal to use randomized value functions to drive exploration in reinforcement learning. These randomized value functions are generated by injecting random noise into the training data, making the approach compatible with many popular methods for estimating parameterized value functions. By providing a worst-case regret bound for tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes, we show that planning with respect to these randomized value functions can induce provably efficient exploration.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need to explore actions whose consequences are not yet well understood. This paper studies an approach that drives exploration by randomizing value functions, the estimates used to assess future returns. The agent plans using these randomized estimates, so uncertainty introduced into value estimation influences which behavior it chooses.

The randomization is produced by injecting noise into the training data. This construction makes the approach compatible with many popular ways of estimating parameterized value functions. Its practical attraction is that exploration can be connected to an existing value-estimation procedure through the data used to train it.

The paper's main result is a worst-case regret bound for tabular Markov decision processes with a finite horizon. Regret tracks the accumulated cost of learning compared with optimal behavior, so such a bound provides evidence of efficient exploration beyond individual successful runs. The result establishes that planning with randomized value functions can be provably efficient in this setting. Compatibility with broader estimation methods does not extend the stated tabular guarantee to every parameterized model.
summary.tldr: A worst-case regret bound shows that noise-generated randomized value functions can drive efficient exploration in finite-horizon tabular decision processes.

title: Worst-Case Regret Bounds for Exploration via Randomized Value Functions

abstract: Linear dimensionality reduction methods are commonly used to extract low-dimensional structure from high-dimensional data. However, popular methods disregard temporal structure, rendering them prone to extracting noise rather than meaningful dynamics when applied to time series data. At the same time, many successful unsupervised learning methods for temporal, sequential and spatial data extract features which are predictive of their surrounding context. Combining these approaches, we introduce Dynamical Components Analysis (DCA), a linear dimensionality reduction method which discovers a subspace of high-dimensional time series data with maximal predictive information, defined as the mutual information between the past and future. We test DCA on synthetic examples and demonstrate its superior ability to extract dynamical structure compared to commonly used linear methods. We also apply DCA to several real-world datasets, showing that the dimensions extracted by DCA are more useful than those extracted by other methods for predicting future states and decoding auxiliary variables. Overall, DCA robustly extracts dynamical structure in noisy, high-dimensional data while retaining the computational efficiency and geometric interpretability of linear dimensionality reduction methods.

paragraphs: Reducing high-dimensional time series to a few coordinates can reveal meaningful dynamics, but methods that ignore time may instead emphasize noise. Dynamical Components Analysis, or DCA, makes temporal predictability central to selecting those coordinates. It combines linear dimensionality reduction with the idea that useful features help predict their surrounding context.

DCA seeks a linear subspace that maximizes predictive information, defined as the mutual information between the past and future. In plain terms, it favors a compact representation whose earlier values retain information about what comes next. The method therefore evaluates the representation through temporal relationships rather than disregarding the order of observations.

On synthetic examples, DCA extracts dynamical structure better than commonly used linear methods. Across several real datasets, its dimensions are more useful for predicting future states and decoding auxiliary variables. The reported results support extracting dynamics from noisy data while keeping the computational efficiency and geometric interpretability associated with linear dimensionality reduction.
summary.tldr: DCA finds linear representations that maximize information shared between past and future, improving extraction of dynamics from noisy time series.

title: Unsupervised Discovery of Temporal Structure in Noisy Data with Dynamical Components Analysis

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) capture long dependencies and context, and 2 hence are the key component of typical sequential data based tasks. However, the sequential nature of RNNs dictates a large inference cost for long sequences even if the hardware supports parallelization. To induce long-term dependencies, and yet admit parallelization, we introduce novel shallow RNNs. In this architecture, the first layer splits the input sequence and runs several independent RNNs. The second layer consumes the output of the first layer using a second RNN thus capturing long dependencies. We provide theoretical justification for our architecture under weak assumptions that we verify on real-world benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that for time-series classification, our technique leads to substantially improved inference time over standard RNNs without compromising accuracy. For example, we can deploy audio-keyword classification on tiny Cortex M4 devices (100MHz processor, 256KB RAM, no DSP available) which was not possible using standard RNN models. Similarly, using SRNN in the popular Listen-Attend-Spell (LAS) architecture for phoneme classification [4], we can reduce the lag inphoneme classification by 10-12x while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks process sequences through dependent steps, so long inputs can remain slow even when hardware supports parallel computation. This paper introduces shallow RNNs to preserve long-range context while enabling parallel work. The goal is faster time-series classification, including deployment on devices with limited processing power and memory.

The architecture first divides the input sequence and processes its parts with independent RNNs. A second RNN consumes the outputs of this first layer to capture dependencies across the parts. The authors provide theoretical justification under weak assumptions and verify those assumptions on real-world benchmarks. This structure combines independent local processing with recurrent integration.

Experiments report substantially faster inference than standard RNNs without sacrificing accuracy. The authors demonstrate audio-keyword classification on a Cortex M4 with a 100 MHz processor, 256 KB of RAM, and no DSP, a deployment they report was infeasible with standard RNNs. In a Listen-Attend-Spell phoneme classifier, shallow RNNs reduce classification lag by 10–12 times while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy.
summary.tldr: Shallow RNNs process sequence segments independently and then combine them recurrently, reducing reported inference latency without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Shallow RNN: Accurate Time-series Classification on Resource Constrained Devices

abstract: Adaptive gradient-based optimizers such as Adagrad and Adam are crucial for achieving state-of-the-art performance in machine translation and language modeling. However, these methods maintain second-order statistics for each parameter, thus introducing significant memory overheads that restrict the size of the model being used as well as the number of examples in a mini-batch. We describe an effective and flexible adaptive optimization method with greatly reduced memory overhead. Our method retains the benefits of per-parameter adaptivity while allowing significantly larger models and batch sizes. We give convergence guarantees for our method, and demonstrate its effectiveness in training very large translation and language models with up to 2-fold speedups compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adagrad and Adam maintain statistics for individual model parameters. These statistics help adapt learning, but they also consume memory alongside the model itself. In large translation and language models, that overhead can restrict both the number of parameters and the number of examples processed in a minibatch.

This paper proposes an adaptive optimization method with substantially reduced memory overhead while retaining the benefits of per-parameter adaptivity. The practical aim is to free capacity for larger models and larger batches. The contribution treats the optimizer's stored information as a resource that directly affects which training configurations are feasible.

The authors provide convergence guarantees and demonstrate the method on very large translation and language models. They report speedups of up to twofold compared with the state of the art. This is an observed upper improvement in their evaluation. Together, the theory and experiments support reducing optimizer memory while preserving useful adaptive behavior and enabling more efficient large-model training.
summary.tldr: A memory-efficient adaptive optimizer supports larger models and batches, with convergence guarantees and reported speedups of up to twofold.

title: Memory Efficient Adaptive Optimization

abstract: The goal of unsupervised image-to-image translation is to map images from one domain to another without the ground truth correspondence between the two domains. State-of-art methods learn the correspondence using large numbers of unpaired examples from both domains and are based on generative adversarial networks. In order to preserve the semantics of the input image, the adversarial objective is usually combined with a cycle-consistency loss that penalizes incorrect reconstruction of the input image from the translated one. However, if the target mapping is many-to-one, e.g. aerial photos to maps, such a restriction forces the generator to hide information in low-amplitude structured noise that is undetectable by human eye or by the discriminator. In this paper, we show how such self-attacking behavior of unsupervised translation methods affects their performance and provide two defense techniques. We perform a quantitative evaluation of the proposed techniques and show that making the translation model more robust to the self-adversarial attack increases its generation quality and reconstruction reliability and makes the model less sensitive to low-amplitude perturbations. Our project page can be found at ai.bu.edu/selfadv.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image translation learns to move between image domains without paired examples showing the correct correspondence. A common training rule asks the model to reconstruct the original image after translating it and then translating back. This cycle-consistency requirement is intended to preserve the meaning of the input, but the paper examines how it can create an unintended behavior.

The problem arises when the desired translation is many-to-one, as with aerial photographs and maps. Different photographs can correspond to the same map, so a proper translation may discard information needed for exact reconstruction. The authors show that cycle consistency can force the generator to conceal that information in faint, structured noise that neither people nor the discriminator detect.

The paper studies the performance consequences of this self-adversarial behavior and introduces two defenses. Quantitative evaluation shows that greater robustness to the hidden-information attack improves generated images and reconstruction reliability while reducing sensitivity to small perturbations. The finding connects a specific conflict in the training objective to both translation quality and fragility.
summary.tldr: Two defenses against information hidden by cycle-consistent image translators improve generation quality, reconstruction reliability, and resistance to small perturbations.

title: Adversarial Self-Defense for Cycle-Consistent GANs

abstract: Intense recent discussions have focused on how to provide individuals with control over when their data can and cannot be used --- the EU’s Right To Be Forgotten regulation is an example of this effort. In this paper we initiate a framework studying what to do when it is no longer permissible to deploy models derivative from specific user data. In particular, we formulate the problem of efficiently deleting individual data points from trained machine learning models. For many standard ML models, the only way to completely remove an individual's data is to retrain the whole model from scratch on the remaining data, which is often not computationally practical. We investigate algorithmic principles that enable efficient data deletion in ML. For the specific setting of $k$-means clustering, we propose two provably deletion efficient algorithms which achieve an average of over $100\times$ improvement in deletion efficiency across 6 datasets, while producing clusters of comparable statistical quality to a canonical $k$-means++ baseline.

paragraphs: Removing a data point from storage does not by itself address a model already trained using that point. This paper formulates the problem of efficiently deleting individual observations from trained machine learning models when continued use of models derived from that data is no longer permissible. Retraining from scratch can accomplish removal for many standard models, but may be computationally impractical.

The authors investigate algorithmic principles that make deletion more efficient and develop two algorithms for k-means clustering. Both come with proofs of deletion efficiency. This gives a concrete setting in which the ability to remove training data can be considered as part of algorithm design.

Across six datasets, the algorithms achieve an average improvement of more than 100 times in deletion efficiency while producing clusters of comparable statistical quality to a canonical k-means++ baseline. The empirical result therefore pairs lower deletion cost with retained clustering quality. The broader framework concerns machine learning data deletion, while the specific algorithms and reported improvements apply to k-means.
summary.tldr: Two deletion-efficient k-means algorithms greatly reduce reported data-removal costs while retaining comparable clustering quality.

title: Making AI Forget You: Data Deletion in Machine Learning

abstract: Sorting is used pervasively in machine learning, either to define elementary algorithms, such as $k$-nearest neighbors ($k$-NN) rules, or to define test-time metrics, such as top-$k$ classification accuracy or ranking losses. Sorting is however a poor match for the end-to-end, automatically differentiable pipelines of deep learning. Indeed, sorting procedures output two vectors, neither of which is differentiable: the vector of sorted values is piecewise linear, while the sorting permutation itself (or its inverse, the vector of ranks) has no differentiable properties to speak of, since it is integer-valued. We propose in this paper to replace the usual \texttt{sort} procedure with a differentiable proxy. Our proxy builds upon the fact that sorting can be seen as an optimal assignment problem, one in which the $n$ values to be sorted are matched to an \emph{auxiliary} probability measure supported on any \emph{increasing} family of $n$ target values. From this observation, we propose extended rank and sort operators by considering optimal transport (OT) problems (the natural relaxation for assignments) where the auxiliary measure can be any weighted measure supported on $m$ increasing values, where $m \ne n$. We recover differentiable operators by regularizing these OT problems with an entropic penalty, and solve them by applying Sinkhorn iterations. Using these smoothed rank and sort operators, we propose differentiable proxies for the classification 0/1 loss as well as for the quantile regression loss.

paragraphs: Sorting and ranking appear throughout machine learning, but their ordinary forms fit poorly into gradient-based training. Ranks are discrete, and sorting values involves changes in their ordering. This paper constructs smooth substitutes so that operations based on ordering can participate in automatically differentiated learning pipelines.

The starting point is to view sorting as an assignment problem: input values are matched to an increasing collection of target values. The authors extend this view using optimal transport, which relaxes the assignment formulation. Their generalized operators allow a weighted target distribution whose number of support points can differ from the number of inputs, expanding the construction beyond ordinary one-to-one sorting.

An entropy penalty smooths the transport problem, and Sinkhorn iterations solve the resulting formulation. This produces differentiable rank and sort operators. The authors use them to construct smooth proxies for classification’s zero-one loss and for quantile regression loss. The contribution provides a way to express ordering-based objectives in a form compatible with end-to-end gradient optimization.
summary.tldr: Entropy-regularized optimal transport turns sorting and ranking into differentiable proxies usable in gradient-based learning objectives.

title: Differentiable Ranking and Sorting using Optimal Transport

abstract: Abstract Neural networks are state-of-the-art classification approaches but are generally difficult to interpret. This issue can be partly alleviated by constructing a precise decision process within the neural network. In this work, a network architecture, denoted as Classification-By-Components network (CBC), is proposed. It is restricted to follow an intuitive reasoning based decision process inspired by Biederman's recognition-by-components theory from cognitive psychology. The network is trained to learn and detect generic components that characterize objects. In parallel, a class-wise reasoning strategy based on these components is learned to solve the classification problem. In contrast to other work on reasoning, we propose three different types of reasoning: positive, negative, and indefinite. These three types together form a probability space to provide a probabilistic classifier. The decomposition of objects into generic components combined with the probabilistic reasoning provides by design a clear interpretation of the classification decision process. The evaluation of the approach on MNIST shows that CBCs are viable classifiers. Additionally, we demonstrate that the inherent interpretability offers a profound understanding of the classification behavior such that we can explain the success of an adversarial attack. The method's scalability is successfully tested using the ImageNet dataset.

paragraphs: Classification-by-Components makes a neural network follow an explicit decision process to improve interpretability. Inspired by recognition-by-components theory in cognitive psychology, the network learns generic components that characterize objects. It also learns a separate reasoning strategy for each class, connecting component detection to the final classification.

The reasoning uses three categories: positive, negative, and indefinite. Together, these form a probability space, allowing the architecture to act as a probabilistic classifier. Because predictions are organized around detected components and learned reasoning, the decision process has an interpretation built into its design. The explanation follows the same structure used to classify the input.

Experiments on MNIST show that the architecture is a viable classifier, and the authors use its interpretability to explain why an adversarial attack succeeds. They also report a successful scalability test on ImageNet. These findings support the practical use of an explicit reasoning architecture while illustrating how its internal structure can reveal the behavior behind a particular prediction.
summary.tldr: Classification-by-Components builds interpretable predictions from learned object components and probabilistic class-specific reasoning.

title: Classification-by-Components: Probabilistic Modeling of Reasoning over a Set of Components

abstract: We study the effects of approximate inference on the performance of Thompson sampling in the $k$-armed bandit problems. Thompson sampling is a successful algorithm for online decision-making but requires posterior inference, which often must be approximated in practice. We show that even small constant inference error (in $\alpha$-divergence) can lead to poor performance (linear regret) due to under-exploration (for $\alpha<1$) or over-exploration (for $\alpha>0$) by the approximation. While for $\alpha > 0$ this is unavoidable, for $\alpha \leq 0$ the regret can be improved by adding a small amount of forced exploration even when the inference error is a large constant.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling makes sequential decisions using a posterior distribution, but computing that posterior often requires approximation. This paper asks whether an approximation that looks statistically close is necessarily good enough for decision-making. It studies the issue in bandit problems with a fixed number of available actions.

The authors show that even small constant error measured by alpha-divergence can produce linear regret, meaning cumulative lost reward can grow proportionally with the number of decisions. Approximation can cause insufficient exploration when alpha is below one or excessive exploration when alpha is above zero. These ranges overlap, so both kinds of failure are relevant for some divergence choices.

For positive alpha, the poor-performance possibility is described as unavoidable. For nonpositive alpha, adding a small amount of forced exploration can improve regret even with large constant inference error. The result shows why posterior approximation quality must be considered together with its effect on action selection: a small divergence error alone need not ensure effective exploration.
summary.tldr: Small posterior approximation errors can cause linear regret in Thompson sampling, while forced exploration helps for nonpositive alpha-divergence settings.

title: Thompson Sampling and Approximate Inference

abstract: Several machine learning models involve mapping a score vector to a probability vector. Usually, this is done by projecting the score vector onto a probability simplex, and such projections are often characterized as Lipschitz continuous approximations of the argmax function, whose Lipschitz constant is controlled by a parameter that is similar to a softmax temperature. The aforementioned parameter has been observed to affect the quality of these models and is typically either treated as a constant or decayed over time. In this work, we propose a method that adapts this parameter to individual training examples. The resulting method exhibits desirable properties, such as sparsity of its support and numerically efficient implementation, and we find that it can significantly outperform competing non-adaptive projection methods.

paragraphs: Many machine learning models turn a vector of scores into probabilities before making predictions or computing a training objective. Such mappings can act as smooth approximations to choosing only the highest-scoring entry. A temperature-like parameter controls their behavior, and the abstract notes that its value can affect the quality of the resulting model.

Common approaches keep that parameter fixed or change it according to a shared schedule over training. Rankmax instead adapts it to each individual training example. The contribution is therefore an example-dependent probability mapping, allowing the approximation to the maximum-selection operation to vary across inputs instead of depending only on a global parameter choice.

The proposed method has sparse support, meaning some output probabilities can be exactly zero, and admits a numerically efficient implementation. The authors find that it can significantly outperform competing non-adaptive projection methods. These results support adapting the score-to-probability transformation as part of model design, with sparsity and efficient computation accompanying the reported empirical improvements.
summary.tldr: Rankmax adapts a temperature-like probability projection parameter per example, providing sparse outputs and reported gains over non-adaptive alternatives.

title: Rankmax: An Adaptive Projection Alternative to the Softmax Function

abstract: Synchronization is a key step in data-parallel distributed machine learning (ML). Different synchronization systems and strategies perform differently, and to achieve optimal parallel training throughput requires synchronization strategies that adapt to model structures and cluster configurations. Existing synchronization systems often only consider a single or a few synchronization aspects, and the burden of deciding the right synchronization strategy is then placed on the ML practitioners, who may lack the required expertise. In this paper, we develop a model- and resource-dependent representation for synchronization, which unifies multiple synchronization aspects ranging from architecture, message partitioning, placement scheme, to communication topology. Based on this representation, we build an end-to-end pipeline, AutoSync, to automatically optimize synchronization strategies given model structures and resource specifications, lowering the bar for data-parallel distributed ML. By learning from low-shot data collected in only 200 trial runs, AutoSync can discover synchronization strategies up to 1.6x better than manually optimized ones. We develop transfer-learning mechanisms to further reduce the auto-optimization cost -- the simulators can transfer among similar model architectures, among similar cluster configurations, or both. We also present a dataset that contains over 10000 synchronization strategies and run-time pairs on a diverse set of models and cluster specifications.

title: AutoSync: Learning to Synchronize for Data-Parallel Distributed Deep Learning

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning addresses the problem of inferring an expert's reward function from demonstrations. However, in many applications, we not only have access to the expert's near-optimal behaviour, but we also observe part of her learning process. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm for this setting, in which the goal is to recover the reward function being optimized by an agent, given a sequence of policies produced during learning. Our approach is based on the assumption that the observed agent is updating her policy parameters along the gradient direction. Then we extend our method to deal with the more realistic scenario where we only have access to a dataset of learning trajectories. For both settings, we provide theoretical insights into our algorithms' performance. Finally, we evaluate the approach in a simulated GridWorld environment and on the MuJoCo environments, comparing it with the state-of-the-art baseline.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks the reward function behind observed behavior. Often, demonstrations show an expert acting near optimally, but some applications also expose how that behavior developed during learning. This paper uses a sequence of changing policies as evidence about the reward an agent is trying to optimize.

The proposed algorithm assumes the observed agent updates its policy parameters along the gradient direction. Under that assumption, changes between policies provide information about the objective guiding learning. The authors then extend the method to a setting where the available evidence consists of recorded learning trajectories rather than direct access to the sequence of policies.

For both settings, the paper provides theoretical insights into algorithm performance. It also evaluates the approach in a simulated GridWorld and in MuJoCo environments, comparing against a state-of-the-art baseline. The contribution is to incorporate the learning process into reward inference. Its central modeling assumption is specifically gradient-directed policy updates, which determines how observed changes are interpreted as evidence.
summary.tldr: The method infers an agent's reward from its learning process by assuming policy updates follow a gradient direction.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning from a Gradient-based Learner

abstract: In recent years, rapid progress has been made on the problem of single-channel sound separation using supervised training of deep neural networks. In such supervised approaches, a model is trained to predict the component sources from synthetic mixtures created by adding up isolated ground-truth sources. Reliance on this synthetic training data is problematic because good performance depends upon the degree of match between the training data and real-world audio, especially in terms of the acoustic conditions and distribution of sources. The acoustic properties can be challenging to accurately simulate, and the distribution of sound types may be hard to replicate. In this paper, we propose a completely unsupervised method, mixture invariant training (MixIT), that requires only single-channel acoustic mixtures. In MixIT, training examples are constructed by mixing together existing mixtures, and the model separates them into a variable number of latent sources, such that the separated sources can be remixed to approximate the original mixtures. We show that MixIT can achieve competitive performance compared to supervised methods on speech separation. Using MixIT in a semi-supervised learning setting enables unsupervised domain adaptation and learning from large amounts of real-world data without ground-truth source waveforms. In particular, we significantly improve reverberant speech separation performance by incorporating reverberant mixtures, train a speech enhancement system from noisy mixtures, and improve universal sound separation by incorporating a large amount of in-the-wild data.

paragraphs: Supervised sound separation commonly requires isolated source recordings that can be combined into synthetic mixtures. Those mixtures may fail to reproduce real acoustic conditions or the range of sounds encountered in practice. Mixture invariant training, or MixIT, removes the requirement for isolated ground-truth sources by learning directly from single-channel mixtures.

Training examples are created by combining existing mixtures. The model separates this combined recording into a variable number of latent sources, which must be remixable to approximate the original mixtures. This reconstruction requirement supplies a learning signal even though the individual sources within those original recordings are unknown.

The authors report improved reverberant speech separation, train speech enhancement from noisy mixtures, and improve universal sound separation using substantial in-the-wild data. These results show how recordings without clean source waveforms can contribute directly to training and help address mismatches between synthetic data and real-world audio.
summary.tldr: MixIT learns sound separation from mixtures alone by requiring separated outputs to reconstruct the original mixtures through remixing.

title: Unsupervised Sound Separation Using Mixture Invariant Training

abstract: We present REVEL, a partially neural reinforcement learning (RL) framework for provably safe exploration in continuous state and action spaces. A key challenge for provably safe deep RL is that repeatedly verifying neural networks within a learning loop is computationally infeasible. We address this challenge using two policy classes: a general, neurosymbolic class with approximate gradients and a more restricted class of symbolic policies that allows efficient verification. Our learning algorithm is a mirror descent over policies: in each iteration, it safely lifts a symbolic policy into the neurosymbolic space, performs safe gradient updates to the resulting policy, and projects the updated policy into the safe symbolic subset, all without requiring explicit verification of neural networks. Our empirical results show that REVEL enforces safe exploration in many scenarios in which Constrained Policy Optimization does not, and that it can discover policies that outperform those learned through prior approaches to verified exploration.

paragraphs: REVEL addresses safe exploration in reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions. The computational obstacle is that repeatedly verifying neural networks during learning is infeasible. The framework uses two policy classes to make progress: a flexible neurosymbolic class with approximate gradients and a more restricted symbolic class that supports efficient verification.

Learning proceeds through a mirror-descent process over policies. Each iteration safely moves a symbolic policy into the neurosymbolic space, applies safe gradient updates, and projects the result back into the safe symbolic subset. This sequence provides a way to use neural policy updates while maintaining the framework’s safety guarantee without explicitly verifying the neural networks themselves.

In the reported experiments, REVEL enforces safe exploration in many scenarios where Constrained Policy Optimization does not. It can also find policies that outperform those produced by earlier verified-exploration approaches. The contribution joins a formally grounded learning procedure with empirical evidence that the symbolic restrictions can coexist with useful policy improvement in the continuous settings studied.
summary.tldr: REVEL combines neural policy updates with verifiable symbolic policies to enable provably safe exploration without repeated neural-network verification.

title: Neurosymbolic Reinforcement Learning with Formally Verified Exploration

abstract: Crowdsourced data used in machine learning services might carry sensitive information about attributes that users do not want to share. Various methods have been proposed to minimize the potential information leakage of sensitive attributes while maximizing the task accuracy. However, little is known about the theory behind these methods. In light of this gap, we develop a novel theoretical framework for attribute obfuscation. Under our framework, we propose a minimax optimization formulation to protect the given attribute and analyze its inference guarantees against worst-case adversaries. Meanwhile, there is a tension between minimizing information leakage and maximizing task accuracy. To understand this, we prove an information-theoretic lower bound to precisely characterize the fundamental trade-off between accuracy and information leakage. We conduct experiments on two real-world datasets to corroborate the inference guarantees and validate the inherent trade-offs therein. Our results indicate that, among several alternatives, the adversarial learning approach achieves the best trade-off in terms of attribute obfuscation and accuracy maximization.

paragraphs: Data useful for a prediction task can also reveal sensitive attributes that contributors would prefer to conceal. This paper develops a theoretical framework for attribute obfuscation, examining how a learned representation can remain useful while reducing an adversary's ability to infer a designated attribute.

The authors formulate the problem as minimax optimization and analyze inference guarantees against worst-case adversaries within their framework. They also establish an information-theoretic lower bound describing the fundamental tension between task accuracy and information leakage. This makes the trade-off an object of analysis, rather than treating usefulness and concealment as goals that can always be improved independently.

Among the alternatives evaluated, adversarial learning achieves the best balance between hiding the attribute and preserving accuracy. The result supports this approach in the reported comparisons while grounding its purpose in a theoretical account of what information must be retained or exposed to maintain predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A minimax framework provides attribute-inference guarantees and characterizes the trade-off between concealing sensitive information and maintaining prediction accuracy.

title: Trade-offs and Guarantees of Adversarial Representation Learning for Information Obfuscation

abstract: We propose a new method for learning with multi-field categorical data. Multi-field categorical data are usually collected over many heterogeneous groups. These groups can reflect in the categories under a field. The existing methods try to learn a universal model that fits all data, which is challenging and inevitably results in learning a complex model. In contrast, we propose a field-wise learning method leveraging the natural structure of data to learn simple yet efficient one-to-one field-focused models with appropriate constraints. In doing this, the models can be fitted to each category and thus can better capture the underlying differences in data. We present a model that utilizes linear models with variance and low-rank constraints, to help it generalize better and reduce the number of parameters. The model is also interpretable in a field-wise manner. As the dimensionality of multi-field categorical data can be very high, the models applied to such data are mostly over-parameterized. Our theoretical analysis can potentially explain the effect of over-parametrization on the generalization of our model. It also supports the variance constraints in the learning objective. The experiment results on two large-scale datasets show the superior performance of our model, the trend of the generalization error bound, and the interpretability of learning outcomes. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzb5600/Field-wise-Learning.

This paper proposes field-wise learning, using the data's existing organization to fit simpler models that respond to category-specific differences.

The proposed approach uses field-focused linear models with variance and low-rank constraints. The constraints are intended to improve generalization and reduce the number of parameters while retaining the ability to capture variation between groups. Because the models are organized around fields, their learned behavior can also be interpreted at that level.

Experiments on two large-scale datasets report superior performance, illustrate the trend predicted by the generalization-error bound, and demonstrate interpretable outcomes. The contribution combines a structured modeling choice with supporting analysis and empirical evidence for learning from high-dimensional categorical data.
summary.tldr: Field-wise learning uses constrained, category-sensitive linear models to capture heterogeneous categorical data while controlling model complexity.

title: Field-wise Learning for Multi-field Categorical Data

abstract: This paper proposes near-optimal algorithms for the pure-exploration linear bandit problem in the fixed confidence and fixed budget settings. Leveraging ideas from the theory of suprema of empirical processes, we provide an algorithm whose sample complexity scales with the geometry of the instance and avoids an explicit union bound over the number of arms. Unlike previous approaches which sample based on minimizing a worst-case variance (e.g. G-optimal design), we define an experimental design objective based on the Gaussian-width of the underlying arm set. We provide a novel lower bound in terms of this objective that highlights its fundamental role in the sample complexity. The sample complexity of our fixed confidence algorithm matches this lower bound, and in addition is computationally efficient for combinatorial classes, e.g. shortest-path, matchings and matroids, where the arm sets can be exponentially large in the dimension. Finally, we propose the first algorithm for linear bandits in the the fixed budget setting. Its guarantee matches our lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: The paper studies pure exploration in linear bandits: how to allocate observations to identify a good choice, rather than maximize rewards during exploration. It considers both a fixed-confidence setting, where reliability is specified, and a fixed-budget setting, where the number of observations is limited. The challenge is especially demanding when the possible choices form a huge combinatorial collection.

Its central idea is to design experiments around the geometry of the choices. The authors use Gaussian width to define a sampling objective, drawing on methods that analyze the largest fluctuations across a collection of related quantities. This avoids an explicit union bound over every choice and differs from designs that minimize the worst individual variance.

A new lower bound establishes the importance of this geometric objective. The fixed-confidence algorithm matches that bound and remains computationally efficient for classes including paths, matchings, and matroids, even when choices are exponentially numerous. The fixed-budget algorithm has a guarantee matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, connecting practical sampling procedures to fundamental statistical requirements.
summary.tldr: Geometry-based experimental design yields near-optimal exploration algorithms for linear bandits, including settings with exponentially many possible choices.

title: An Empirical Process Approach to the Union Bound: Practical Algorithms for Combinatorial and Linear Bandits

abstract: Imitation learning is a popular approach for teaching motor skills to robots. However, most approaches focus on extracting policy parameters from execution traces alone (i.e., motion trajectories and perceptual data). No adequate communication channel exists between the human expert and the robot to describe critical aspects of the task, such as the properties of the target object or the intended shape of the motion. Motivated by insights into the human teaching process, we introduce a method for incorporating unstructured natural language into imitation learning. At training time, the expert can provide demonstrations along with verbal descriptions in order to describe the underlying intent (e.g., "go to the large green bowl"). The training process then interrelates these two modalities to encode the correlations between language, perception, and motion. The resulting language-conditioned visuomotor policies can be conditioned at runtime on new human commands and instructions, which allows for more fine-grained control over the trained policies while also reducing situational ambiguity. We demonstrate in a set of simulation experiments how our approach can learn language-conditioned manipulation policies for a seven-degree-of-freedom robot arm and compare the results to a variety of alternative methods.

paragraphs: A robot demonstration shows what a person did, but may leave unclear which object properties or movement choices mattered. Imitation learning based only on motion and perception must infer that intent indirectly. This paper adds natural language as a channel through which an expert can explain important aspects of a demonstration.

During training, the system receives verbal descriptions alongside demonstrated actions. It learns relationships among the language, the visual scene, and the motion. The resulting visuomotor policy can then take new instructions at runtime, allowing a person to specify details such as the intended target and reduce ambiguity about how the learned behavior should be used.

The authors demonstrate the approach in simulation with a seven-degree-of-freedom robot arm and compare it with alternative methods. The contribution is the integration of unstructured language into learning from demonstrations and subsequent policy control. The reported setting supports the feasibility of language-conditioned manipulation policies, with language providing information that execution traces alone may leave unresolved.
summary.tldr: Pairing demonstrations with natural-language descriptions teaches robot policies that can be directed more precisely through runtime instructions.

title: Language-Conditioned Imitation Learning for Robot Manipulation Tasks

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been shown to be effective models for different predictive tasks on graph-structured data. Recent work on their expressive power has focused on isomorphism tasks and countable feature spaces. We extend this theoretical framework to include continuous features---which occur regularly in real-world input domains and within the hidden layers of GNNs---and we demonstrate the requirement for multiple aggregation functions in this context. Accordingly, we propose Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA), a novel architecture combining multiple aggregators with degree-scalers (which generalize the sum aggregator). Finally, we compare the capacity of different models to capture and exploit the graph structure via a novel benchmark containing multiple tasks taken from classical graph theory, alongside existing benchmarks from real-world domains, all of which demonstrate the strength of our model. With this work we hope to steer some of the GNN research towards new aggregation methods which we believe are essential in the search for powerful and robust models.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks update node representations by collecting information from neighboring nodes. How that information is aggregated affects what graph patterns the network can distinguish. This paper extends expressiveness analysis beyond countable feature spaces to continuous features, which appear both in real inputs and in the internal representations of graph networks.

Within that extended framework, the authors demonstrate a requirement for multiple aggregation functions. They translate the result into Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation, an architecture that combines several aggregators with degree scalers. These scalers account for neighborhood size and generalize the role of summation, giving the network multiple ways to summarize the information surrounding each node.

The evaluation includes a new collection of tasks drawn from classical graph theory and existing benchmarks from real-world domains. The reported results demonstrate the model's strength across those evaluations. The contribution connects a theoretical issue about continuous features to an architectural choice, then tests whether that choice helps models capture and use graph structure in predictive tasks.
summary.tldr: PNA combines multiple neighborhood aggregators and degree scalers, motivated by expressiveness requirements for graph networks with continuous features.

title: Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation for Graph Nets

abstract: We study the fundamental problems of agnostically learning halfspaces and ReLUs under Gaussian marginals. In the former problem, given labeled examples $(\bx, y)$ from an unknown distribution on $\R^d \times \{ \pm 1\}$, whose marginal distribution on $\bx$ is the standard Gaussian and the labels $y$ can be arbitrary, the goal is to output a hypothesis with 0-1 loss $\opt+\eps$, where $\opt$ is the 0-1 loss of the best-fitting halfspace. In the latter problem, given labeled examples $(\bx, y)$ from an unknown distribution on $\R^d \times \R$, whose marginal distribution on $\bx$ is the standard Gaussian and the labels $y$ can be arbitrary, the goal is to output a hypothesis with square loss $\opt+\eps$, where $\opt$ is the square loss of the best-fitting ReLU. We prove Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds of $d^{\poly(1/\eps)}$ for both of these problems. Our SQ lower bounds provide strong evidence that current upper bounds for these tasks are essentially best possible.

paragraphs: The paper studies how difficult it is to learn halfspaces and ReLU functions when inputs follow a standard Gaussian distribution but labels can be arbitrary. This is an agnostic setting: the learner cannot assume that any function in the target class explains the labels perfectly. Instead, it aims to approach the best fit available within that class.

For halfspaces, success means a classification error at most epsilon above that of the best halfspace. For ReLUs, the corresponding target uses squared error. These definitions separate unavoidable error in the best-fitting function from the learner's additional error, making epsilon the required closeness to the best attainable fit.

The authors prove lower bounds of d raised to a polynomial in 1/epsilon in the Statistical Query model for both problems. Thus, the bounds express substantial difficulty as dimension and accuracy demands increase. They provide strong evidence that existing upper bounds are essentially optimal, while remaining bounds within the Statistical Query framework rather than unrestricted impossibility results for every learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Statistical Query lower bounds suggest existing algorithms for agnostic halfspace and ReLU learning under Gaussian inputs are essentially optimal.

title: Near-Optimal SQ Lower Bounds for Agnostically Learning Halfspaces and ReLUs under Gaussian Marginals

abstract: In this paper, we provide a theory of using graph neural networks (GNNs) for multi-node representation learning (where we are interested in learning a representation for a set of more than one node, such as link). We know that GNN is designed to learn single-node representations. When we want to learn a node set representation involving multiple nodes, a common practice in previous works is to directly aggregate the single-node representations obtained by a GNN into a joint node set representation. In this paper, we show a fundamental constraint of such an approach, namely the inability to capture the dependence between nodes in the node set, and argue that directly aggregating individual node representations does not lead to an effective joint representation for multiple nodes. Then, we notice that a few previous successful works for multi-node representation learning, including SEAL, Distance Encoding, and ID-GNN, all used node labeling. These methods first label nodes in the graph according to their relationships with the target node set before applying a GNN. Then, the node representations obtained in the labeled graph are aggregated into a node set representation. By investigating their inner mechanisms, we unify these node labeling techniques into a single and most general form---labeling trick. We prove that with labeling trick a sufficiently expressive GNN learns the most expressive node set representations, thus in principle solves any joint learning tasks over node sets. Experiments on one important two-node representation learning task, link prediction, verified our theory. Our work explains the superior performance of previous node-labeling-based methods, and establishes a theoretical foundation of using GNNs for multi-node representation learning.

The paper identifies a fundamental limitation of this construction: it cannot capture the dependence among the nodes in the target set.

Representations from this labeled graph are then combined. The paper unifies these techniques as the labeling trick, explaining how information about the joint target can enter representation learning before aggregation.

summary.tldr: Labeling nodes relative to a target set lets sufficiently expressive GNNs learn maximally expressive joint representations.

title: Labeling Trick: A Theory of Using Graph Neural Networks for Multi-Node Representation Learning

abstract: Neural agents trained in reinforcement learning settings can learn to communicate among themselves via discrete tokens, accomplishing as a team what agents would be unable to do alone. However, the current standard of using one-hot vectors as discrete communication tokens prevents agents from acquiring more desirable aspects of communication such as zero-shot understanding. Inspired by word embedding techniques from natural language processing, we propose neural agent architectures that enables them to communicate via discrete tokens derived from a learned, continuous space. We show in a decision theoretic framework that our technique optimizes communication over a wide range of scenarios, whereas one-hot tokens are only optimal under restrictive assumptions. In self-play experiments, we validate that our trained agents learn to cluster tokens in semantically-meaningful ways, allowing them communicate in noisy environments where other techniques fail. Lastly, we demonstrate both that agents using our method can effectively respond to novel human communication and that humans can understand unlabeled emergent agent communication, outperforming the use of one-hot communication.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can develop discrete messages that help them cooperate. However, representing every message as an unrelated one-hot symbol gives the communication system no built-in way to express similarity between meanings. The paper investigates whether discrete messages drawn from a learned continuous space can support more flexible understanding.

Inspired by word embeddings, the proposed architectures retain discrete communication while learning relationships among the tokens. A decision-theoretic analysis shows that this technique optimizes communication across a broad range of scenarios, whereas one-hot messages are optimal only under restrictive assumptions. The distinction concerns how messages are represented, not simply whether agents are allowed to communicate.

In self-play experiments, agents organize tokens into meaningful semantic groups and communicate successfully in noisy settings where other techniques fail. Further experiments show responses to novel human messages and human understanding of agent messages without labels, outperforming one-hot communication. Together, these results suggest that learned semantic relationships can make an emergent communication system more robust and more accessible across unfamiliar exchanges.
summary.tldr: Learning semantic relationships among discrete communication tokens improves agents' robustness and supports exchanges with humans in the reported experiments.

title: Emergent Discrete Communication in Semantic Spaces

abstract: Despite the advances in extracting local features achieved by handcrafted and learning-based descriptors, they are still limited by the lack of invariance to non-rigid transformations. In this paper, we present a new approach to compute features from still images that are robust to non-rigid deformations to circumvent the problem of matching deformable surfaces and objects. Our deformation-aware local descriptor, named DEAL, leverages a polar sampling and a spatial transformer warping to provide invariance to rotation, scale, and image deformations. We train the model architecture end-to-end by applying isometric non-rigid deformations to objects in a simulated environment as guidance to provide highly discriminative local features. The experiments show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art handcrafted, learning-based image, and RGB-D descriptors in different datasets with both real and realistic synthetic deformable objects in still images. The source code and trained model of the descriptor are publicly available at https://www.verlab.dcc.ufmg.br/descriptors/neurips2021.

paragraphs: Matching corresponding regions across images becomes difficult when an object bends or otherwise changes shape. Local image descriptors need to recognize the same surface region despite these changes. This paper introduces DEAL, a descriptor designed to handle non-rigid deformation while extracting features directly from still images.

DEAL combines polar sampling with spatial transformer warping to provide invariance to rotation, scale, and image deformation. Its architecture is trained end to end using simulated objects subjected to isometric non-rigid deformations. These training transformations guide the model toward features that remain recognizable as surfaces deform while still distinguishing different local regions.

Experiments cover datasets containing real and realistically simulated deformable objects. The authors report better results than leading handcrafted descriptors, learned image descriptors, and descriptors using color and depth. The findings support teaching a feature extractor about deformation during training and building deformation handling into its architecture. This offers a way to improve correspondence matching when ordinary appearance changes are compounded by changes in an object's shape.
summary.tldr: DEAL learns local image descriptors using simulated deformations and spatial warping to improve matching of deformable objects.

title: Extracting Deformation-Aware Local Features by Learning to Deform

abstract: Most real world applications require dealing with stochasticity like sensor noise or predictive uncertainty, where formal specifications of desired behavior are inherently probabilistic. Despite the promise of formal verification in ensuring the reliability of neural networks, progress in the direction of probabilistic specifications has been limited. In this direction, we first introduce a general formulation of probabilistic specifications for neural networks, which captures both probabilistic networks (e.g., Bayesian neural networks, MC-Dropout networks) and uncertain inputs (distributions over inputs arising from sensor noise or other perturbations). We then propose a general technique to verify such specifications by generalizing the notion of Lagrangian duality, replacing standard Lagrangian multipliers with "functional multipliers" that can be arbitrary functions of the activations at a given layer. We show that an optimal choice of functional multipliers leads to exact verification (i.e., sound and complete verification), and for specific forms of multipliers, we develop tractable practical verification algorithms. We empirically validate our algorithms by applying them to Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) and MC Dropout Networks, and certifying properties such as adversarial robustness and robust detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) data. On these tasks we are able to provide significantly stronger guarantees when compared to prior work -- for instance, for a VGG-64 MC-Dropout CNN trained on CIFAR-10 in a verification-agnostic manner, we improve the certified AUC (a verified lower bound on the true AUC) for robust OOD detection (on CIFAR-100) from $0 \% \rightarrow 29\%$. Similarly, for a BNN trained on MNIST, we improve on the $\ell_\infty$ robust accuracy from $60.2 \% \rightarrow 74.6\%$. Further, on a novel specification -- distributionally robust OOD detection -- we improve on the certified AUC from $5\% \rightarrow 23\%$.

summary.tldr: Functional multipliers extend neural network verification to probabilistic requirements and produce stronger practical robustness certificates.

title: Make Sure You're Unsure: A Framework for Verifying Probabilistic Specifications

abstract: Several issues in machine learning and inverse problems require to generate discrete data, as if sampled from a model probabilitydistribution. A common way to do so relies on the construction of a uniform probability distribution over a set of $N$ points whichminimizes the Wasserstein distance to the model distribution. This minimization problem, where the unknowns are the positions of the atoms, is non-convex. Yet, in most cases, a suitably adjusted version of Lloyd's algorithm in which Voronoi cells are replaced by Power cells, leads to configurations with small Wasserstein error. This is surprising because, again, of the non-convex nature of the problem, which moreover admits spurious critical points. We provide explicit upper bounds for the convergence speed of this Lloyd-type algorithm, starting from a cloud of points sufficiently far from each other. This already works after one step of the iteration procedure, and similar bounds can be deduced, for the corresponding gradient descent. These bounds naturally lead to a sort of Poliak-Łojasiewicz inequality for the Wasserstein distance cost, with an error term depending on the distances between Dirac masses in the discrete distribution.

paragraphs: Some learning and inverse problems require a finite set of points that represents a target probability distribution. One approach assigns equal probability to N points and adjusts their locations to minimize Wasserstein distance from the target. The optimization is non-convex and can contain spurious critical points, making practical success theoretically surprising.

The paper analyzes an adjusted Lloyd algorithm that replaces Voronoi cells with Power cells. Although this procedure often produces low-error configurations, non-convexity makes its convergence behavior difficult to explain. The authors provide explicit bounds on convergence speed when the starting points are sufficiently separated from one another.

The bounds already apply after a single iteration, and related bounds follow for the corresponding gradient descent procedure. They also yield a form of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality for the Wasserstein objective, including an error term determined by distances between the discrete point masses. The result provides finite-iteration control under a concrete geometric starting condition, helping explain why useful approximation can occur despite the optimization landscape's difficulties.
summary.tldr: Explicit convergence bounds explain Wasserstein point-cloud approximation by a Lloyd-type algorithm when its initial points are sufficiently separated.

title: Non-asymptotic convergence bounds for Wasserstein approximation using point clouds

abstract: Decision trees have been widely used as classifiers in many machine learning applications thanks to their lightweight and interpretable decision process. This paper introduces Tree in Tree decision graph (TnT), a framework that extends the conventional decision tree to a more generic and powerful directed acyclic graph. TnT constructs decision graphs by recursively growing decision trees inside the internal or leaf nodes instead of greedy training. The time complexity of TnT is linear to the number of nodes in the graph, therefore it can construct decision graphs on large datasets. Compared to decision trees, we show that TnT achieves better classification performance with reduced model size, both as a stand-alone classifier and as a base-estimator in bagging/AdaBoost ensembles. Our proposed model is a novel, more efficient and accurate alternative to the widely-used decision trees.

paragraphs: Decision trees classify examples through a sequence of branching decisions and are popular for their lightweight, interpretable operation. This paper introduces Tree in Tree, or TnT, which expands that structure into a directed acyclic decision graph. The aim is to obtain stronger classifiers while using smaller models.

TnT constructs its graph by recursively growing decision trees inside internal nodes or leaf nodes. This gives the construction a richer building block than a single greedy decision at each step. The reported time complexity grows linearly with the number of nodes in the resulting graph, supporting the use of the method on large datasets.

These benefits appear both when TnT is used as an individual classifier and when it supplies the base estimators in bagging or AdaBoost ensembles. The findings suggest that changing the structure and construction of a tree-based classifier can improve both predictive performance and model compactness.
summary.tldr: Tree in Tree recursively builds decision graphs that improve classification performance while using smaller models than the compared decision trees.

title: Tree in Tree: from Decision Trees to Decision Graphs

abstract: Attention is sparse in vision transformers. We observe the final prediction in vision transformers is only based on a subset of most informative tokens, which is sufficient for accurate image recognition. Based on this observation, we propose a dynamic token sparsification framework to prune redundant tokens progressively and dynamically based on the input. Specifically, we devise a lightweight prediction module to estimate the importance score of each token given the current features. The module is added to different layers to prune redundant tokens hierarchically. To optimize the prediction module in an end-to-end manner, we propose an attention masking strategy to differentiably prune a token by blocking its interactions with other tokens. Benefiting from the nature of self-attention, the unstructured sparse tokens are still hardware friendly, which makes our framework easy to achieve actual speed-up. By hierarchically pruning 66% of the input tokens, our method greatly reduces 31% $\sim$ 37% FLOPs and improves the throughput by over 40% while the drop of accuracy is within 0.5% for various vision transformers. Equipped with the dynamic token sparsification framework, DynamicViT models can achieve very competitive complexity/accuracy trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art CNNs and vision transformers on ImageNet. Code is available at https://github.com/raoyongming/DynamicViT

paragraphs: DynamicViT starts from the observation that a vision transformer's final prediction often relies on only a subset of its most informative tokens. Processing every token through every layer can therefore spend computation on information that contributes little to the decision. The paper proposes removing redundant tokens progressively, with the selection adapted to each input image.

Lightweight prediction modules estimate token importance from the current features at several layers. This allows pruning to happen hierarchically as representations develop. To train these decisions end to end, the authors use attention masking: a token is differentiably pruned by blocking its interactions with other tokens. The resulting irregular token sets remain compatible with efficient computation because of how self-attention operates.

Across the evaluated vision transformers, pruning 66% of input tokens reduces FLOPs by 31–37% and increases throughput by more than 40%, with an accuracy drop within 0.5%. These measurements matter together: the method delivers actual processing gains alongside reduced arithmetic work. ImageNet results show competitive accuracy-versus-complexity trade-offs against contemporary convolutional networks and vision transformers.
summary.tldr: DynamicViT progressively removes input-dependent redundant tokens, substantially accelerating tested vision transformers with a small accuracy drop.

title: DynamicViT: Efficient Vision Transformers with Dynamic Token Sparsification

abstract: A generic video summary is an abridged version of a video that conveys the whole story and features the most important scenes. Yet the importance of scenes in a video is often subjective, and users should have the option of customizing the summary by using natural language to specify what is important to them. Further, existing models for fully automatic generic summarization have not exploited available language models, which can serve as an effective prior for saliency. This work introduces CLIP-It, a single framework for addressing both generic and query-focused video summarization, typically approached separately in the literature. We propose a language-guided multimodal transformer that learns to score frames in a video based on their importance relative to one another and their correlation with a user-defined query (for query-focused summarization) or an automatically generated dense video caption (for generic video summarization). Our model can be extended to the unsupervised setting by training without ground-truth supervision. We outperform baselines and prior work by a significant margin on both standard video summarization datasets (TVSum and SumMe) and a query-focused video summarization dataset (QFVS). Particularly, we achieve large improvements in the transfer setting, attesting to our method's strong generalization capabilities.
