paragraphs: EVAAA is a three-dimensional environment for studying reinforcement learning agents whose behavior is driven by internal needs. Its motivation is that conventional environments often provide fixed tasks and externally specified goals, whereas biological agents must continuously adapt their behavior to remain viable under changing conditions.

Agents in EVAAA maintain internal variables such as satiation, hydration, body temperature, and tissue integrity within viable ranges. Rewards come from changes in these internal states, allowing goals to arise from the agent's condition without separately engineering a reward for each task. The environment becomes harder across training stages, connecting physiological regulation to increasingly demanding survival situations.

Built with Unity ML-Agents, the platform supports first-person embodiment and sensory inputs including vision, smell, temperature, and collisions. It combines environments for staged training with unseen test settings for evaluating adaptation. The contribution is a benchmark platform that brings internal regulation, embodiment, continual learning, and generalization into the same experimental setting, enabling study of how autonomous behavior emerges from internal needs and environmental constraints.
summary.tldr: EVAAA provides virtual survival environments where embodied agents learn from internal physiological needs and face unseen tests of adaptation.

title: EVAAA: A Virtual Environment Platform for Essential Variables in Autonomous and Adaptive Agents

abstract: Loss of plasticity (LoP) is the primary cause of cognitive decline in normal aging brains next to cell loss. Recent works show that similar LoP also plagues neural networks during deep continual learning (DCL). While it has been shown that random perturbations of learned weights can alleviate LoP, its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Here we offer a unique view of LoP and dissect its mechanisms through the lenses of an innovative framework combining the theory of neural collapse and finite-time Lyapunov exponents (FTLE) analysis. We show that LoP actually consists of two contrasting types: (i) type-1 LoP is characterized by highly negative FTLEs, where the network is prevented from learning due to the collapse of representations; (ii) while type-2 LoP is characterized by excessively positive FTLEs, where the network can train well but the growingly chaotic behaviors reduce its test accuracy. Based on these understandings, we introduce Generalized Mixup, designed to relax the representation space for prolonged DCL and demonstrate its superior efficacy vs. existing methods.

paragraphs: Neural networks can lose their ability to adapt during continual learning. Although random changes to learned weights can alleviate this loss of plasticity, its mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This paper develops an analysis combining neural collapse theory with finite-time Lyapunov exponents, using these tools to distinguish two contrasting forms of deterioration.

In type-1 loss of plasticity, strongly negative exponents accompany collapsed representations that prevent the network from learning effectively. Type-2 has excessively positive exponents: the network can still fit its training data, but increasingly chaotic behavior reduces test accuracy. The distinction matters because successful training performance can coexist with one form of declining adaptability.

Based on this account, the authors introduce Generalized Mixup to relax the representation space during prolonged continual learning. They report superior effectiveness compared with existing methods. The work therefore contributes both a diagnosis and a mitigation strategy: it separates a failure to learn from a failure to generalize associated with unstable behavior, then uses that understanding to guide changes to the learned representation space.
summary.tldr: The paper separates continual-learning plasticity loss into representation collapse and chaotic generalization failure, then introduces Generalized Mixup to mitigate it.

title: The Dual Nature of Plasticity Loss in Deep Continual Learning: Dissection and Mitigation

abstract: Sign Language Video Generation (SLVG) seeks to generate identity-preserving sign language videos from spoken language texts. Existing methods primarily rely on the single coarse condition (e.g., skeleton sequences) as the intermediary to bridge the translation model and the video generation model, which limits both the naturalness and expressiveness of the generated videos. To overcome these limitations, we propose SignViP, a novel SLVG framework that incorporate multiple fine-grained conditions for improved generation fidelity. Rather than directly translating error-prone high-dimensional conditions, SignViP adopts a discrete tokenization paradigm to integrate and represent fine-grained conditions (i.e., fine-grained poses and 3D hands). SignViP contains three core components. (1) Sign Video Diffusion Model is jointly trained with a multi-condition encoder to learn continuous embeddings that encapsulate fine-grained motion and appearance. (2) Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) Autoencoder is further trained to compress and quantize these embeddings into discrete tokens for compact representation of the conditions. (3) Multi-Condition Token Translator is trained to translate spoken language text to discrete multi-condition tokens. During inference, Multi-Condition Token Translator first translates the spoken language text into discrete multi-condition tokens. These tokens are then decoded to continuous embeddings by FSQ Autoencoder, which are subsequently injected into Sign Video Diffusion Model to guide video generation. Experimental results show that SignViP achieves state-of-the-art performance across metrics, including video quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. The code is available at https://github.com/umnooob/signvip/.

paragraphs: SignViP generates sign language videos from spoken-language text while aiming to preserve the signer’s identity. Existing approaches often connect text translation to video generation through a single coarse representation, such as a skeleton sequence. The paper instead uses detailed poses and three-dimensional hand information to provide richer guidance for natural and expressive signing.

The framework learns this guidance in stages. A video diffusion model and a multi-condition encoder first learn continuous representations of motion and appearance. An autoencoder then compresses these representations and converts them into discrete tokens using finite scalar quantization. A separate translator learns to predict those tokens from text. This makes the translation target compact rather than requiring direct prediction of high-dimensional conditions.

At generation time, the predicted tokens are decoded into continuous representations that guide the video diffusion model. Reported experiments show state-of-the-art performance across video quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. These findings support the proposed combination of detailed motion guidance and compact tokenization for producing videos that remain coherent over time and faithful to the intended signing content.
summary.tldr: SignViP translates text into compact tokens encoding detailed pose and hand information to guide higher-quality sign language video generation.

title: Advanced Sign Language Video Generation with Compressed and Quantized Multi-Condition Tokenization

abstract: From clinical healthcare to daily living, continuous sensor monitoring across multiple modalities has shown great promise for real-world intelligent decision-making but also faces various challenges. In this work, we argue for modeling such heterogeneous data sources under the multimodal paradigm and introduce a new framework, MAESTRO. We introduce MAESTRO, a novel framework that overcomes key limitations of existing multimodal learning approaches: (1) reliance on a single primary modality for alignment, (2) pairwise modeling of modalities, and (3) assumption of complete modality observations. These limitations hinder the applicability of these approaches in real-world multimodal time-series settings, where primary modality priors are often unclear, the number of modalities can be large (making pairwise modeling impractical), and sensor failures often result in arbitrary missing observations. At its core, MAESTRO facilitates dynamic intra- and cross-modal interactions based on task relevance, and leverages symbolic tokenization and adaptive attention budgeting to construct long multimodal sequences, which are processed via sparse cross-modal attention. The resulting cross-modal tokens are routed through a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism, enabling black-box specialization under varying modality combinations. We evaluate MAESTRO against 10 baselines on four diverse datasets spanning three applications, and observe average relative improvements of 4% and 8% over the best existing multimodal and multivariate approaches, respectively, under complete observations. Under partial observations—with up to 40% of missing modalities—MAESTRO achieves an average 9% improvement. Further analysis also demonstrates the robustness and efficiency of MAESTRO's sparse, modality-aware design for learning from dynamic time series.

paragraphs: MAESTRO addresses continuous monitoring with multiple types of sensors, where useful relationships change and some observations may be missing. The paper challenges approaches that require a designated primary modality, model every pair of modalities separately, or assume complete observations. These assumptions become restrictive when many sensors contribute and failures remove arbitrary inputs.

The framework forms long multimodal sequences using symbolic tokenization and allocates attention adaptively according to task relevance. Sparse cross-modal attention supports interactions within and between modalities. The resulting tokens then pass through a sparse mixture of experts, allowing specialized processing under different combinations of available modalities.

With complete observations, MAESTRO reports average relative improvements of 4% over the best multimodal approaches and 8% over the best multivariate approaches. With up to 40% of modalities missing, it reports an average improvement of 9%. Further analysis supports the robustness and efficiency of its sparse design, connecting flexible sensor interaction with practical handling of incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: MAESTRO uses adaptive sparse attention and expert routing to learn from changing combinations of sensor modalities, including missing observations.

title: MAESTRO : Adaptive Sparse Attention and Robust Learning for Multimodal Dynamic Time Series

abstract: The brain is made up of a vast set of heterogeneous regions that dynamically organize into pathways as a function of task demands. Examples of such pathways can be found in the interactions between cortical and subcortical networks during learning, or in sub-networks specializing for task characteristics such as difficulty or modality. Despite the large role these pathways play in cognition, the mechanisms through which brain regions organize into pathways remain unclear. In this work, we use an extension of the Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts architecture to show that heterogeneous regions do not form processing pathways by themselves, implying that the brain likely implements specific constraints which result in the reliable formation of pathways. We identify three biologically relevant inductive biases that encourage pathway formation: a routing cost imposed on the use of more complex regions, a scaling factor that reduces this cost when task performance is low, and randomized expert dropout. When comparing our resulting Mixture-of-Pathways model with the brain, we observe that the artificial pathways in our model match how the brain uses cortical and subcortical systems to learn and solve tasks of varying difficulty. In summary, we introduce a novel framework for investigating how the brain forms task-specific pathways through inductive biases, and the effects these biases have on the behavior of Mixture-of-Experts models.

paragraphs: Different brain regions cooperate in pathways that change with learning and task demands. This paper investigates how such organization might arise using a model containing heterogeneous experts: computational components with different capabilities. In the authors’ extended architecture, simply providing different kinds of experts does not by itself produce organized processing pathways.

The authors identify three biases that encourage pathways to form. Using more complex experts incurs a routing cost, but that cost is reduced when task performance is poor. Randomly dropping experts provides another constraint on how the system distributes computation. Together, these mechanisms shape when particular components are used and how they cooperate.

The resulting Mixture-of-Pathways model develops artificial pathways whose behavior resembles the use of cortical and subcortical systems during learning and across tasks of different difficulty. This correspondence motivates the suggestion that specific constraints may help the brain reliably organize pathways. The contribution is a modeling framework for investigating that possibility and for studying how these biases affect mixture-of-experts behavior.
summary.tldr: Costs, performance-sensitive routing, and expert dropout encourage heterogeneous experts to form pathways resembling patterns of brain organization.

title: Brain-Like Processing Pathways Form in Models With Heterogeneous Experts

abstract: Open-vocabulary learning requires modeling the data distribution in open environments, which consists of both seen-class and unseen-class data. Existing methods estimate the distribution in open environments using seen-class data, where the absence of unseen classes makes the estimation error inherently unidentifiable. Intuitively, learning beyond the seen classes is crucial for distribution estimation to bound the estimation error. We theoretically demonstrate that the distribution can be effectively estimated by generating unseen-class data, through which the estimation error is upper-bounded. Building on this theoretical insight, we propose a novel open-vocabulary learning method, which generates unseen-class data for estimating the distribution in open environments. The method consists of a class-domain-wise data generation pipeline and a distribution alignment algorithm. The data generation pipeline generates unseen-class data under the guidance of a hierarchical semantic tree and domain information inferred from the seen-class data, facilitating accurate distribution estimation. With the generated data, the distribution alignment algorithm estimates and maximizes the posterior probability to enhance generalization in open-vocabulary learning. Extensive experiments on 11 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches by up to 14%, highlighting its effectiveness and superiority.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary learning must handle categories absent from its observed training examples. Estimating the distribution of this broader environment using only familiar categories leaves a fundamental gap: the missing categories prevent the estimation error from being identified. This paper investigates whether generating examples of unseen categories can make that error more tractable.

The authors provide a theoretical argument that generating unseen-class data can enable distribution estimation with an upper bound on its error. Their method turns this insight into a data generation pipeline organized around both categories and domains. A hierarchical semantic tree guides which categories to generate, while information inferred from the observed data guides the domain characteristics of those examples.

A distribution alignment algorithm then uses the generated examples to estimate and maximize posterior probabilities, with the aim of improving generalization beyond observed categories. Experiments across 11 datasets report improvements over baseline approaches of up to 14%. This maximum reported gain supports the method's effectiveness in the evaluated settings; the theoretical contribution concerns bounding estimation error through inclusion of generated unseen-class data.
summary.tldr: Generating unseen-category examples enables bounded distribution estimation and improves open-vocabulary learning in experiments across 11 datasets.

title: Beyond the Seen: Bounded Distribution Estimation for Open-Vocabulary Learning

abstract: Chain of thought is a natural inference-time method for increasing the computational power of transformer-based large language models (LLMs), but comes at the cost of sequential decoding. Are there more efficient alternatives to expand a transformer's expressive power without adding parameters? We consider transformers with *padding* tokens as a form of parallelizable test-time compute. We show that averaging-hard-attention, masked-pre-norm transformers with polynomial padding recognize precisely the class $\mathsf{FO}$-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ of extremely parallelizable problems. While the $\mathsf{TC}^0$ upper bound was known, proving a matching lower bound had been elusive. Further, our novel analysis reveals the precise expanded power of padded transformers when coupled with another form of inference-time compute, namely dynamically increasing depth via *looping*. Our core technical contribution is to show how padding helps bring the notions of *complete problems* and *reductions*, which have been a cornerstone of classical complexity theory, to the formal study of transformers. Armed with this new tool, we prove that padded transformers with $\mathrm{O}(\log^d n)$ looping on inputs of length $n$ recognize exactly the class $\mathsf{FO}$-uniform $\mathsf{TC}^d$ of moderately parallelizable problems. Thus, padding and looping together systematically expand transformers' expressive power: with polylogarithmic looping, polynomially padded transformers recognize precisely the class $\mathsf{FO}$-uniform $\mathsf{NC}$, the best that could be expected without losing parallelism (unless $\mathsf{NC} = \mathsf{P}$). Our results thus motivate further exploration of padding and looping as parallelizable alternatives to chain of thought for test-time compute.

They motivate investigating padding and looping as parallelizable forms of test-time computation alongside sequential reasoning.
summary.tldr: The paper exactly characterizes how polynomial padding and inference-time looping expand the expressive power of a specified transformer architecture.

title: Exact Expressive Power of Transformers with Padding

abstract: Inspired by the workings of biological brains, humans have designed artificial neural networks (ANNs), sparking profound advancements across various fields. However, the biological brain possesses high plasticity, enabling it to develop simple, efficient, and powerful structures to cope with complex external environments. In contrast, the superior performance of ANNs often relies on meticulously crafted architectures, which can make them vulnerable when handling complex inputs. Moreover, overparameterization often characterizes the most advanced ANNs. This paper explores the path toward building streamlined and plastic ANNs. Firstly, we introduce the Graph Perceptron (GP), which extends the most fundamental ANN, the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Subsequently, we incorporate a self-assembly mechanism on top of GP called Self-Assembling Graph Perceptron (SAGP). During training, SAGP can autonomously adjust the network's number of neurons and synapses and their connectivity. SAGP achieves comparable or even superior performance with only about 5% of the size of an MLP. We also demonstrate the SAGP's advantages in enhancing model interpretability and feature selection.

paragraphs: This paper explores neural networks that can change their structure during training. Its motivation comes from biological plasticity and from the dependence of many artificial networks on carefully designed, often oversized architectures. The aim is to develop networks that remain capable while using a more streamlined and adaptable structure.

The authors first introduce the Graph Perceptron as an extension of the multilayer perceptron. They then add a self-assembly mechanism to create the Self-Assembling Graph Perceptron, or SAGP. During training, SAGP can adjust how many neurons and connections it contains, as well as how those components connect to one another.

The reported results show comparable or better performance using about 5% of the size of an MLP. The authors also demonstrate advantages for interpretability and feature selection. These findings support learning aspects of network structure alongside the training process, allowing model size and connectivity to adapt. The size comparison concerns the MLP comparison reported in the study; its significance is that substantial structural reduction can coexist with strong performance in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: SAGP adapts its neurons and connections during training, achieving comparable or better performance at about 5% of an MLP’s size.

title: Self-Assembling Graph Perceptrons

abstract: The steep computational cost of diffusion models at inference hinders their use as fast physics emulators. In the context of image and video generation, this computational drawback has been addressed by generating in the latent space of an autoencoder instead of the pixel space. In this work, we investigate whether a similar strategy can be effectively applied to the emulation of dynamical systems and at what cost. We find that the accuracy of latent-space emulation is surprisingly robust to a wide range of compression rates (up to 1000x). We also show that diffusion-based emulators are consistently more accurate than non-generative counterparts and compensate for uncertainty in their predictions with greater diversity. Finally, we cover practical design choices, spanning from architectures to optimizers, that we found critical to train latent-space emulators.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can emulate dynamical systems, but their inference cost makes fast physics emulation difficult. This paper investigates an approach already used in image and video generation: performing generation in an autoencoder’s compressed latent space. The central question is how well this compression preserves the accuracy needed for dynamical-system emulation.

The empirical study finds that emulation accuracy remains surprisingly robust across a broad range of compression rates, reaching up to 1,000 times compression. This suggests that, in the studied settings, a much smaller representation can still retain information useful for emulation. The compression figure describes representation compression, rather than a stated equivalent increase in runtime speed.

The authors also find diffusion-based emulators consistently more accurate than the non-generative alternatives they evaluate. When predictions are uncertain, the generative models compensate with greater diversity. Alongside these findings, the paper discusses architecture and optimizer choices that proved important for training latent-space emulators, connecting its empirical conclusions to practical decisions involved in constructing such systems.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds latent diffusion physics emulators retain accuracy across compression rates up to 1,000 times and outperform evaluated non-generative alternatives.

title: Lost in Latent Space: An Empirical Study of Latent Diffusion Models for Physics Emulation

abstract: Modern machine learning models struggle to maintain performance in dynamic environments where temporal distribution shifts, \textit{i.e., concept drift}, are prevalent. Temporal Domain Generalization (TDG) seeks to enable model generalization across evolving domains, yet existing approaches typically assume smooth incremental changes, struggling with complex real-world drifts involving both long-term structure (incremental evolution/periodicity) and local uncertainties. To overcome these limitations, we introduce FreKoo, which tackles these challenges through a novel frequency-domain analysis of parameter trajectories. It leverages the Fourier transform to disentangle parameter evolution into distinct spectral bands. Specifically, the low-frequency components with dominant dynamics are learned and extrapolated using the Koopman operator, robustly capturing diverse drift patterns including both incremental and periodic drifts. Simultaneously, potentially disruptive high-frequency variations are smoothed via targeted temporal regularization, preventing overfitting to transient noise and domain uncertainties. In addition, this dual-spectral strategy is rigorously grounded through theoretical analysis, providing stability guarantees for the Koopman prediction, a principled Bayesian justification for the high-frequency regularization, and culminating in a multiscale generalization bound connecting spectral dynamics to improved generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate FreKoo's significant superiority over state-of-the-art TDG methods, particularly excelling in real-world streaming scenarios with complex drifts and uncertainties.

paragraphs: FreKoo addresses prediction when data distributions evolve over time. Such changes can combine gradual trends, recurring patterns, and short-lived uncertainty. The paper argues that approaches built around smooth incremental change struggle with this mixture, and instead studies the evolution of model parameters through their frequency components.

A Fourier transform separates parameter trajectories into spectral bands. FreKoo learns and extrapolates dominant low-frequency dynamics with a Koopman operator, aiming to capture both incremental and periodic drift. It handles potentially disruptive high-frequency variations through targeted temporal regularization. This gives persistent structure and transient fluctuations different treatment within one approach.

Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art temporal domain generalization methods, particularly on real-world streams with complex drift and uncertainty. The results support separating predictable evolution from rapid variation when preparing models for future domains, rather than relying only on smooth-change assumptions.
summary.tldr: FreKoo predicts persistent parameter dynamics in the frequency domain while regularizing rapid fluctuations to improve generalization under temporal drift.

title: Learning Robust Spectral Dynamics for Temporal Domain Generalization

abstract: Linear classiffers are much faster to learn and test than non-linear ones. On the other hand, non-linear kernels offer improved performance, albeit at the increased cost of training kernel classiffers. To use non-linear mappings with efficient linear learning algorithms, explicit embeddings that approximate popular kernels have recently been proposed. However, the embedding process itself is often costly and the results are usually less accurate than kernel methods. In this work we propose a non-linear feature map that is both very efficient, but at the same time highly expressive. The method is based on discretization and interpolation of individual features values and feature pairs. The discretization allows us to model different regions of the feature space separately, while the interpolation preserves the original continuous values. Using this embedding is strictly more general than a linear model and as efficient as the second-order polynomial explicit feature map. An extensive empirical evaluation shows that our method consistently signiffcantly outperforms other methods, including a wide range of kernels. This is in contrast to other proposed embeddings that were faster than kernel methods, but with lower accuracy.
originalAbstract: Linear classiffers are much faster to learn and test than non-linear ones. On the other hand, non-linear kernels offer improved performance, albeit at the increased cost of training kernel classiffers. To use non-linear mappings with efficient linear learning algorithms, explicit embeddings that approximate popular kernels have recently been proposed. However, the embedding process itself is often costly and the results are usually less accurate than kernel methods. In this work we propose a non-linear feature map that is both very efficient, but at the same time highly expressive. The method is based on discretization and interpolation of individual features values and feature pairs. The discretization allows us to model different regions of the feature space separately, while the interpolation preserves the original continuous values. Using this embedding is strictly more general than a linear model and as efficient as the second-order polynomial explicit feature map. An extensive empirical evaluation shows that our method consistently signiffcantly outperforms other methods, including a wide range of kernels. This is in contrast to other proposed embeddings that were faster than kernel methods, but with lower accuracy.

Explicit feature embeddings offer a way to combine nonlinear representations with linear learning, but their construction can be expensive and their accuracy can fall below kernel methods. This paper proposes a different nonlinear feature map.

The map discretizes and interpolates individual feature values and pairs of features. Discretization lets different regions of feature space be modeled separately, while interpolation preserves the original continuous values. The resulting representation is strictly more general than a linear model and is reported to be as efficient as an explicit second-order polynomial feature map.

An extensive empirical evaluation finds that the method consistently and significantly outperforms the compared alternatives, including a broad range of kernels. The contribution is an expressive feature representation with efficient computation, supported by strong results in the evaluated settings. Its regional modeling and treatment of feature pairs provide the mechanism for using nonlinear structure with linear learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: A feature map based on discretization and interpolation combines efficient linear learning with strong nonlinear classification results.

title: The Pairwise Piecewise-Linear Embedding for Efficient Non-Linear Classification

abstract: In this paper we address the widely-experienced difficulty in tuning Hamiltonian-based Monte Carlo samplers. We develop an algorithm that allows for the adaptation of Hamiltonian and Riemann manifold Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samplers using Bayesian optimization that allows for infinite adaptation of the parameters of these samplers. We show that the resulting sampling algorithms are ergodic, and demonstrate on several models and data sets that the use of our adaptive algorithms makes it is easy to obtain more efficient samplers, in some precluding the need for more complex models. Hamiltonian-based Monte Carlo samplers are widely known to be an excellent choice of MCMC method, and we aim with this paper to remove a key obstacle towards the more widespread use of these samplers in practice.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods can be effective sampling tools, but their practical performance depends on tuning their parameters. This paper addresses that tuning burden for both ordinary Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and its Riemann manifold version. Its goal is to make efficient sampling easier to obtain without requiring the user to manage the tuning process manually.

The proposed algorithm uses Bayesian optimization to adapt sampler parameters. A central feature is that adaptation can continue indefinitely. The authors show that the resulting sampling algorithms are ergodic, providing a theoretical foundation for continuing to adjust parameters while sampling. This connects automated tuning to a property needed for the sampler's long-run statistical behavior.

Experiments across several models and datasets demonstrate improved sampling efficiency with the adaptive methods. In some cases, the improvement also removes the need for more complex models. The contribution combines a practical parameter-selection procedure with an ergodicity result, addressing an obstacle to wider use of Hamiltonian sampling.
summary.tldr: Bayesian optimization automates ongoing tuning of Hamiltonian samplers while preserving ergodicity and improving efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Adaptive Hamiltonian and Riemann Manifold Monte Carlo

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of differentially private risk minimization where the goal is to provide differentially private algorithms that have small excess risk. In particular we address the following open problem: \emphIs it possible to design computationally efficient differentially private risk minimizers with excess risk bounds that do not explicitly depend on dimensionality (p) and do not require structural assumptions like restricted strong convexity? In this paper, we answer the question in the affirmative for a variant of the well-known \emphoutput and \emphobjective perturbation algorithms [Chaudhuri et al., 2011]. In particular, we show that in generalized linear model, variants of both output and objective perturbation algorithms have no \em explicit dependence on p. Our results assume that the underlying loss function is a 1-Lipschitz convex function and we show that the excess risk depends only on L_2 norm of the true risk minimizer and that of training points. Next, we present a novel privacy preserving algorithm for risk minimization over simplex in the generalized linear model, where the loss function is a doubly differentiable convex function. Assuming that the training points have bounded L_∞-norm, our algorithm provides risk bound that has only \em logarithmic dependence on p. We also apply our technique to the online learning setting and obtain a regret bound with similar logarithmic dependence on p. In contrast, the existing differentially private online learning methods incur O(\sqrtp) dependence.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning seeks useful predictors while protecting information about individual training examples. This paper asks whether computationally efficient private risk minimization can avoid an explicit dependence on the number of input dimensions without requiring structural conditions such as restricted strong convexity. It gives affirmative results for particular generalized linear model settings.

For variants of output and objective perturbation, the authors establish excess risk bounds with no explicit dimension term. These results assume a convex, 1-Lipschitz loss. The bounds depend instead on the L2 norms of the true risk minimizer and training points, identifying the quantities that control the guarantee.

The paper also develops a private algorithm for optimization over the simplex with a twice-differentiable convex loss. When training points have bounded L-infinity norm, its risk bound depends only logarithmically on dimension. An online extension obtains a similarly logarithmic dimension dependence in regret, compared with the square-root dependence reported for existing private online methods. These are distinct conditional guarantees showing that ambient dimension need not enter privacy-related error bounds as strongly as before.
summary.tldr: Under specified loss and norm assumptions, private generalized linear learning admits risk bounds with no explicit or only logarithmic dimension dependence.

title: (Near) Dimension Independent Risk Bounds for Differentially Private Learning

abstract: The problem of change point estimation is considered in a general framework where the data are generated by arbitrary unknown stationary ergodic process distributions. This means that the data may have long-range dependencies of an arbitrary form. In this context the consistent estimation of the number of change points is provably impossible. A formulation is proposed which overcomes this obstacle: it is possible to find the correct number of change points at the expense of introducing the additional constraint that the correct number of process distributions that generate the data is provided. This additional parameter has a natural interpretation in many real-world applications. It turns out that in this formulation change point estimation can be reduced to time series clustering. Based on this reduction, an algorithm is proposed that finds the number of change points and locates the changes. This algorithm is shown to be asymptotically consistent. The theoretical results are complemented with empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify changes in time series whose observations may have arbitrary long-range dependencies. The generating distributions are unknown stationary ergodic processes, a broad setting that permits substantial dependence over time. In this framework, consistently estimating the number of change points is provably impossible without additional information.

The authors overcome that obstacle by supplying the algorithm with the correct number of distinct process distributions generating the data. This is different from supplying the number of changes: the same distribution can be relevant to multiple portions of a sequence. The extra information constrains how many underlying sources must be distinguished while leaving the changes themselves to be discovered.

Under this formulation, the paper reduces change point estimation to time series clustering. Its algorithm both counts the changes and estimates their locations, with a proof of asymptotic consistency. Empirical evaluations complement the theory. The result shows how a specific piece of prior information can make reliable estimation possible in a dependence setting where the original problem cannot be solved consistently.
summary.tldr: Knowing the number of generating process distributions enables consistent change point estimation for highly dependent time series.

title: Asymptotically consistent estimation of the number of change points in highly dependent time series

abstract: We consider LSTD(λ), the least-squares temporal-difference algorithm with eligibility traces algorithm proposed by Boyan (2002). It computes a linear approximation of the value function of a fixed policy in a large Markov Decision Process. Under a β-mixing assumption, we derive, for any value of λ∈(0,1), a high-probability bound on the rate of convergence of this algorithm to its limit. We deduce a high-probability bound on the error of this algorithm, that extends (and slightly improves) that derived by Lazaric et al. (2012) in the specific case where λ=0. In the context of temporal-difference algorithms with value function approximation, this analysis is to our knowledge the first to provide insight on the choice of the eligibility-trace parameter λwith respect to the approximation quality of the space and the number of samples.

paragraphs: LSTD(λ) estimates the value function of a fixed policy using a linear approximation in a large Markov decision process. Its eligibility-trace parameter λ affects how information is used during estimation. This paper analyzes how quickly the algorithm approaches its limit and how much error remains in its value estimate.

Under a β-mixing assumption, which controls temporal dependence in the data, the authors derive a high-probability convergence-rate bound for every λ strictly between zero and one. They then obtain a high-probability error bound. This extends and slightly improves an earlier result that addressed the special case λ equals zero.

The analysis also provides insight into choosing λ in relation to the quality of the available approximation space and the number of samples. This connects a tuning parameter to both representation and data availability. The contribution is consequently more than a convergence statement: it helps explain how those ingredients enter value estimation together. The guarantees remain tied to the stated mixing assumption and are probabilistic rather than unconditional.
summary.tldr: High-probability bounds for LSTD(λ) connect convergence and estimation error to eligibility traces, approximation quality, and sample size.

title: On the Rate of Convergence and Error Bounds for LSTD(λ)

abstract: We present Deep Voice, a production-quality text-to-speech system constructed entirely from deep neural networks. Deep Voice lays the groundwork for truly end-to-end neural speech synthesis. The system comprises five major building blocks: a segmentation model for locating phoneme boundaries, a grapheme-to-phoneme conversion model, a phoneme duration prediction model, a fundamental frequency prediction model, and an audio synthesis model. For the segmentation model, we propose a novel way of performing phoneme boundary detection with deep neural networks using connectionist temporal classification (CTC) loss. For the audio synthesis model, we implement a variant of WaveNet that requires fewer parameters and trains faster than the original. By using a neural network for each component, our system is simpler and more flexible than traditional text-to-speech systems, where each component requires laborious feature engineering and extensive domain expertise. Finally, we show that inference with our system can be performed faster than real time and describe optimized WaveNet inference kernels on both CPU and GPU that achieve up to 400x speedups over existing implementations.

paragraphs: Deep Voice is presented as a production-quality text-to-speech system whose components are all deep neural networks. It includes models for phoneme segmentation, text-to-phoneme conversion, phoneme duration, fundamental frequency, and audio synthesis. Replacing each component with a neural model reduces reliance on the extensive feature engineering and domain expertise associated with traditional systems.

Two technical contributions address segmentation and sound generation. The segmentation model detects phoneme boundaries using connectionist temporal classification loss. For audio synthesis, the system uses a WaveNet variant with fewer parameters and faster training than the original. These changes support a neural speech pipeline spanning linguistic processing through waveform generation.

The authors demonstrate inference faster than real time and describe optimized WaveNet inference kernels for both CPUs and GPUs. Those kernels achieve speedups of up to 400 times over existing implementations. The upper-bound wording matters: it is the reported maximum speedup. The system establishes groundwork for fully end-to-end neural speech synthesis while demonstrating a practical pipeline built entirely from neural components.
summary.tldr: Deep Voice builds every text-to-speech component with neural networks and demonstrates faster-than-real-time synthesis with optimized inference.

title: Deep Voice: Real-time Neural Text-to-Speech

abstract: We present a reinforcement learning framework, called Programmatically Interpretable Reinforcement Learning (PIRL), that is designed to generate interpretable and verifiable agent policies. Unlike the popular Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) paradigm, which represents policies by neural networks, PIRL represents policies using a high-level, domain-specific programming language. Such programmatic policies have the benefits of being more easily interpreted than neural networks, and being amenable to verification by symbolic methods. We propose a new method, called Neurally Directed Program Search (NDPS), for solving the challenging nonsmooth optimization problem of finding a programmatic policy with maximal reward. NDPS works by first learning a neural policy network using DRL, and then performing a local search over programmatic policies that seeks to minimize a distance from this neural “oracle”. We evaluate NDPS on the task of learning to drive a simulated car in the TORCS car-racing environment. We demonstrate that NDPS is able to discover human-readable policies that pass some significant performance bars. We also show that PIRL policies can have smoother trajectories, and can be more easily transferred to environments not encountered during training, than corresponding policies discovered by DRL.

paragraphs: Programmatically Interpretable Reinforcement Learning represents an agent’s policy as a program in a high-level, domain-specific language. The aim is to produce behavior that people can inspect and that symbolic methods can potentially verify. This choice makes the policy’s representation central to both interpretability and the process of learning it.

Finding a high-reward program is a challenging nonsmooth optimization problem. The proposed Neurally Directed Program Search first trains a neural policy with deep reinforcement learning. It then searches locally among programmatic policies, seeking programs close to that neural policy. The trained network serves as an oracle that guides the search through possible programs.

In the TORCS simulated car-racing environment, the method discovers human-readable policies that meet significant performance requirements. The authors also show that these policies can produce smoother trajectories and transfer more easily to previously unseen environments than corresponding deep reinforcement-learning policies. These results demonstrate useful programmatic behavior while retaining the qualified nature of the smoothness and transfer advantages.
summary.tldr: PIRL uses a trained neural policy to guide the search for readable program policies, demonstrated in simulated driving.

title: Programmatically Interpretable Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce an off-policy evaluation procedure for highlighting episodes where applying a reinforcement learned (RL) policy is likely to have produced a substantially different outcome than the observed policy. In particular, we introduce a class of structural causal models (SCMs) for generating counterfactual trajectories in finite partially observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). We see this as a useful procedure for off-policy “debugging” in high-risk settings (e.g., healthcare); by decomposing the expected difference in reward between the RL and observed policy into specific episodes, we can identify episodes where the counterfactual difference in reward is most dramatic. This in turn can be used to facilitate review of specific episodes by domain experts. We demonstrate the utility of this procedure with a synthetic environment of sepsis management.

paragraphs: This paper makes policy evaluation useful for inspecting individual episodes. Instead of only summarizing how a learned policy might perform overall, the procedure highlights observed episodes for which using that policy would likely have produced a substantially different outcome. This provides a way to focus expert attention on consequential differences between policies.

The authors introduce structural causal models for generating counterfactual trajectories in finite, partially observable decision processes. These trajectories represent how an episode might have unfolded under another policy. The procedure decomposes the expected reward difference between the learned policy and the observed policy into contributions associated with specific episodes.

Episodes with especially dramatic estimated differences can then be reviewed by domain experts. The authors frame this as off-policy debugging for high-risk settings, including healthcare, and demonstrate its utility in a synthetic sepsis-management environment. The demonstration supports a targeted review workflow: counterfactual evaluation identifies cases worth examining, with the reported evidence coming from a synthetic environment.
summary.tldr: A counterfactual policy-evaluation procedure identifies episodes where a learned policy would likely change outcomes substantially, helping experts target their review.

title: Counterfactual Off-Policy Evaluation with Gumbel-Max Structural Causal Models

abstract: An important property for lifelong-learning agents is the ability to combine existing skills to solve new unseen tasks. In general, however, it is unclear how to compose existing skills in a principled manner. Under the assumption of deterministic dynamics, we prove that optimal value function composition can be achieved in entropy-regularised reinforcement learning (RL), and extend this result to the standard RL setting. Composition is demonstrated in a high-dimensional video game, where an agent with an existing library of skills is immediately able to solve new tasks without the need for further learning.

Under the assumption of deterministic dynamics, we prove that optimal value function composition can be achieved in entropy-regularised reinforcement learning (RL), and extend this result to the standard RL setting. Composition is demonstrated in a high-dimensional video game, where an agent with an existing library of skills is immediately able to solve new tasks without the need for further learning.

paragraphs: An agent that learns over its lifetime should be able to reuse existing skills when a new task appears. This paper asks how to combine those skills in a principled way. Its focus is value functions, which express the value of behavior in a task and provide a basis for composing previously learned capabilities.

Under the assumption of deterministic dynamics, the authors prove that optimal value functions can be composed in entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. They also extend the result to standard reinforcement learning. The deterministic-dynamics assumption is part of the theoretical claim: the abstract does not establish the same result for environments whose transitions are inherently random.

The authors demonstrate composition in a high-dimensional video game. An agent equipped with a library of skills solves new tasks immediately, without further learning. This connects the mathematical result to a concrete example of skill reuse: learning the component skills in advance can enable new behavior through composition when the task and environment support it.
summary.tldr: Under deterministic dynamics, composing optimal value functions enables principled skill reuse, demonstrated on new video-game tasks without further learning.

title: Composing Value Functions in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We revisit the optimization from samples (OPS) model, which studies the problem of optimizing objective functions directly from the sample data. Previous results showed that we cannot obtain a constant approximation ratio for the maximum coverage problem using polynomially many independent samples of the form $\{S_i, f(S_i)\}_{i=1}^t$ (Balkanski et al., 2017), even if coverage functions are $(1 - \epsilon)$-PMAC learnable using these samples (Badanidiyuru et al., 2012), which means most of the function values can be approximately learned very well with high probability. In this work, to circumvent the impossibility result of OPS, we propose a stronger model called optimization from structured samples (OPSS) for coverage functions, where the data samples encode the structural information of the functions. We show that under three general assumptions on the sample distributions, we can design efficient OPSS algorithms that achieve a constant approximation for the maximum coverage problem. We further prove a constant lower bound under these assumptions, which is tight when not considering computational efficiency. Moreover, we also show that if we remove any one of the three assumptions, OPSS for the maximum coverage problem has no constant approximation.

Previous results showed that we cannot obtain a constant approximation ratio for the maximum coverage problem using polynomially many independent samples of the form $\{S_i, f(S_i)\}_{i=1}^t$ (Balkanski et al., 2017), even if coverage functions are $(1 - \epsilon)$-PMAC learnable using these samples (Badanidiyuru et al., 2012), which means most of the function values can be approximately learned very well with high probability. We show that under three general assumptions on the sample distributions, we can design efficient OPSS algorithms that achieve a constant approximation for the maximum coverage problem. We further prove a constant lower bound under these assumptions, which is tight when not considering computational efficiency. Moreover, we also show that if we remove any one of the three assumptions, OPSS for the maximum coverage problem has no constant approximation.

paragraphs: Learning a function’s values accurately does not necessarily provide enough information to optimize it. For maximum coverage, earlier results ruled out constant-factor approximation from polynomially many independent samples containing only a set and its value. This difficulty can remain even when most function values can be approximately learned with high probability.

The paper proposes optimization from structured samples, a stronger model in which observations also reveal structural information about the coverage function. Under three assumptions on the sampling distributions, the authors construct efficient algorithms that achieve constant-factor approximations. The change in what the samples reveal makes a provable optimization guarantee possible.

The authors also establish a constant lower bound that is tight when computational efficiency is set aside. Removing any one of the three distributional assumptions eliminates the constant-approximation guarantee in this model. These results identify both the value and the limits of structured observations: useful optimization depends on the information samples contain and on the conditions governing how those samples are obtained.
summary.tldr: Structural information in samples enables constant-factor maximum-coverage approximation under three assumptions that are essential to the stated guarantee.

title: Optimization from Structured Samples for Coverage Functions

abstract: Exploration is widely regarded as one of the most challenging aspects of reinforcement learning (RL), with many naive approaches succumbing to exponential sample complexity. To isolate the challenges of exploration, we propose the following “reward-free RL” framework. In the exploration phase, the agent first collects trajectories from an MDP $M$ without a pre-specified reward function. After exploration, it is tasked with computing a near-policies under the transitions of $\mathcal{M}$ for a collection of given reward functions. This framework is particularly suitable where there are many reward functions of interest, or where the reward function is shaped by an external agent to elicit desired behavior. We give an efficient algorithm that conducts $\widetilde{O}(S^2A\mathrm{poly}(H)/\epsilon^2)$ episodes of exploration, and returns $\epsilon$-suboptimal policies for an arbitrary number of reward functions. We achieve this by finding exploratory policies that jointly visit each “significant” state with probability proportional to its maximum visitation probability under any possible policy. Moreover, our planning procedure can be instantiated by any black-box approximate planner, such as value iteration or natural policy gradient. Finally, we give a nearly-matching $\Omega(S^2AH^2/\epsilon^2)$ lower bound, demonstrating the near-optimality of our algorithm in this setting.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates learning about an environment from choosing what to achieve in it. During exploration, the agent collects trajectories without a predetermined reward function. Afterwards, it uses that experience to compute policies for supplied rewards. This is useful when many objectives matter or another agent later specifies the desired behavior.

The algorithm finds exploratory policies that collectively visit each significant state with probability proportional to the greatest visitation probability achievable by any policy. This organizes exploration around which states can meaningfully be reached. The subsequent planning step can use a black-box approximate planner, including value iteration or natural policy gradient.

The authors guarantee epsilon-suboptimal policies for arbitrarily many reward functions after an exploration budget scaling as S squared times A times a polynomial in H, divided by epsilon squared, up to logarithmic factors. Here S counts states, A actions, and H the horizon. A nearly matching lower bound establishes near-optimality in this setting, although the stated upper and lower bounds do not specify identical horizon dependence.
summary.tldr: Reward-free exploration gathers reusable experience for many later reward functions with a provably near-optimal exploration budget.

title: Reward-Free Exploration for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The input to the \emph{sets-$k$-means} problem is an integer $k\geq 1$ and a set $\mathcal{P}=\{P_1,\cdots,P_n\}$ of fixed sized sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The goal is to compute a set $C$ of $k$ centers (points) in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that minimizes the sum $\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}} \min_{p\in P, c\in C}\left\|{p}-c \right\|^2$ of squared distances to these sets. An \emph{$\varepsilon$-core-set} for this problem is a weighted subset of $\mathcal{P}$ that approximates this sum up to $1\pm\varepsilon$ factor, for \emph{every} set $C$ of $k$ centers in $\mathbb{R}^d$. We prove that such a core-set of $O(\log^2{n})$ sets always exists, and can be computed in $O(n\log{n})$ time, for every input $\mathcal{P}$ and every fixed $d,k\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The result easily generalized for any metric space, distances to the power of $z>0$, and M-estimators that handle outliers. Applying an inefficient but optimal algorithm on this coreset allows us to obtain the first PTAS ($1+\varepsilon$ approximation) for the sets-$k$-means problem that takes time near linear in $n$. This is the first result even for sets-mean on the plane ($k=1$, $d=2$). Open source code and experimental results for document classification and facility locations are also provided.
originalAbstract: The input to the \emph{sets-$k$-means} problem is an integer $k\geq 1$ and a set $\mathcal{P}=\{P_1,\cdots,P_n\}$ of fixed sized sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The goal is to compute a set $C$ of $k$ centers (points) in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that minimizes the sum $\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}} \min_{p\in P, c\in C}\left\|{p}-c \right\|^2$ of squared distances to these sets. An \emph{$\varepsilon$-core-set} for this problem is a weighted subset of $\mathcal{P}$ that approximates this sum up to $1\pm\varepsilon$ factor, for \emph{every} set $C$ of $k$ centers in $\mathbb{R}^d$. We prove that such a core-set of $O(\log^2{n})$ sets always exists, and can be computed in $O(n\log{n})$ time, for every input $\mathcal{P}$ and every fixed $d,k\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The result easily generalized for any metric space, distances to the power of $z>0$, and M-estimators that handle outliers. Applying an inefficient but optimal algorithm on this coreset allows us to obtain the first PTAS ($1+\varepsilon$ approximation) for the sets-$k$-means problem that takes time near linear in $n$. This is the first result even for sets-mean on the plane ($k=1$, $d=2$). Open source code and experimental results for document classification and facility locations are also provided.

paragraphs: Sets-k-means clusters a collection whose individual objects are fixed-size sets of points. For each input set, its cost is the smallest squared distance between any point in that set and any chosen center. The objective sums these costs, so each set contributes through its closest point-center pair.

The authors construct a small weighted subset, called a coreset, that approximates this objective for every possible choice of k centers. For fixed dimension, center count, and approximation tolerance, its size grows as the square of the logarithm of the number of input sets. Construction takes time proportional to n log n.

An expensive optimal algorithm can then run on the small coreset, yielding a near-linear-time approximation scheme for the full problem. The results extend to general metric spaces, positive powers of distance, and outlier-handling M-estimators. Experiments and open-source code cover document classification and facility location, complementing the central guarantee that one compact summary preserves all candidate clustering costs.
summary.tldr: Small coresets preserve sets-k-means costs for every center choice and enable a near-linear-time approximation scheme for fixed parameters.

title: Sets Clustering

abstract: To acquire a new skill, humans learn better and faster if a tutor, based on their current knowledge level, informs them of how much attention they should pay to particular content or practice problems. Similarly, a machine learning model could potentially be trained better with a scorer that “adapts” to its current learning state and estimates the importance of each training data instance. Training such an adaptive scorer efficiently is a challenging problem; in order to precisely quantify the effect of a data instance at a given time during the training, it is typically necessary to first complete the entire training process. To efficiently optimize data usage, we propose a reinforcement learning approach called Differentiable Data Selection (DDS). In DDS, we formulate a scorer network as a learnable function of the training data, which can be efficiently updated along with the main model being trained. Specifically, DDS updates the scorer with an intuitive reward signal: it should up-weigh the data that has a similar gradient with a dev set upon which we would finally like to perform well. Without significant computing overhead, DDS delivers strong and consistent improvements over several strong baselines on two very different tasks of machine translation and image classification.

paragraphs: A training example's usefulness can depend on what a model has already learned. This paper studies how to adapt the attention given to training data as learning progresses. Precisely measuring an example's eventual effect would typically require completing training first, making direct evaluation expensive when the scoring system must change alongside the model.

Differentiable Data Selection, or DDS, addresses this with a reinforcement learning approach that trains a scorer network together with the main model. Its reward favors examples whose gradients resemble gradients from a development set where good performance is desired. In plain terms, it increases the weight of training data that suggests parameter updates similar to those suggested by that development set.

Experiments on machine translation and image classification show strong, consistent improvements over several strong baselines without significant computing overhead. The findings support gradient similarity as a useful signal for adapting data usage during training. The development set has a central role: it supplies the reference for deciding which training examples deserve greater emphasis.
summary.tldr: DDS learns to weight training examples using gradient similarity with a development set, improving data usage during training.

title: Optimizing Data Usage via Differentiable Rewards

abstract: This work addresses the problem of optimizing communications between server and clients in federated learning (FL). Current sampling approaches in FL are either biased, or non optimal in terms of server-clients communications and training stability. To overcome this issue, we introduce clustered sampling for clients selection. We prove that clustered sampling leads to better clients representatitivity and to reduced variance of the clients stochastic aggregation weights in FL. Compatibly with our theory, we provide two different clustering approaches enabling clients aggregation based on 1) sample size, and 2) models similarity. Through a series of experiments in non-iid and unbalanced scenarios, we demonstrate that model aggregation through clustered sampling consistently leads to better training convergence and variability when compared to standard sampling approaches. Our approach does not require any additional operation on the clients side, and can be seamlessly integrated in standard FL implementations. Finally, clustered sampling is compatible with existing methods and technologies for privacy enhancement, and for communication reduction through model compression.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from multiple clients, making client selection important for both communication and training behavior. If the selected clients represent the population unevenly, their contributions can fluctuate in ways that affect aggregation. This paper proposes clustered sampling as a way to improve which clients participate in that process.

The authors prove that their sampling approach improves client representativity and reduces the variance of the random aggregation weights assigned to clients. They provide two clustering approaches consistent with the theory: one uses client sample sizes, while the other uses similarity between client models. These give different ways to organize selection around information relevant to aggregation.

Experiments with uneven client data sizes and differing data distributions show consistently improved convergence and training variability compared with standard sampling methods. The method requires no additional operations on clients and can fit into standard federated-learning implementations. It is also compatible with existing privacy-enhancement and model-compression approaches, making the selection mechanism usable alongside other communication and privacy measures.
summary.tldr: Clustered client sampling improves representation and reduces aggregation-weight variance, yielding more stable federated-learning training in the evaluated settings.

title: Clustered Sampling: Low-Variance and Improved Representativity for Clients Selection in Federated Learning

abstract: Active search is a learning paradigm where we seek to identify as many members of a rare, valuable class as possible given a labeling budget. Previous work on active search has assumed access to a faithful (and expensive) oracle reporting experimental results. However, some settings offer access to cheaper surrogates such as computational simulation that may aid in the search. We propose a model of multifidelity active search, as well as a novel, computationally efficient policy for this setting that is motivated by state-of-the-art classical policies. Our policy is nonmyopic and budget aware, allowing for a dynamic tradeoff between exploration and exploitation. We evaluate the performance of our solution on real-world datasets and demonstrate significantly better performance than natural benchmarks.

paragraphs: Active search aims to find as many rare, valuable examples as possible before a labeling budget runs out. Earlier work assumes access to an accurate but expensive source of experimental results. This paper considers settings where cheaper sources, such as computational simulations, can also provide information that helps guide the search.

The authors formulate multifidelity active search and develop a computationally efficient policy for choosing how to proceed. The policy is nonmyopic, meaning it considers the value of information for later decisions, and explicitly accounts for the remaining budget. These features allow the balance between exploration and exploitation to change as the search progresses.

The approach is evaluated on real-world datasets and performs significantly better than natural benchmarks. The result supports combining different information sources within a single budget-aware search strategy. Its central contribution is a way to decide how cheaper surrogate information can aid the continuing effort to discover valuable members of the target class.
summary.tldr: A budget-aware, forward-looking search policy uses cheaper surrogate information to improve the discovery of rare valuable examples.

title: Nonmyopic Multifidelity Acitve Search

abstract: Performing reliable Bayesian inference on a big data scale is becoming a keystone in the modern era of machine learning. A workhorse class of methods to achieve this task are Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms and their design to handle distributed datasets has been the subject of many works. However, existing methods are not completely either reliable or computationally efficient. In this paper, we propose to fill this gap in the case where the dataset is partitioned and stored on computing nodes within a cluster under a master/slaves architecture. We derive a user-friendly centralised distributed MCMC algorithm with provable scaling in high-dimensional settings. We illustrate the relevance of the proposed methodology on both synthetic and real data experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference on large datasets needs methods that are both computationally manageable and reliable. Markov chain Monte Carlo provides a major family of methods for this purpose, but distributing the computation creates additional design challenges. This paper addresses the tension between inference reliability and computational efficiency when data are stored across a cluster.

The setting is specific: the dataset is partitioned among computing nodes, and a central coordinating node manages the workers. DG-LMC is a synchronous, centralized distributed MCMC algorithm. As its title indicates, it combines Langevin Monte Carlo with a Gibbs structure, placing the sampling method within this coordinated computing arrangement.

The authors derive provable scaling results for high-dimensional settings and illustrate the method on synthetic and real datasets. The theoretical contribution concerns how the algorithm scales, while the experiments demonstrate its relevance in concrete inference problems. The stated architecture matters to interpreting the work: its contribution addresses distributed data under central coordination, where the organization of computation is part of the method's design.
summary.tldr: DG-LMC provides a centrally coordinated distributed MCMC method with provable high-dimensional scaling for data partitioned across computing nodes.

title: DG-LMC: A Turn-key and Scalable Synchronous Distributed MCMC Algorithm via Langevin Monte Carlo within Gibbs

abstract: We show that learning can be improved by using loss functions that evolve cyclically during training to emphasize one class at a time. In underparameterized networks, such dynamical loss functions can lead to successful training for networks that fail to find deep minima of the standard cross-entropy loss. In overparameterized networks, dynamical loss functions can lead to better generalization. Improvement arises from the interplay of the changing loss landscape with the dynamics of the system as it evolves to minimize the loss. In particular, as the loss function oscillates, instabilities develop in the form of bifurcation cascades, which we study using the Hessian and Neural Tangent Kernel. Valleys in the landscape widen and deepen, and then narrow and rise as the loss landscape changes during a cycle. As the landscape narrows, the learning rate becomes too large and the network becomes unstable and bounces around the valley. This process ultimately pushes the system into deeper and wider regions of the loss landscape and is characterized by decreasing eigenvalues of the Hessian. This results in better regularized models with improved generalization performance.

paragraphs: This paper changes the training objective over time by cyclically emphasizing one class after another. The authors show that these dynamical losses can help underparameterized networks train successfully when standard cross-entropy training fails to reach deep minima. For overparameterized networks, they can improve generalization.

The explanation centers on the interaction between a moving loss landscape and the network’s optimization dynamics. During a cycle, valleys widen and deepen, then narrow and rise. When a valley narrows, the learning rate becomes too large for stable motion within it, causing the network to move around the valley. The authors study the resulting instabilities and bifurcation cascades using the Hessian and Neural Tangent Kernel.

This process pushes the system toward deeper, wider regions of the landscape and is associated with decreasing Hessian eigenvalues. The paper links that behavior to stronger regularization and improved generalization. Its contribution is both a training strategy and an account of how deliberately varying class emphasis can reshape the optimization trajectory.
summary.tldr: Cyclically changing class emphasis can improve training and generalization by altering the loss landscape and the network’s optimization dynamics.

title: Tilting the playing field: Dynamical loss functions for machine learning

abstract: Kernel mean embeddings are a powerful tool to represent probability distributions over arbitrary spaces as single points in a Hilbert space. Yet, the cost of computing and storing such embeddings prohibits their direct use in large-scale settings. We propose an efficient approximation procedure based on the Nystr{ö}m method, which exploits a small random subset of the dataset. Our main result is an upper bound on the approximation error of this procedure. It yields sufficient conditions on the subsample size to obtain the standard (1/sqrt(n)) rate while reducing computational costs. We discuss applications of this result for the approximation of the maximum mean discrepancy and quadrature rules, and we illustrate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: A kernel mean embedding represents a probability distribution as a single point in a Hilbert space. This makes distributions available to methods that operate on such representations, even when their original data live in varied kinds of spaces. Computing and storing the embeddings, however, can become too expensive for large datasets.

The paper proposes a Nyström approximation that uses a small random subset of the dataset. Its central theoretical result bounds the error introduced by this approximation. From that bound, the authors derive sufficient conditions on subset size for retaining the standard inverse-square-root sample-size rate while reducing computational costs.

The distinction between sufficient conditions and an unconditional promise matters: the result explains when a smaller representation can preserve the desired rate. The authors also discuss approximating maximum mean discrepancy, a comparison between distributions, and quadrature rules for approximating integrals. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory. Together, these contributions show how one efficient representation procedure can support several uses of kernel embeddings, with an explicit account of its approximation error.
summary.tldr: A Nyström approximation uses a small random subset to reduce kernel-embedding costs while retaining the standard error rate under sufficient conditions.

title: Nyström Kernel Mean Embeddings

abstract: An ideal learned representation should display transferability and robustness. Supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) is a promising method for training accurate models, but produces representations that do not capture these properties due to class collapse—when all points in a class map to the same representation. Recent work suggests that "spreading out" these representations improves them, but the precise mechanism is poorly understood. We argue that creating spread alone is insufficient for better representations, since spread is invariant to permutations within classes. Instead, both the correct degree of spread and a mechanism for breaking this invariance are necessary. We first prove that adding a weighted class-conditional InfoNCE loss to SupCon controls the degree of spread. Next, we study three mechanisms to break permutation invariance: using a constrained encoder, adding a class-conditional autoencoder, and using data augmentation. We show that the latter two encourage clustering of latent subclasses under more realistic conditions than the former. Using these insights, we show that adding a properly-weighted class-conditional InfoNCE loss and a class-conditional autoencoder to SupCon achieves 11.1 points of lift on coarse-to-fine transfer across 5 standard datasets and 4.7 points on worst-group robustness on 3 datasets, setting state-of-the-art on CelebA by 11.5 points.

paragraphs: Supervised contrastive learning can collapse all examples of a class to the same representation, losing distinctions useful for transfer and robustness. The paper argues that simply spreading examples apart is insufficient: the same spread can remain after arbitrary rearrangements within a class. Useful representations also need a mechanism that gives this internal arrangement meaningful structure.

They then examine three ways to break the permutation invariance: constraining the encoder, adding a class-conditional autoencoder, and using data augmentation. The reported CelebA result improves the state of the art by 11.5 points. These findings support treating both the amount of within-class variation and its organization as central design choices.
summary.tldr: Controlling within-class spread while organizing latent subclasses improves transfer and worst-group robustness in the reported supervised contrastive learning experiments.

title: Perfectly Balanced: Improving Transfer and Robustness of Supervised Contrastive Learning

abstract: Understanding a decision-maker’s priorities by observing their behavior is critical for transparency and accountability in decision processes{—}such as in healthcare. Though conventional approaches to policy learning almost invariably assume stationarity in behavior, this is hardly true in practice: Medical practice is constantly evolving as clinical professionals fine-tune their knowledge over time. For instance, as the medical community’s understanding of organ transplantations has progressed over the years, a pertinent question is: How have actual organ allocation policies been evolving? To give an answer, we desire a policy learning method that provides interpretable representations of decision-making, in particular capturing an agent’s non-stationary knowledge of the world, as well as operating in an offline manner. First, we model the evolving behavior of decision-makers in terms of contextual bandits, and formalize the problem of Inverse Contextual Bandits ("ICB"). Second, we propose two concrete algorithms as solutions, learning parametric and non-parametric representations of an agent’s behavior. Finally, using both real and simulated data for liver transplantations, we illustrate the applicability and explainability of our method, as well as benchmarking and validating the accuracy of our algorithms.
