paragraphs: Inferring a decision-maker's priorities from observed actions becomes harder when their knowledge changes over time. A fixed behavioral model can miss that evolution. This paper focuses on learning interpretable accounts of changing decisions from offline data, motivated by questions about how clinical practice and organ-allocation policies develop.

The authors model evolving decision-making with contextual bandits and formulate the inverse problem: using observed behavior to learn a representation of the agent's changing behavior and knowledge. They propose two algorithms, one learning a parametric representation and the other a nonparametric representation. Both address the need to describe nonstationary behavior rather than assume a single unchanging policy.

The methods are evaluated using real and simulated liver-transplantation data. These studies illustrate applicability and explainability, and they benchmark and validate algorithmic accuracy. The contribution is a framework for examining how decision processes evolve from historical observations. In the motivating setting, that provides a way to study changes in allocation behavior alongside changes in the decision-maker's understanding of the world.
summary.tldr: Inverse Contextual Bandits learns interpretable representations of how decision-makers' behavior and knowledge evolve from offline observations.

title: Inverse Contextual Bandits: Learning How Behavior Evolves over Time

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable achievements in simulated environments. However, carrying this success to real environments requires the important attribute of robustness, which the existing RL algorithms often lack as they assume that the future deployment environment is the same as the training environment (i.e. simulator) in which the policy is learned. This assumption often does not hold due to the discrepancy between the simulator and the real environment and, as a result, and hence renders the learned policy fragile when deployed. In this paper, we propose a novel distributionally robust $Q$-learning algorithm that learns the best policy in the worst distributional perturbation of the environment. Our algorithm first transforms the infinite-dimensional learning problem (since the environment MDP perturbation lies in an infinite-dimensional space) into a finite-dimensional dual problem and subsequently uses a multi-level Monte-Carlo scheme to approximate the dual value using samples from the simulator. Despite the complexity, we show that the resulting distributionally robust $Q$-learning algorithm asymptotically converges to optimal worst-case policy, thus making it robust to future environment changes. Simulation results further demonstrate its strong empirical robustness.

paragraphs: A policy learned in a simulator can become fragile when deployment conditions differ from training. This paper changes the learning objective to account for distributional changes in the environment. Instead of optimizing only for the training environment, it seeks the policy with the best performance under the worst perturbation considered by its formulation.

Directly solving this problem involves an infinite-dimensional space of possible environment perturbations. The authors transform it into a finite-dimensional dual problem, making the robust objective more manageable. They then use a multilevel Monte Carlo method to approximate the dual value from simulator samples, connecting the transformed optimization problem to a sample-based Q-learning algorithm.

The theoretical result establishes asymptotic convergence to the optimal worst-case policy. That is a convergence statement about the robust objective, rather than a claim of immediate optimality after a finite amount of training. Simulation experiments additionally report strong robustness. Together, the results support learning policies that explicitly account for the distributional environment changes represented in the problem.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust Q-learning uses simulator samples to learn a worst-case policy and asymptotically converges to the robust optimum.

title: Distributionally Robust $Q$-Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study nonconvex tensor robust principal component analysis (RPCA) based on the $t$-SVD. We first propose an alternating projection method, i.e., APT, which converges linearly to the ground-truth under the incoherence conditions of tensors. However, as the projection to the low-rank tensor space in APT can be slow, we further propose to speedup such a process by utilizing the property of the tangent space of low-rank. The resulting algorithm, i.e., EAPT, is not only more efficient than APT but also keeps the linear convergence. Compared with existing tensor RPCA works, the proposed method, especially EAPT, is not only more effective due to the recovery guarantee and adaption in the transformed (frequency) domain but also more efficient due to faster convergence rate and lower iteration complexity. These benefits are also empirically verified both on synthetic data, and real applications, e.g., hyperspectral image denoising and video background subtraction.

paragraphs: This paper studies robust principal component analysis for tensors using a decomposition framework called t-SVD. The aim is to recover underlying low-rank structure, with both a mathematical recovery guarantee and an efficient computation. The authors first introduce APT, an alternating projection method that converges to the ground truth under tensor incoherence conditions.

APT has linear convergence, meaning its error contracts at a geometric rate, but its projection onto the low-rank tensor space can still be expensive. The authors therefore develop EAPT, which uses the tangent space associated with low-rank structure to accelerate that operation. The resulting method retains linear convergence while reducing the computational burden of the projection step.

The reported advantages combine recovery guarantees, adaptation in the transformed frequency domain, and faster computation through convergence speed and lower per-iteration complexity. Experiments support these benefits on synthetic data and on hyperspectral image denoising and video background subtraction. The theory and applications address complementary questions: when recovery is guaranteed under the stated conditions, and whether the resulting algorithms provide practical benefits on the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: APT and its accelerated variant EAPT recover low-rank tensor structure with linear convergence under incoherence conditions, with EAPT reducing projection costs.

title: Fast and Provable Nonconvex Tensor RPCA

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) can learn control policies from static datasets but, like standard RL methods, it requires reward annotations for every transition. In many cases, labeling large datasets with rewards may be costly, especially if those rewards must be provided by human labelers, while collecting diverse unlabeled data might be comparatively inexpensive. How can we best leverage such unlabeled data in offline RL? One natural solution is to learn a reward function from the labeled data and use it to label the unlabeled data. In this paper, we find that, perhaps surprisingly, a much simpler method that simply applies zero rewards to unlabeled data leads to effective data sharing both in theory and in practice, without learning any reward model at all. While this approach might seem strange (and incorrect) at first, we provide extensive theoretical and empirical analysis that illustrates how it trades off reward bias, sample complexity and distributional shift, often leading to good results. We characterize conditions under which this simple strategy is effective, and further show that extending it with a simple reweighting approach can further alleviate the bias introduced by using incorrect reward labels. Our empirical evaluation confirms these findings in simulated robotic locomotion, navigation, and manipulation settings.

In many cases, labeling large datasets with rewards may be costly, especially if those rewards must be provided by human labelers, while collecting diverse unlabeled data might be comparatively inexpensive. How can we best leverage such unlabeled data in offline RL? One natural solution is to learn a reward function from the labeled data and use it to label the unlabeled data. In this paper, we find that, perhaps surprisingly, a much simpler method that simply applies zero rewards to unlabeled data leads to effective data sharing both in theory and in practice, without learning any reward model at all. While this approach might seem strange (and incorrect) at first, we provide extensive theoretical and empirical analysis that illustrates how it trades off reward bias, sample complexity and distributional shift, often leading to good results. We characterize conditions under which this simple strategy is effective, and further show that extending it with a simple reweighting approach can further alleviate the bias introduced by using incorrect reward labels. Our empirical evaluation confirms these findings in simulated robotic locomotion, navigation, and manipulation settings.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns behavior from an existing dataset, but it usually requires a reward annotation for every transition. Obtaining those annotations can be expensive even when additional unlabeled experience is easy to collect. This paper investigates how such experience can help without first training a model to predict its missing rewards.

The proposed strategy assigns zero rewards to unlabeled transitions and incorporates them into learning. These assigned rewards may be incorrect, so the approach introduces reward bias. The authors analyze how that bias interacts with sample complexity and distributional shift, showing why additional data can still help. They characterize conditions under which this simple strategy is effective.

The paper also extends the method with reweighting to reduce the bias caused by incorrect reward labels. Experiments in simulated robotic locomotion, navigation, and manipulation support the theoretical findings. The result is a conditional case for a very simple data-sharing procedure: useful additional experience can outweigh the harm of imperfect reward labels in the settings analyzed, without requiring a learned reward model.
summary.tldr: Assigning zero rewards to unlabeled offline experience can improve learning under characterized conditions, with reweighting helping reduce reward bias.

title: How to Leverage Unlabeled Data in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Traditional federated optimization methods perform poorly with heterogeneous data (i.e. , accuracy reduction), especially for highly skewed data. In this paper, we investigate the label distribution skew in FL, where the distribution of labels varies across clients. First, we investigate the label distribution skew from a statistical view. We demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that previous methods based on softmax cross-entropy are not suitable, which can result in local models heavily overfitting to minority classes and missing classes. Additionally, we theoretically introduce a deviation bound to measure the deviation of the gradient after local update. At last, we propose FedLC (\textbf{Fed}erated learning via \textbf{L}ogits \textbf{C}alibration), which calibrates the logits before softmax cross-entropy according to the probability of occurrence of each class. FedLC applies a fine-grained calibrated cross-entropy loss to local update by adding a pairwise label margin. Extensive experiments on federated datasets and real-world datasets demonstrate that FedLC leads to a more accurate global model and much improved performance. Furthermore, integrating other FL methods into our approach can further enhance the performance of the global model.

paragraphs: In federated learning, different clients can see very different proportions of each class, including classes with few or no local examples. This paper examines how that label imbalance affects local training and the shared model. Its theoretical and empirical analysis identifies problems with previous methods based on ordinary softmax cross-entropy.

The authors also derive a bound measuring how much the gradient deviates after a local update. Their proposed method, FedLC, adjusts the model's class scores before applying softmax cross-entropy. The adjustment depends on each class's occurrence probability and introduces a margin between pairs of labels, making the local loss sensitive to label distribution skew.

Experiments on federated and real-world datasets show that this calibrated training objective produces a more accurate global model than the compared approaches. The abstract also reports further gains when other federated learning methods are integrated with FedLC. The findings suggest that correcting the local classification objective is a useful way to address unequal class distributions across clients.
summary.tldr: FedLC adjusts local class scores using label frequencies to improve federated learning under unequal client label distributions.

title: Federated Learning with Label Distribution Skew via Logits Calibration

abstract: Pipeline parallelism is a key technique for training large language models within GPU clusters. However, it often leads to a memory imbalance problem, where certain GPUs face high memory pressure while others underutilize their capacity. This imbalance results in suboptimal training performance, even when the overall GPU memory capacity is sufficient for more efficient setups. To address this inefficiency, we propose BPipe, a novel approach for achieving memory balance in pipeline parallelism. BPipe employs an activation balancing method to transfer intermediate activations between GPUs during training, enabling all GPUs to utilize comparable amounts of memory. With balanced memory utilization, BPipe enhances the training efficiency of large language models like GPT-3 by eliminating redundant recomputations or increasing the micro-batch size. Our evaluation conducted on 48 A100 GPUs across six nodes interconnected with HDR InfiniBand shows that BPipe accelerates the training of GPT-3 96B and GPT-3 134B models by 1.25x-2.17x compared to Megatron-LM, a state-of-the-art framework for training large language models.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallelism spreads large language model training across GPUs, but it can leave their memory usage uneven. Some devices face heavy memory pressure while others have spare capacity. Consequently, sufficient memory across the cluster does not necessarily translate into an efficient training configuration: the uneven distribution can still constrain training.

BPipe addresses this problem by moving intermediate activations between GPUs during training. These activations are the intermediate results produced as data passes through the model. Redistributing them makes memory consumption more comparable across devices. The method therefore treats available memory as a resource that can be balanced across the pipeline.

That balance can improve efficiency by removing redundant recomputation or allowing a larger micro-batch size. In an evaluation using 48 A100 GPUs across six nodes connected with HDR InfiniBand, BPipe accelerated GPT-3 96B and 134B training by 1.25 to 2.17 times relative to Megatron-LM. The result demonstrates that better placement of intermediate training data can yield substantial speed improvements in the evaluated large-model configurations.
summary.tldr: BPipe redistributes intermediate activations across GPUs to balance memory and accelerate large language model training.

title: BPipe: Memory-Balanced Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Language Models

abstract: Autonomous driving systems require High-Definition (HD) semantic maps to navigate around urban roads. Existing solutions approach the semantic mapping problem by offline manual annotation, which suffers from serious scalability issues. Recent learning-based methods produce dense rasterized segmentation predictions to construct maps. However, these predictions do not include instance information of individual map elements and require heuristic post-processing to obtain vectorized maps. To tackle these challenges, we introduce an end-to-end vectorized HD map learning pipeline, termed VectorMapNet. VectorMapNet takes onboard sensor observations and predicts a sparse set of polylines in the bird’s-eye view. This pipeline can explicitly model the spatial relation between map elements and generate vectorized maps that are friendly to downstream autonomous driving tasks. Extensive experiments show that VectorMapNet achieve strong map learning performance on both nuScenes and Argoverse2 dataset, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by 14.2 mAP and 14.6mAP. Qualitatively, VectorMapNet is capable of generating comprehensive maps and capturing fine-grained details of road geometry. To the best of our knowledge, VectorMapNet is the first work designed towards end-to-end vectorized map learning from onboard observations.

VectorMapNet addresses this representation gap by learning to predict a vector map directly from observations collected by onboard sensors.

The system outputs a sparse set of polylines in a bird’s-eye view. These connected line segments represent map geometry in a form suited to downstream driving tasks. The pipeline can explicitly model spatial relationships between map elements, bringing element structure and geometry into the prediction process instead of relying on heuristic conversion from raster segmentation.

Qualitative results show comprehensive maps and fine road-geometry details. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first work aimed at end-to-end vectorized map learning from onboard observations, with the reported results supporting that direct prediction approach.
summary.tldr: VectorMapNet predicts vectorized road maps directly from onboard sensor observations, improving map learning on nuScenes and Argoverse2.

title: VectorMapNet: End-to-end Vectorized HD Map Learning

abstract: We study the variance of stochastic policy gradients (SPGs) with many action samples per state. We derive a many-actions optimality condition, which determines when many-actions SPG yields lower variance as compared to a single-action agent with proportionally extended trajectory. We propose Model-Based Many-Actions (MBMA), an approach leveraging dynamics models for many-actions sampling in the context of SPG. MBMA addresses issues associated with existing implementations of many-actions SPG and yields lower bias and comparable variance to SPG estimated from states in model-simulated rollouts. We find that MBMA bias and variance structure matches that predicted by theory. As a result, MBMA achieves improved sample efficiency and higher returns on a range of continuous action environments as compared to model-free, many-actions, and model-based on-policy SPG baselines.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient learning estimates how an agent should change its behavior from sampled experience. This paper asks when sampling several actions at the same state is more useful than sampling one action at each state along a proportionally longer trajectory. The comparison focuses on variance, which measures the variability of the resulting gradient estimates.

The authors derive an optimality condition identifying when the many-action approach yields lower variance. This makes the benefit conditional on the structure of the estimation problem. They also propose Model-Based Many-Actions, or MBMA, which uses a learned dynamics model to support action sampling and addresses issues in existing many-action implementations.

Compared with gradient estimates based on states from model-simulated rollouts, MBMA achieves lower bias and comparable variance. Its observed bias and variance structure agrees with the theoretical predictions. Across a range of continuous-action environments, it improves sample efficiency and returns relative to the evaluated model-free, many-action, and model-based on-policy baselines. The work links a theoretical sampling comparison to a practical model-assisted learning method.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies when multiple action samples reduce policy-gradient variance and introduces MBMA to exploit this with dynamics models.

title: On Many-Actions Policy Gradient

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has made significant advancements in artificial intelligence. However, its real-world applications are limited due to differences between simulated environments and the actual world. Consequently, it is crucial to systematically analyze how each component of the RL system can affect the final model performance. In this study, we propose an adversarial learning framework for distributional reinforcement learning, which adopts the concept of influence measure from the statistics community. This framework enables us to detect performance loss caused by either the internal policy structure or the external state observation. The proposed influence measure is based on information geometry and has desirable properties of invariance. We demonstrate that the influence measure is useful for three diagnostic tasks: identifying fragile states in trajectories, determining the instability of the policy architecture, and pinpointing anomalously sensitive policy parameters.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system can perform differently when its observations or internal policy components change. This matters when moving between simulated and real environments, where conditions do not match perfectly. The paper develops an adversarial learning framework for distributional reinforcement learning that helps diagnose which parts of a system contribute to performance loss.

The central tool is an influence measure adapted from statistics. It is constructed using information geometry and has invariance properties. The framework considers influences arising both outside the policy, through state observations, and inside it, through policy structure. This provides a shared way to examine sources of sensitivity that might otherwise be analyzed separately.

The authors demonstrate three diagnostic uses: locating fragile states along trajectories, assessing instability associated with policy architecture, and identifying unusually sensitive policy parameters. These findings concern understanding vulnerability within a learned system. They make the framework useful for identifying where performance is sensitive, without establishing that the resulting diagnoses alone solve the broader challenge of deployment outside simulation.
summary.tldr: An information-geometric influence measure diagnoses sensitivity in distributional reinforcement learning observations, architectures, and policy parameters.

title: Adversarial Learning of Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sampling approaches like Markov chain Monte Carlo were once popular for combinatorial optimization, but the inefficiency of classical methods and the need for problem-specific designs curtailed ongoing development. Recent work has favored data-driven approaches that mitigate the need for hand-craft heuristics, but these are often not usable as out-of-the-box solvers due to dependence on in-distribution training and limited scalability to large instances. In this paper, we revisit the idea of using sampling for combinatorial optimization, motivated by the significant recent advances of gradient-based discrete MCMC and new techniques for parallel neighborhood exploration on accelerators. Remarkably, we find that modern sampling strategies can leverage landscape information to provide general-purpose solvers that require no training and yet are competitive with state of the art combinatorial solvers. In particular, experiments on cover vertex selection, graph partition and routing demonstrate better speed-quality trade-offs over current learning based approaches, and sometimes even superior performance to commercial solvers and specialized algorithms.

More recent learned solvers reduce dependence on hand-crafted heuristics, yet may depend on matching their training distribution and struggle with large instances. This paper revisits sampling in light of newer computational techniques.

The approach draws on advances in gradient-based discrete Markov chain Monte Carlo and parallel exploration of neighboring solutions on accelerators. These methods use information about the optimization landscape to guide search. The authors find that modern sampling can provide general-purpose solvers that require no training while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art combinatorial optimization methods.

Experiments cover vertex-cover selection, graph partitioning, and routing. They show better speed-quality trade-offs than the learning-based approaches considered, and sometimes better performance than commercial solvers or specialized algorithms. The qualified comparison matters: the finding is competitive performance across the studied tasks, with occasional wins over stronger solver categories, rather than universal superiority. It makes sampling a credible option for training-free optimization.
summary.tldr: Modern discrete sampling and parallel search provide training-free combinatorial solvers with competitive speed-quality trade-offs.

title: Revisiting Sampling for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful technique that allows an autonomous agent to learn an optimal policy to maximize the expected return. The optimality of various RL algorithms relies on the stationarity assumption, which requires time-invariant state transition and reward functions. However, deviations from stationarity over extended periods often occur in real-world applications like robotics control, health care and digital marketing, resulting in suboptimal policies learned under stationary assumptions. In this paper, we propose a model-based doubly robust procedure for testing the stationarity assumption and detecting change points in offline RL settings with certain degree of homogeneity. Our proposed testing procedure is robust to model misspecifications and can effectively control type-I error while achieving high statistical power, especially in high-dimensional settings. Extensive comparative simulations and a real-world interventional mobile health example illustrate the advantages of our method in detecting change points and optimizing long-term rewards in high-dimensional, non-stationary environments.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning methods assume that the environment follows the same rules over time: actions have stable effects, and rewards are assigned consistently. Real applications can violate this assumption, making a policy learned from earlier experience less effective later. This paper develops a way to test whether those rules have changed and locate the times when changes occurred.

The proposed procedure uses a model-based, doubly robust approach in offline reinforcement learning, working with previously collected data. Its stated setting requires a certain degree of homogeneity. The method is designed to tolerate model misspecification while controlling false alarms, known as type-I errors, and retaining strong ability to detect actual changes, particularly with high-dimensional data.

Comparative simulations and an interventional mobile health example illustrate the method’s advantages. The findings connect detecting environmental changes with improving long-term rewards: identifying when historical experience reflects different conditions can matter for sequential decisions. The evidence supports this approach in the studied nonstationary settings.
summary.tldr: A doubly robust test detects changes in offline reinforcement learning environments while controlling false alarms under the studied conditions.

title: A Robust Test for the Stationarity Assumption in Sequential Decision Making

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become more integrated into our daily lives, it is crucial to identify and mitigate their risks, especially when the risks can have profound impacts on human users and societies. Guardrails, which filter the inputs or outputs of LLMs, have emerged as a core safeguarding technology. This position paper takes a deep look at current open-source solutions (Llama Guard, Nvidia NeMo, Guardrails AI), and discusses the challenges and the road towards building more complete solutions. Drawing on robust evidence from previous research, we advocate for a systematic approach to construct guardrails for LLMs, based on comprehensive consideration of diverse contexts across various LLMs applications. We propose employing socio-technical methods through collaboration with a multi-disciplinary team to pinpoint precise technical requirements, exploring advanced neural-symbolic implementations to embrace the complexity of the requirements, and developing verification and testing to ensure the utmost quality of the final product.

This position paper argues that building effective guardrails requires systematic design that takes the application context seriously. It examines open-source approaches, including Llama Guard, Nvidia NeMo, and Guardrails AI, to discuss challenges and paths toward more complete solutions.

The proposed process begins with socio-technical work involving a multidisciplinary team. The aim is to translate the needs and risks of an application into precise technical requirements. This matters because guardrail behavior depends on what a system is being used for and how its outputs affect people, so requirements must account for diverse contexts.

The authors then advocate exploring neural-symbolic implementations to handle complex requirements and developing verification and testing to assess the resulting product. The paper’s contribution is a design position grounded in previous research. It brings requirements, implementation, and assurance into one process, arguing that all three deserve attention when building safeguards for language-model applications.
summary.tldr: This position paper advocates context-sensitive guardrail design combining multidisciplinary requirements work, neural-symbolic implementation, and verification.

title: Position: Building Guardrails for Large Language Models Requires Systematic Design

abstract: Domain incremental learning (DIL) poses a significant challenge in real-world scenarios, as models need to be sequentially trained on diverse domains over time, all the while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Mitigating representation drift, which refers to the phenomenon of learned representations undergoing changes as the model adapts to new tasks, can help alleviate catastrophic forgetting. In this study, we propose a novel DIL method named DARE, featuring a three-stage training process: Divergence, Adaptation, and REfinement. This process gradually adapts the representations associated with new tasks into the feature space spanned by samples from previous tasks, simultaneously integrating task-specific decision boundaries. Additionally, we introduce a novel strategy for buffer sampling and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, combined with this sampling strategy, in reducing representation drift within the feature encoder. This contribution effectively alleviates catastrophic forgetting across multiple DIL benchmarks. Furthermore, our approach prevents sudden representation drift at task boundaries, resulting in a well-calibrated DIL model that maintains the performance on previous tasks.

paragraphs: Domain incremental learning asks a model to learn from changing domains over time while retaining performance on earlier ones. One source of forgetting is representation drift: the features used to describe inputs change as training proceeds. DARE addresses this by controlling how new-task representations are incorporated into the space already shaped by previous tasks.

The method uses three training stages called Divergence, Adaptation, and Refinement. Together, they gradually adapt representations for new tasks into the feature space spanned by previous-task samples while incorporating task-specific decision boundaries. The paper also introduces a buffer-sampling strategy and evaluates its combination with this staged process for reducing drift in the feature encoder.

Across multiple domain incremental learning benchmarks, the combined approach reduces representation drift and alleviates catastrophic forgetting. The authors also report that it prevents abrupt feature changes at task boundaries, produces a well-calibrated model, and maintains earlier-task performance. These findings connect the way adaptation unfolds over time with both retention and calibration, supporting gradual representation adjustment as a useful component of continual domain learning.
summary.tldr: DARE combines staged adaptation and buffer sampling to reduce representation drift and forgetting as models learn successive domains.

title: Gradual Divergence for Seamless Adaptation: A Novel Domain Incremental Learning Method

abstract: Traveling waves are a fundamental phenomenon in the brain, playing a crucial role in short-term information storage. In this study, we leverage the concept of traveling wave dynamics within a neural lattice to formulate a theoretical model of neural working memory in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), study its properties, and its real world implications in AI. The proposed model diverges from traditional approaches, which assume information storage in static, register-like locations updated by interference. Instead, the model stores data as waves that is updated by the wave’s boundary conditions. We rigorously examine the model’s capabilities in representing and learning state histories, which are vital for learning history-dependent dynamical systems. The findings reveal that the model reliably stores external information and enhances the learning process by addressing the diminishing gradient problem of RNNs. To understand the model’s real-world applicability, we explore two cases: linear boundary condition and non-linear, self-attention-driven boundary condition. The experiments reveal that the linear scenario is effectively learned by RNNs through backpropagation when modeling history-dependent dynamical systems. Conversely, the non-linear scenario parallels an attention-only transformer. Collectively, our findings suggest the broader relevance of traveling waves in AI and its potential in advancing neural network architectures.

paragraphs: This paper develops a model of working memory in recurrent neural networks using traveling waves on a neural lattice. Its central idea is that information can persist as moving wave patterns. Memory updates occur through the waves’ boundary conditions, offering a different account from storing information in fixed, register-like locations.

The authors analyze how this mechanism represents and learns histories of states, which matter when a system’s behavior depends on its past. Their findings indicate that the model reliably retains external information and improves learning by addressing diminishing gradients in recurrent networks. This links a proposed memory mechanism to a difficulty in learning dependencies across time.

These results suggest a potential architectural role for traveling waves and connect recurrent memory and attention through a shared dynamical perspective.
summary.tldr: A traveling-wave memory model retains state histories, addresses diminishing gradients, and connects recurrent dynamics with attention-based architectures.

title: Hidden Traveling Waves bind Working Memory Variables in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: In real-world continual learning (CL) scenarios, tasks often exhibit intricate and unpredictable semantic shifts, posing challenges for fixed prompt management strategies which are tailored to only handle semantic shifts of uniform degree (i.e., uniformly mild or uniformly abrupt). To address this limitation, we propose an adaptive prompting approach that effectively accommodates semantic shifts of varying degree where mild and abrupt shifts are mixed. AdaPromptCL employs the assign-and-refine semantic grouping mechanism that dynamically manages prompt groups in accordance with the semantic similarity between tasks, enhancing the quality of grouping through continuous refinement. Our experiment results demonstrate that AdaPromptCL outperforms existing prompting methods by up to 21.3%, especially in the benchmark datasets with diverse semantic shifts between tasks.

paragraphs: Continual learning involves encountering tasks over time, and the semantic differences between successive tasks can vary considerably. Some changes are mild, while others are abrupt. The paper argues that fixed prompt-management strategies, designed around a uniform degree of change, struggle when a task sequence mixes both kinds of shifts.

AdaPromptCL responds by adapting how prompts are grouped. Its assign-and-refine mechanism manages prompt groups according to semantic similarity between tasks. Grouping is also continuously refined, allowing the organization to change as learning proceeds. This makes task relationships an ongoing part of prompt management instead of treating the initial grouping strategy as permanently appropriate.

Experiments report improvements of up to 21.3% over existing prompting methods, especially on benchmarks with diverse semantic shifts. The reported findings support adapting prompt organization to the variation actually present across tasks. The contribution is particularly relevant to sequences where one fixed assumption about task similarity is inadequate: the method aims to accommodate both closely related and sharply different tasks within the same continual-learning process.
summary.tldr: AdaPromptCL adaptively groups and refines prompts to handle continual-learning tasks with mixed mild and abrupt semantic shifts.

title: One Size Fits All for Semantic Shifts: Adaptive Prompt Tuning for Continual Learning

abstract: This paper studies sample average approximation (SAA) and its simple regularized variation in solving convex or strongly convex stochastic programming problems. Under heavy-tailed assumptions and comparable regularity conditions as in the typical SAA literature, we show — perhaps for the first time — that the sample complexity can be completely free from any complexity measure (e.g., logarithm of the covering number) of the feasible region. As a result, our new bounds can be more advantageous than the state-of-the-art in terms of the dependence on the problem dimensionality.

paragraphs: Sample average approximation solves a stochastic optimization problem by replacing an expected objective with an average over sampled observations. A central theoretical question is how many samples are needed for a useful solution. This paper studies that question for convex and strongly convex problems, including a simple regularized version of the method.

The analysis works under heavy-tailed assumptions and regularity conditions comparable to those in typical sample-average-approximation research. Its main result removes any complexity measure of the feasible region from the sample-complexity bounds. Such measures include the logarithm of a covering number, which describes how extensively the allowable solution set must be represented at a chosen resolution.

Removing that dependence changes what drives the theoretical sample requirement. The resulting bounds can have more favorable dependence on problem dimensionality than state-of-the-art bounds. This is a conditional advantage under the paper’s assumptions, rather than a claim that every high-dimensional problem needs fewer samples. The contribution is a sharper theoretical assessment of familiar approximation procedures, including their regularized variation.
summary.tldr: The paper derives heavy-tailed sample-average-approximation bounds free of feasible-region complexity measures, potentially improving dependence on dimensionality.

title: New Sample Complexity Bounds for Sample Average Approximation in Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Programming

abstract: The existing definitions of graph convolution, either from spatial or spectral perspectives, are inflexible and not unified. Defining a general convolution operator in the graph domain is challenging due to the lack of canonical coordinates, the presence of irregular structures, and the properties of graph symmetries. In this work, we propose a novel and general graph convolution framework by parameterizing the kernels as continuous functions of pseudo-coordinates derived via graph positional encoding. We name this Continuous Kernel Graph Convolution (CKGConv). Theoretically, we demonstrate that CKGConv is flexible and expressive. CKGConv encompasses many existing graph convolutions, and exhibits a stronger expressiveness, as powerful as graph transformers in terms of distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. Empirically, we show that CKGConv-based Networks outperform existing graph convolutional networks and perform comparably to the best graph transformers across a variety of graph datasets. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/networkslab/CKGConv.

paragraphs: Convolution is difficult to define uniformly on graphs because graphs have irregular structures and lack a standard coordinate system. Existing spatial and spectral definitions provide different, relatively inflexible ways to combine information. This paper proposes Continuous Kernel Graph Convolution, or CKGConv, as a more general framework for defining that operation.

CKGConv uses graph positional encodings to derive pseudo-coordinates. It then represents convolution kernels as continuous functions of those coordinates. This gives the kernel a structured way to depend on graph position despite the absence of ordinary coordinates. The authors show theoretically that the framework includes many existing graph convolutions and has substantial expressive power.

In particular, their expressiveness result places CKGConv on par with graph transformers for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, meaning graphs with genuinely different connectivity structures. Experiments across multiple graph datasets show networks built with CKGConv outperforming existing graph convolutional networks and performing comparably to leading graph transformers. These results support continuous kernels as a flexible basis for graph learning, with both theoretical and empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: CKGConv defines graph convolution through continuous kernels over positional pseudo-coordinates, combining broad theoretical expressiveness with competitive empirical performance.

title: CKGConv: General Graph Convolution with Continuous Kernels

abstract: Learning in deep weight spaces (DWS), where neural networks process the weights of other neural networks, is an emerging research direction, with applications to 2D and 3D neural fields (INRs, NeRFs), as well as making inferences about other types of neural networks. Unfortunately, weight space models tend to suffer from substantial overfitting. We empirically analyze the reasons for this overfitting and find that a key reason is the lack of diversity in DWS datasets. While a given object can be represented by many different weight configurations, typical INR training sets fail to capture variability across INRs that represent the same object. To address this, we explore strategies for data augmentation in weight spaces and propose a MixUp method adapted for weight spaces. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in two setups. In classification, they improve performance similarly to having up to 10 times more data. In self-supervised contrastive learning, they yield substantial 5-10% gains in downstream classification.

paragraphs: Weight-space learning trains neural networks to process the weights of other neural networks. Applications include reasoning about networks that represent images or three-dimensional scenes. The paper examines why these models often overfit and identifies limited diversity in their training datasets as an important empirical explanation for the problem.

One object can be represented by many different neural-network weight configurations. Typical datasets of implicit neural representations do not adequately capture this variation among networks representing the same object. The authors investigate augmentation strategies in weight space and introduce a version of MixUp adapted to these inputs, aiming to expose the learner to more varied weight representations.

The methods are evaluated in classification and self-supervised contrastive learning. In classification, their improvements are comparable to those obtained with up to ten times more data. In the contrastive setting, they produce reported downstream classification gains of 5–10%. The results support augmentation as a way to address insufficient representation diversity, with the stated benefits established in these evaluated setups.
summary.tldr: Weight-space augmentation, including an adapted MixUp method, improves generalization by increasing the diversity of neural-network representations.

title: Improved Generalization of Weight Space Networks via Augmentations

abstract: Language models often exhibit undesirable behavior, e.g., generating toxic or gender-biased text. In the case of neural language models, an encoding of the undesirable behavior is often present in the model’s representations. Thus, one natural (and common) approach to prevent the model from exhibiting undesirable behavior is to steer the model’s representations in a manner that reduces the probability of it generating undesirable text. This paper investigates the formal and empirical properties of steering functions, i.e., transformation of the neural language model’s representations that alter its behavior. First, we derive two optimal, in the least-squares sense, affine steering functions under different constraints. Our theory provides justification for existing approaches and offers a novel, improved steering approach. Second, we offer a series of experiments that demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of the methods in mitigating bias and reducing toxic generation.

paragraphs: Language models can generate toxic or gender-biased text, and information associated with those behaviors can appear in their internal representations. This paper studies steering functions that transform those representations to change the model's behavior. The goal is to reduce the probability of undesirable output by intervening in how the model represents information.

The authors derive two affine steering functions under different constraints. An affine transformation combines a linear transformation with a shift, giving a structured family of interventions to analyze. The derived functions are optimal in the least-squares sense for their respective constraints. That qualification matters: the formal result concerns a particular mathematical objective, rather than every possible measure of behavioral improvement.

The theory provides justification for existing steering approaches and yields a new, improved approach. Experiments then demonstrate effectiveness in mitigating bias and reducing toxic generation. Together, the theoretical and empirical components connect a precisely defined representation transformation with observed changes in generated text, providing both a rationale for steering and evidence of its behavioral usefulness.
summary.tldr: The paper derives two constrained least-squares-optimal affine steering functions and demonstrates reductions in biased and toxic language generation.

title: Representation Surgery: Theory and Practice of Affine Steering

abstract: We introduce a multiple target optimization framework for DP-SGD referred to as pro-active DP. In contrast to traditional DP accountants, which are used to track the expenditure of privacy budgets, the pro-active DP scheme allows one to a-priori select parameters of DP-SGD based on a fixed privacy budget (in terms of $\epsilon$ and $\delta$) in such a way to optimize the anticipated utility (test accuracy) the most. To achieve this objective, we first propose significant improvements to the moment account method, presenting a closed-form $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP guarantee that connects all parameters in the DP-SGD setup. Generally, DP-SGD is $(\epsilon\leq 1/2,\delta=1/N)$-DP if $\sigma=\sqrt{2(\epsilon +\ln(1/\delta))/\epsilon}$ with $T$ at least $\approx 2k^2/\epsilon$ and $(2/e)^2k^2-1/2\geq \ln(N)$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, and $K=kN$ is the total number of gradient computations where $k$ measures $K$ in number of epochs of size $N$ of the local data set. We prove that our expression is close to tight in that if $T$ is more than a constant factor $\approx 4$ smaller than the lower bound $\approx 2k^2/\epsilon$, then the $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP guarantee is violated. Our enhanced DP theory allows us to create a utility graph and DP calculator. These tools link privacy and utility objectives and search for optimal experiment setups, efficiently taking into account both accuracy and privacy objectives, as well as implementation goals. We furnish a comprehensive implementation flow of our proactive DP, with rigorous experiments to showcase the proof-of-concept.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent involves choices that jointly affect privacy, accuracy, and implementation. Privacy accountants usually track how much privacy budget training consumes. Proactive DP instead uses a fixed privacy budget to help choose training parameters in advance, with the goal of optimizing anticipated test accuracy alongside practical objectives.

The authors improve the moment accounting method and derive a closed-form privacy guarantee linking the training parameters. Their stated sufficient conditions connect noise, training rounds, dataset size, and gradient computations measured in epochs, within a specified privacy regime. They also show a form of near-tightness: reducing the number of rounds sufficiently below the stated threshold, by roughly a factor of four, violates the guarantee under their analysis.

The framework turns this theory into a utility graph and a DP calculator that search for experiment configurations satisfying multiple objectives. A full implementation flow and proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate the approach. The main benefit is planning: privacy becomes a constraint used to design a training setup, together with expected utility and implementation requirements.
summary.tldr: Proactive DP uses improved privacy accounting to select DP-SGD parameters in advance for a fixed privacy budget and anticipated utility.

title: Proactive DP: A Multiple Target Optimization Framework for DP-SGD

abstract: We present Langevin Predictive Coding (LPC), a novel algorithm for deep generative model learning that builds upon the predictive coding framework of computational neuroscience. By injecting Gaussian noise into the predictive coding inference procedure and incorporating an encoder network initialization, we reframe the approach as an amortized Langevin sampling method for optimizing a tight variational lower bound. To increase robustness to sampling step size, we present a lightweight preconditioning technique inspired by Riemannian Langevin methods and adaptive SGD. We compare LPC against VAEs by training generative models on benchmark datasets; our experiments demonstrate superior sample quality and faster convergence for LPC in a fraction of SGD training iterations, while matching or exceeding VAE performance across key metrics like FID, diversity and coverage.

By injecting Gaussian noise into the predictive coding inference procedure and incorporating an encoder network initialization, we reframe the approach as an amortized Langevin sampling method for optimizing a tight variational lower bound. To increase robustness to sampling step size, we present a lightweight preconditioning technique inspired by Riemannian Langevin methods and adaptive SGD. We compare LPC against VAEs by training generative models on benchmark datasets; our experiments demonstrate superior sample quality and faster convergence for LPC in a fraction of SGD training iterations, while matching or exceeding VAE performance across key metrics like FID, diversity and coverage.

paragraphs: Predictive coding provides a computational-neuroscience framework for inference and learning. This paper adapts it into Langevin Predictive Coding, or LPC, for training deep generative models. The key change is to make the inference procedure perform sampling, connecting predictive coding to a probabilistic learning objective.

LPC injects Gaussian noise into predictive-coding inference and uses an encoder network to initialize the process. Together, these changes yield an amortized Langevin sampling method that optimizes a tight variational lower bound. The authors also introduce lightweight preconditioning, inspired by Riemannian Langevin methods and adaptive stochastic gradient descent, to make sampling less sensitive to step size.

In benchmark experiments, LPC generates higher-quality samples and converges in a fraction of the stochastic-gradient training iterations used by the compared variational autoencoders. It matches or exceeds their performance on FID, diversity, and coverage. These results support combining encoder-based initialization with noisy iterative inference, while the reported iteration reduction specifically measures training iterations rather than establishing an equivalent reduction in total runtime.
summary.tldr: LPC turns predictive-coding inference into Langevin sampling and reports improved generative quality with fewer training iterations than compared VAEs.

title: Sample as you Infer: Predictive Coding with Langevin Dynamics

abstract: Image retrieval, i.e., finding desired images given a reference image, inherently encompasses rich, multi-faceted search intents that are difficult to capture solely using image-based measures. Recent works leverage text instructions to allow users to more freely express their search intents. However, they primarily focus on image pairs that are visually similar and/or can be characterized by a small set of pre-defined relations. The core thesis of this paper is that text instructions can enable retrieving images with richer relations beyond visual similarity. To show this, we introduce MagicLens, a series of self-supervised image retrieval models that support open-ended instructions. MagicLens is built on a key novel insight: image pairs that naturally occur on the same web pages contain a wide range of implicit relations (e.g., inside view of), and we can bring those implicit relations explicit by synthesizing instructions via foundation models. Trained on 36.7M (query image, instruction, target image) triplets with rich semantic relations mined from the web, MagicLens achieves results comparable with or better than prior best on eight benchmarks of various image retrieval tasks, while maintaining high parameter efficiency with a significantly smaller model size. Additional human analyses on a 1.4M-image unseen corpus further demonstrate the diversity of search intents supported by MagicLens. Code and models are publicly available at the https://open-vision-language.github.io/MagicLens/.

paragraphs: Searching from a reference image can involve intentions that visual similarity alone cannot express. Someone may want an image related to the reference through a semantic relationship, such as an inside view. MagicLens supports searches that combine a query image with an open-ended text instruction, expanding the range of relationships a retrieval model can handle.

The training approach uses image pairs found on the same web pages. The authors argue that these pairs contain diverse implicit relationships, which foundation models can turn into explicit instructions. This produces 36.7 million training triplets consisting of a query image, an instruction, and a target image. The web-derived relationships supply supervision for the retrieval task.

Across eight image-retrieval benchmarks, MagicLens matches or exceeds the prior best results while using a significantly smaller model. Human analyses on an unseen collection of 1.4 million images further demonstrate varied supported search intentions. Together, these findings support the central idea that instruction-guided retrieval can capture rich relationships beyond visual resemblance, and that naturally co-occurring web images can help train that capability.
summary.tldr: MagicLens learns from web image pairs and synthesized instructions to retrieve images through diverse relationships beyond visual similarity.

title: MagicLens: Self-Supervised Image Retrieval with Open-Ended Instructions

abstract: The maximum entropy encoding framework provides a unified perspective for many non-contrastive learning methods like SimSiam, Barlow Twins, and MEC. Inspired by this framework, we introduce Matrix-SSL, a novel approach that leverages matrix information theory to interpret the maximum entropy encoding loss as matrix uniformity loss. Furthermore, Matrix-SSL enhances the maximum entropy encoding method by seamlessly incorporating matrix alignment loss, directly aligning covariance matrices in different branches. Experimental results reveal that Matrix-SSL outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the ImageNet dataset under linear evaluation settings and on MS-COCO for transfer learning tasks. Specifically, when performing transfer learning tasks on MS-COCO, our method outperforms previous SOTA methods such as MoCo v2 and BYOL up to 3.3% with only 400 epochs compared to 800 epochs pre-training. We also try to introduce representation learning into the language modeling regime by fine-tuning a 7B model using matrix cross-entropy loss, with a margin of 3.1% on the GSM8K dataset over the standard cross-entropy loss.

paragraphs: Matrix-SSL develops a matrix-based perspective on self-supervised representation learning. It starts from maximum entropy encoding, a framework that already connects several non-contrastive learning methods. The authors interpret its loss as a matrix uniformity objective, providing a way to understand the training criterion through matrix information theory.

The method then adds matrix alignment, directly bringing covariance matrices from different branches into agreement. This extends the existing objective with a requirement on the relationships captured by those covariance matrices. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods on ImageNet under linear evaluation and on MS-COCO transfer tasks.

For MS-COCO transfer, the authors report improvements of up to 3.3% over methods including MoCo v2 and BYOL, using 400 pretraining epochs compared with 800. They also explore language modeling by fine-tuning a 7B model with matrix cross-entropy, reporting a 3.1% margin on GSM8K over standard cross-entropy. These findings support the matrix-based objectives in the tested vision settings and provide an additional language-modeling example.
summary.tldr: Matrix-SSL combines matrix uniformity and covariance alignment, reporting improved visual representations and a promising language-model fine-tuning result.

title: Matrix Information Theory for Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Hindsight experience replay and goal relabeling are successful in reinforcement learning (RL) since they enable agents to learn from failures. Despite their successes, we lack a theoretical understanding, such as (i) why hindsight experience replay improves sample efficiency and (ii) how to design a relabeling method that achieves sample efficiency. To this end, we construct an example to show the information-theoretical improvement in sample efficiency achieved by goal relabeling. Our example reveals that goal relabeling can enhance sample efficiency and exploit the rich information in observations through better hypothesis elimination. Based on these insights, we develop an RL algorithm called GOALIVE. To analyze the sample complexity of GOALIVE, we introduce a complexity measure, the goal-conditioned Bellman-Eluder (GOAL-BE) dimension, which characterizes the sample complexity of goal-conditioned RL problems. Compared to the Bellman-Eluder dimension, the goal-conditioned version offers an exponential improvement in the best case. To the best of our knowledge, our work provides the first characterization of the theoretical improvement in sample efficiency achieved by goal relabeling.

paragraphs: Goal relabeling allows a reinforcement-learning agent to learn from an attempt that failed to achieve its original goal. This paper asks why that reuse can reduce the amount of experience needed for learning. It constructs an example demonstrating an information-theoretic improvement, providing a theoretical explanation for a technique already successful in practice.

The example shows how relabeling can extract richer information from observations by eliminating more hypotheses about the learning problem. Building on this insight, the authors introduce an algorithm called GOALIVE. They also define the goal-conditioned Bellman–Eluder dimension, a complexity measure designed to characterize the number of samples required in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

Compared with the existing Bellman–Eluder dimension, the goal-conditioned measure offers an exponential improvement in the best case. That qualification matters: the result establishes how large the benefit can be, rather than promising exponential savings for every task. Together, the construction, algorithm, and complexity measure connect the practical reuse of failed attempts to a formal account of sample efficiency.
summary.tldr: The paper explains goal relabeling through improved hypothesis elimination and develops GOALIVE with a complexity measure offering best-case exponential improvement.

title: How Does Goal Relabeling Improve Sample Efficiency?

abstract: Catastrophic forgetting emerges as a critical challenge when fine-tuning multi-modal large language models (MLLMs), where improving performance on unseen tasks often leads to a significant performance drop on the original tasks. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of catastrophic forgetting in MLLMs and introduces a post-training adjustment method called Model Tailor. Our method primarily preserves the pre-trained parameters while replacing a small number ($\leq$ 10%) of fine-tuned parameters, maintaining $\sim$ 99% effectiveness on original tasks versus pre-training, and achieving $\sim$ 97% on new tasks compared to standard fine-tuning. Specifically, we derive a sparse mask to identify the model patch, based on a fusion strategy that integrates salience and sensitivity analysis. Subsequently, a compensation mechanism is introduced to decorate the patch, enhancing the model’s performance on both target and original tasks. Additionally, our method is adaptable to multi-task scenarios. Through extensive experiments on InstructBLIP and LLaVA-1.5 in both image captioning and visual question answering tasks, our approach demonstrates significant task adaptability while preserving inherent pre-trained capabilities.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a multimodal language model for new tasks can damage abilities it already had, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Model Tailor addresses this through a post-training adjustment. It retains most pretrained parameters while incorporating a small selected patch of fine-tuned parameters, seeking to preserve original capabilities alongside newly learned ones.

The patch is identified with a sparse mask that combines salience and sensitivity analysis. A compensation mechanism then adjusts the patch to improve performance on both original and target tasks. The method uses no more than 10% of fine-tuned parameters in this selective replacement strategy and can also be applied in multi-task settings.

The authors report approximately 99% of pretrained effectiveness on original tasks and approximately 97% of standard fine-tuning effectiveness on new tasks. These are relative comparisons to different reference models. Experiments on InstructBLIP and LLaVA-1.5 cover image captioning and visual question answering, supporting the approach’s ability to balance adaptation with preservation of pretrained capabilities.
summary.tldr: Model Tailor selectively incorporates and compensates a small fine-tuned parameter patch to preserve old capabilities while retaining new-task performance.

title: Model Tailor: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Multi-modal Large Language Models

abstract: Hierarchical clustering (HC) is an important data analysis technique in which the goal is to recursively partition a dataset into a tree-like structure while grouping together similar data points at each level of granularity. Unfortunately, for many of the proposed HC objectives, there exist strong barriers to approximation algorithms with the hardness of approximation. We consider the problem of hierarchical clustering given auxiliary information from natural oracles in the learning-augmented framework. Our main results are algorithms that, given learning-augmented oracles, compute efficient approximate HC trees for the celebrated Dasgupta’s and Moseley-Wang objectives that overcome known hardness barriers.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into a tree of progressively finer groups. Similar points should remain together at appropriate levels, allowing the same dataset to be examined at several granularities. The difficulty is that several mathematical objectives for choosing such a tree have strong barriers to efficient approximation.

This paper studies what becomes possible when the algorithm receives auxiliary information from oracles in a learning-augmented framework. The additional information changes the setting in which the clustering problem is solved. The authors develop efficient algorithms for two established objectives, Dasgupta's and Moseley-Wang's, using these oracles to construct approximate hierarchical trees.

The resulting approximation guarantees overcome known hardness barriers in this augmented setting. The role of the oracle is essential to interpreting the claim: the algorithms are given information beyond the ordinary clustering input. The contribution is therefore a demonstration that appropriately structured auxiliary guidance can change what efficient hierarchical clustering can achieve. It connects the quality of a clustering hierarchy to the information available during its construction, across two prominent ways of evaluating such trees.
summary.tldr: Oracle-provided auxiliary information enables efficient hierarchical clustering approximations that overcome known barriers in the learning-augmented setting.

title: Learning-Augmented Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: Model reprogramming adapts pretrained models to downstream tasks by modifying only the input and output spaces. Visual reprogramming (VR) is one instance for vision tasks that adds a trainable noise pattern (i.e., a visual prompt) to input images to facilitate downstream classification. The existing VR approaches for CLIP train a single visual prompt using all descriptions of different downstream classes. However, the limited learning capacity may result in (1) a failure to capture diverse aspects of the descriptions (e.g., shape, color, and texture), and (2) a possible bias toward less informative attributes that do not help distinguish between classes. In this paper, we introduce a decoupling-and-reweighting framework. Our decoupled visual prompts (DVP) are optimized using descriptions grouped by explicit causes (DVP-cse) or unsupervised clusters (DVP-cls). Then, we integrate the outputs of these visual prompts with a probabilistic reweighting matrix (PRM) that measures their contributions to each downstream class. Theoretically, DVP lowers the empirical risk bound. Experimentally, DVP outperforms baselines on average across 11 downstream datasets. Notably, the DVP-PRM integration enables insights into how individual visual prompts influence classification decisions, providing a probabilistic framework for understanding reprogramming.

title: Understanding Model Reprogramming for CLIP via Decoupling Visual Prompts

abstract: The rapid advancement of code large language models (Code LLMs) underscores the critical need for effective and transparent benchmarking methods. However, current benchmarking predominantly relies on publicly available, human-created datasets. The widespread use of these static benchmark datasets makes the evaluation process particularly susceptible to data contamination—an unavoidable consequence of the extensive data collection processes employed during LLM training. Existing methods for addressing data contamination typically face significant limitations, including reliance on substantial human effort and difficulty in managing class imbalances. To overcome these challenges, we propose DyCodeEval, a novel benchmarking suite specifically designed to evaluate Code LLMs under realistic contamination scenarios. Given an initial seed programming problem, DyCodeEval utilizes multiple agents to systematically extract and modify contextual information without changing the core logic, generating semantically equivalent variations. We introduce a dynamic data generation method and conduct extensive empirical studies on two seed datasets involving 18 Code LLMs. The results demonstrate that DyCodeEval effectively assesses the reasoning capabilities of Code LLMs under contamination conditions while producing diverse problem variants, thereby ensuring robust and consistent benchmarking outcomes.

paragraphs: Code models are often evaluated on public programming problems that may also appear in their training data. This contamination complicates the interpretation of benchmark scores as evidence of reasoning ability. Existing responses can require substantial human work and struggle with class imbalance, motivating a more dynamic way to construct evaluation problems.

DyCodeEval begins with a seed programming problem and uses multiple agents to extract and modify its contextual information. The intended result is a collection of semantically equivalent variants that preserve the original problem's core logic. Changing context while retaining logic lets the evaluation examine performance across different presentations of the same underlying reasoning task.

The authors study the approach using two seed datasets and 18 code language models. They report that it produces diverse variants and effectively evaluates reasoning under contamination conditions, with robust and consistent benchmarking outcomes. Its contribution is an automated evaluation suite that treats contamination as part of the setting being studied. The reported evidence supports dynamic variation as a useful tool for assessing code models in that setting.
summary.tldr: DyCodeEval generates contextually varied programming problems with preserved core logic to assess code models under benchmark contamination.

title: DyCodeEval: Dynamic Benchmarking of Reasoning Capabilities in Code Large Language Models Under Data Contamination

abstract: We present any4, a learned 4-bit weight quantization solution for large language models (LLMs) providing arbitrary numeric representations without requiring pre-processing of weights or activations. any4 yields higher accuracy compared to other related 4-bit numeric representation types: int4, fp4 and nf4, as evaluated on a range of model sizes, generations and families (Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral and Mixtral). While any4 does not require preprocessing of weights or activations, it is also competitive with orthogonal techniques that require such preprocessing (e.g., AWQ and GPTQ). We also experiment with any3 and any2 and show competitiveness at lower bits. Additionally, we show that we can calibrate using a single curated diverse sample rather than hundreds of samples from a dataset as done in most quantization approaches. We also open source tinygemm, a latency optimized GPU matrix multiplication library for LLMs, that implements any4 using a GPU-efficient lookup table strategy along with other common quantization methods. We open source our code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/any4.

paragraphs: Compressing language-model weights to four bits requires choosing which numerical values those bits represent. any4 learns that representation instead of relying on fixed formats such as int4, fp4, or nf4. The method supports arbitrary numerical representations and does not require preprocessing either the model weights or its activations.

Across the evaluated model sizes, generations, and families, including Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, and Mixtral, any4 achieves higher accuracy than those other four-bit formats. It is also competitive with AWQ and GPTQ, which involve preprocessing. Experiments with three-bit and two-bit variants report competitive results as well, extending the investigation to more aggressive compression.

The authors also show calibration using one curated, diverse sample instead of the hundreds of dataset samples commonly used by quantization approaches. To support execution, they release tinygemm, a GPU matrix multiplication library optimized for latency. It implements any4 through a GPU-efficient lookup table strategy, connecting the learned numerical format with a concrete implementation for language-model computation.
summary.tldr: any4 learns four-bit weight representations that improve accuracy over fixed formats and supports efficient GPU execution without weight or activation preprocessing.

title: any4: Learned 4-bit Numeric Representation for LLMs

abstract: Human body restoration, as a specific application of image restoration, is widely applied in practice and plays a vital role across diverse fields. However, thorough research remains difficult, particularly due to the lack of benchmark datasets. In this study, we propose a high-quality dataset automated cropping and filtering (HQ-ACF) pipeline. This pipeline leverages existing object detection datasets and other unlabeled images to automatically crop and filter high-quality human images. Using this pipeline, we constructed a person-based restoration with sophisticated objects and natural activities (PERSONA) dataset, which includes training, validation, and test sets. The dataset significantly surpasses other human-related datasets in both quality and content richness. Finally, we propose OSDHuman, a novel one-step diffusion model for human body restoration. Specifically, we propose a high-fidelity image embedder (HFIE) as the prompt generator to better guide the model with low-quality human image information, effectively avoiding misleading prompts. Experimental results show that OSDHuman outperforms existing methods in both visual quality and quantitative metrics. The dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/gobunu/OSDHuman.

paragraphs: Restoring images of human bodies is a practical image-restoration problem, but dedicated research has been constrained by a shortage of benchmark data. This paper addresses both the data problem and the restoration model. It introduces an automated process for building a human-image dataset and a one-step diffusion approach for restoring low-quality human images.

The high-quality automated cropping and filtering pipeline draws on existing object-detection datasets and other unlabeled images. It selects and crops high-quality human imagery to construct PERSONA, with training, validation, and test splits. The authors report that PERSONA substantially exceeds other human-related datasets in image quality and content richness, providing a broader basis for restoration research.

The proposed OSDHuman model uses a high-fidelity image embedder to generate its conditioning prompt from the low-quality input. This guides restoration using information from the actual image and helps avoid misleading prompts. Experiments show better visual quality and quantitative results than existing methods. Together, the dataset and model contribute a benchmark foundation and an improved restoration approach.
summary.tldr: PERSONA supplies a richer human-restoration benchmark, while OSDHuman uses image-derived guidance for improved one-step diffusion restoration.

title: Human Body Restoration with One-Step Diffusion Model and A New Benchmark

abstract: Graph-based social recommendation (SR) models suffer from various noises of the social graphs, hindering their recommendation performances. Either graph-level redundancy or graph-level missing will indeed influence the social graph structures, further influencing the message propagation procedure of graph neural networks (GNNs). Generative models, especially diffusion-based models, are usually used to reconstruct and recover the data in better quality from original data with noises. Motivated by it, a few works take attempts on it for social recommendation. However, they can only handle isotropic Gaussian noises but fail to leverage the anisotropic ones. Meanwhile the anisotropic relational structures in social graphs are commonly seen, so that existing models cannot sufficiently utilize the graph structures, which constraints the capacity of noise removal and recommendation performances. Compared to the diffusion strategy, the flow matching strategy shows better ability to handle the data with anisotropic noises since they can better preserve the data structures during the learning procedure. Inspired by it, we propose RecFlow which is the first flow-matching based SR model. Concretely, RecFlow performs flow matching on the structure representations of social graphs. Then, a conditional learning procedure is designed for optimization. Extensive performances prove the promising performances of our RecFlow from six aspects, including superiority, effectiveness, robustnesses, sensitivity, convergence and visualization.
