paragraphs: Social recommendation models use relationships between users to help make recommendations. Redundant or missing relationships alter the graph and affect how graph neural networks pass information. The paper argues that existing diffusion-based denoising approaches are limited by their treatment of isotropic Gaussian noise, whereas social relationships commonly exhibit direction-dependent, or anisotropic, structure.

RecFlow applies flow matching to representations of the social graph’s structure. The motivation is that flow matching can better preserve data structure during learning when noise is anisotropic. A conditional learning procedure is then used to optimize the model. The intended benefit is to recover more useful relational information for recommendation while accounting for the uneven structure of graph noise.

The authors evaluate RecFlow through comparisons of performance, component effectiveness, robustness, sensitivity, convergence, and visualizations, reporting promising results across these analyses. The contribution connects the choice of generative denoising approach to the kind of corruption present in social graphs. Its findings support flow matching as a useful approach for the recommendation settings investigated.
summary.tldr: RecFlow uses flow matching to denoise social graph representations while preserving relational structure relevant to recommendations.

title: Flow Matching for Denoised Social Recommendation

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs’ basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs’ utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders try to turn a language model’s internal activations into a collection of interpretable features. But an appealing interpretation is difficult to verify when researchers do not know the model’s underlying concepts. This paper asks a practical question: do those features help predict concepts from activations better than established alternatives?

The authors test activation probing under four challenging conditions: limited training data, uneven class frequencies, noisy labels, and changes in the input distribution. Their hypothesis is that concept-like features could provide useful structure when learning from difficult data. Although sparse autoencoders sometimes improve results on individual datasets, ensembles incorporating them do not consistently beat ensembles built entirely from baseline methods.

The authors also examine identifying misleading correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and probing across multiple tokens. Simple alternatives achieve similar results in these settings. The findings therefore challenge the demonstrated practical advantage of current sparse autoencoders for these tasks, while leaving their usefulness elsewhere open. They also show why strong downstream comparisons matter when evaluating interpretability methods.
summary.tldr: Sparse autoencoders offer occasional probing gains, but the tested combinations do not consistently outperform strong alternatives without them.

title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing

abstract: Open-source pre-trained models hold great potential for diverse applications, but their utility declines when their training data is unavailable. Data-Free Image Synthesis (DFIS) aims to generate images that approximate the learned data distribution of a pre-trained model without accessing the original data. However, existing DFIS methods produce samples that deviate from the training data distribution due to the lack of prior knowledge about natural images. To overcome this limitation, we propose DDIS, the first Diffusion-assisted Data-free Image Synthesis method that leverages a text-to-image diffusion model as a powerful image prior, improving synthetic image quality. DDIS extracts knowledge about the learned distribution from the given model and uses it to guide the diffusion model, enabling the generation of images that accurately align with the training data distribution. To achieve this, we introduce Domain Alignment Guidance (DAG) that aligns the synthetic data domain with the training data domain during the diffusion sampling process. Furthermore, we optimize a single Class Alignment Token (CAT) embedding to effectively capture class-specific attributes in the training dataset. Experiments on PACS and ImageNet demonstrate that DDIS outperforms prior DFIS methods by generating samples that better reflect the training data distribution, achieving SOTA performance in data-free applications.

paragraphs: Data-free image synthesis aims to recover images resembling a pretrained model’s learned distribution without accessing its original training data. The paper identifies limited knowledge of natural images as a reason existing methods produce mismatched samples. DDIS addresses this by using a text-to-image diffusion model as an image prior.

The method extracts distributional knowledge from the given pretrained model and uses it to guide image generation. Domain Alignment Guidance steers diffusion sampling toward the original training domain. Separately, an optimized Class Alignment Token embedding captures class-specific attributes. These components address both the broader characteristics of the source domain and the details associated with individual classes.

Experiments on PACS and ImageNet show that DDIS generates samples that better reflect the training distribution than earlier data-free synthesis methods. The authors also report state-of-the-art performance in data-free applications. The findings support combining a diffusion model’s image-generation prior with knowledge retained in another trained model, using explicit domain and class alignment to make synthetic data relevant to that model’s unavailable training set.
summary.tldr: DDIS guides a diffusion model with domain and class knowledge from a pretrained model to synthesize better-aligned images without original training data.

title: When Model Knowledge meets Diffusion Model: Diffusion-assisted Data-free Image Synthesis with Alignment of Domain and Class

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique has proven effective in improving the performance of large language models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks. However, the performance gains are inconsistent across different tasks, and the underlying mechanism remains a long-standing research question. In this work, we make a preliminary observation that the monotonicity of token probability distributions may be correlated with the gains achieved through CoT reasoning. Leveraging this insight, we propose two indicators based on the token probability distribution to assess CoT effectiveness across different tasks. By combining instance-level indicators with logistic regression model, we introduce Dynamic CoT, a method that dynamically select between CoT and direct answer. Furthermore, we extend Dynamic CoT to closed-source models by transferring decision strategies learned from open-source models. Our indicators for assessing CoT effectiveness achieve an accuracy of 89.2%, and Dynamic CoT reduces token consumption by more than 35% while maintaining high accuracy. Overall, our work offers a novel perspective on the underlying mechanisms of CoT reasoning and provides a framework for its more efficient deployment.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting can improve language-model reasoning, but its benefits vary across tasks. This paper investigates whether token probability distributions can help predict when it will be useful. Its starting observation is preliminary: the monotonicity of those distributions may correlate with the performance gains from chain-of-thought reasoning.

The authors construct two indicators from token probabilities and combine instance-level signals with logistic regression. The resulting Dynamic CoT method chooses between generating a chain of thought and answering directly. They also extend the approach to closed-source models by transferring decision strategies learned from open-source models. The indicators thus become a mechanism for allocating extra reasoning selectively.

The reported indicators assess chain-of-thought effectiveness with 89.2% accuracy, while Dynamic CoT reduces token consumption by more than 35% and maintains high accuracy. These findings support the usefulness of the signals for selective deployment. They do not turn the preliminary correlation into a complete explanation of why chain-of-thought works; the contribution is both an investigative perspective and an empirically effective selection method.
summary.tldr: Dynamic CoT uses token-probability indicators to choose when to reason step by step, cutting reported token use by over 35% while maintaining high accuracy.

title: Token Signature: Predicting Chain-of-Thought Gains with Token Decoding Feature in Large Language Models

abstract: Previous studies have extensively addressed the attribution problem for binary outcome variables. However, in many practical scenarios, the outcome variable is continuous, and simply binarizing it may result in information loss or biased conclusions. To address this issue, we propose a series of posterior causal estimands for retrospectively evaluating multiple correlated causes from a continuous outcome. These estimands include posterior intervention effects, posterior total causal effects, and posterior natural direct effects. Under assumptions of sequential ignorability, monotonicity, and perfect positive rank, we show that the posterior causal estimands of interest are identifiable and present the corresponding identification equations. We also provide a simple but effective estimation procedure and establish asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators. An artificial hypertension example and a real developmental toxicity dataset are employed to illustrate our method.

paragraphs: Causal attribution asks how causes contributed to an outcome that has already been observed. Much prior work treats outcomes as binary, but many practical outcomes vary continuously. Converting these measurements into two categories can discard information or distort conclusions. This paper develops a framework for retrospective causal analysis that retains the continuous outcome and accommodates multiple correlated causes.

The authors define several posterior causal quantities, including intervention effects, total causal effects, and natural direct effects. These provide different ways to describe causal contributions after observing an outcome. The paper supplies equations showing how the quantities can be identified under sequential ignorability, monotonicity, and perfect positive rank assumptions. Those assumptions are central to the identification result.

The work also introduces an estimation procedure and establishes asymptotic properties describing its behavior as sample sizes grow. An artificial hypertension example and a real developmental toxicity dataset illustrate the approach. The contribution combines definitions, conditional identification, and estimation tools for attribution without first reducing a continuous measurement to a binary label.
summary.tldr: The paper develops retrospective causal attribution for continuous outcomes, with identification guarantees under explicit assumptions and an accompanying estimation procedure.

title: Causal Attribution Analysis for Continuous Outcomes

abstract: Foundation models serve as the backbone for numerous specialized models developed through fine-tuning. However, when the underlying pretrained model is updated or retrained (e.g., on larger and more curated datasets), the fine-tuned model becomes obsolete, losing its utility and requiring retraining. This raises the question: is it possible to transfer fine-tuning to a new release of the model? In this work, we investigate how to transfer fine-tuning to a new checkpoint without having to re-train, in a data-free manner. To do so, we draw principles from model re-basin and provide a recipe based on weight permutations to re-base the modifications made to the original base model, often called task vector. In particular, our approach tailors model re-basin for Transformer models, taking into account the challenges of residual connections and multi-head attention layers. Specifically, we propose a two-level method rooted in spectral theory, initially permuting the attention heads and subsequently adjusting parameters within select pairs of heads. Through extensive experiments on visual and textual tasks, we achieve the seamless transfer of fine-tuned knowledge to new pre-trained backbones without relying on a single training step or datapoint. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/TransFusion.

paragraphs: When a pretrained model receives a new checkpoint, specialized fine-tuning performed on an older version may need to be repeated. This paper investigates transferring that specialization without training again or accessing training data. It represents the fine-tuning changes as a task vector: the modifications made relative to the original base model.

The approach adapts model re-basin techniques to transformers, using weight permutations to align the task vector with a new backbone. Residual connections and multi-head attention create structural challenges for this alignment. The proposed method uses two levels grounded in spectral theory, first permuting attention heads and then adjusting parameters within selected pairs of heads.

Experiments on visual and textual tasks demonstrate transfer of fine-tuned knowledge to new pretrained backbones without any training steps or datapoints. The significance is that specialization can be carried forward through parameter alignment in the evaluated settings. This offers a route to benefiting from an updated base model while reusing work already encoded in an older model’s fine-tuning changes.
summary.tldr: Transformer-specific weight alignment transfers fine-tuning changes to updated pretrained checkpoints without additional training or data in the reported experiments.

title: Update Your Transformer to the Latest Release: Re-Basin of Task Vectors

abstract: Predicting molecular ground-state conformation (i.e., energy-minimized conformation) is crucial for many chemical applications such as molecular docking and property prediction. Classic energy-based simulation is time-consuming when solving this problem, while existing learning-based methods have advantages in computational efficiency but sacrifice accuracy and interpretability. In this work, we propose a novel and effective method to bridge the energy-based simulation and the learning-based strategy, which designs and learns a Wasserstein gradient flow-driven SE(3)-Transformer, called WGFormer, for ground-state conformation prediction. Specifically, our method tackles this task within an auto-encoding framework, which encodes low-quality conformations by the proposed WGFormer and decodes corresponding ground-state conformations by an MLP. The architecture of WGFormer corresponds to Wasserstein gradient flows — it optimizes conformations by minimizing an energy function defined on the latent mixture models of atoms, thereby significantly improving performance and interpretability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art competitors, providing a new and insightful paradigm to predict ground-state conformation. The code is available at https://github.com/FanmengWang/WGFormer.

abstract: Bridge models in image restoration construct a diffusion process from degraded to clear images. However, existing methods typically require training a bridge model from scratch for each specific type of degradation, resulting in high computational costs and limited performance. This work aims to efficiently leverage pretrained generative priors within existing image restoration bridges to eliminate this requirement. The main challenge is that standard generative models are typically designed for a diffusion process that starts from pure noise, while restoration tasks begin with a low-quality image, resulting in a mismatch in the state distributions between the two processes. To address this challenge, we propose a transition equation that bridges two diffusion processes with the same endpoint distribution. Based on this, we introduce the IRBridge framework, which enables the direct utilization of generative models within image restoration bridges, offering a more flexible and adaptable approach to image restoration. Extensive experiments on six image restoration tasks demonstrate that IRBridge efficiently integrates generative priors, resulting in improved robustness and generalization performance. Code will be available at GitHub.

paragraphs: Image-restoration bridge models define a diffusion process that takes a degraded image toward a clear one. Existing approaches typically train a separate bridge for each degradation type, which creates substantial computational cost. IRBridge investigates how to reuse pretrained generative models within these restoration processes.

The central obstacle is a mismatch between starting points. Standard generative diffusion begins from pure noise, whereas restoration begins from an image that already contains degraded visual information. Consequently, the states encountered along the two processes have different distributions. The authors derive a transition equation connecting diffusion processes that share the same endpoint distribution, providing the basis for transferring generative knowledge between them.

IRBridge uses this connection to incorporate generative models directly into restoration bridges, removing the stated need to train each bridge from scratch. Experiments across six restoration tasks report improved robustness and generalization through efficient integration of pretrained generative priors. The approach matters because it provides a principled connection between existing image generators and restoration processes with different starting conditions.
summary.tldr: IRBridge connects diffusion processes with a shared endpoint so pretrained image generators can be reused in image-restoration bridges.

title: IRBridge: Solving Image Restoration Bridge with Pre-trained Generative Diffusion Models

abstract: Merging multiple expert models offers a promising approach for performing multi-task learning without accessing their original data. Existing methods attempt to alleviate task conflicts by sparsifying task vectors or promoting orthogonality among them. However, they overlook the fundamental target of model merging: the merged model performs as closely as possible to task-specific models on respective tasks. We find these methods inevitably discard task-specific information that, while causing conflicts, is crucial for performance. Based on our findings, we frame model merging as a constrained optimization problem ($\textit{i.e.}$, minimizing the gap between the merged model and individual models, subject to the constraint of retaining shared knowledge) and solve it via adaptive projective gradient descent. Specifically, we align the merged model with individual models by decomposing and reconstituting the loss function, alleviating conflicts through $\textit{data-free}$ optimization of task vectors. To retain shared knowledge, we optimize this objective by projecting gradients within a $\textit{shared subspace}$ spanning all tasks. Moreover, we view merging coefficients as adaptive learning rates and propose a task-aware, training-free strategy. Experiments show that our plug-and-play approach consistently outperforms previous methods, achieving state-of-the-art results across diverse architectures and tasks in both vision and NLP domains.

paragraphs: Combining expert models can create a multitask model without using their original training data. However, reducing conflicts between experts by removing or separating parts of their task vectors can also discard information needed for individual tasks. This paper argues that merging should directly target agreement with each expert on its respective task.

The authors formulate that goal as constrained optimization: reduce the gap between the merged model and the individual models while preserving shared knowledge. Their method decomposes and reconstructs the loss to optimize task vectors without data. It projects gradients into a shared subspace spanning the tasks, using that constraint to retain common knowledge while addressing conflicts.

The approach also interprets merging coefficients as adaptive learning rates and supplies a task-aware strategy that does not require training. Experiments across vision and language tasks and multiple architectures report consistent improvements over previous methods and state-of-the-art results. The main contribution is an optimization view that treats task-specific information as something to preserve while managing interference, rather than simply removing conflicting components.
summary.tldr: The method merges experts through data-free constrained optimization that preserves shared knowledge while reducing disagreement with task-specific models.

title: Modeling Multi-Task Model Merging as Adaptive Projective Gradient Descent

abstract: Modern language models are trained on large, unstructured datasets consisting of trillions of tokens and obtained by crawling the web. The unstructured nature makes it difficult to reason about their contents and develop systematic approaches to data curation. In this paper, we unpack monolithic web corpora by developing taxonomies of their contents and organizing them into domains. We introduce WebOrganizer, a framework for organizing web pages in terms of both their topic and format. Using these two complementary notions of domains, we automatically annotate pre-training data by distilling annotations from a large language model into efficient classifiers. This allows us to study how data from different domains should be mixed to improve models on downstream tasks, and we show that we can combine insights about effective topics and formats to further boost performance. We demonstrate that our domain mixing also improves existing methods that select data based on quality. Furthermore, we study and compare how quality-based methods will implicitly change the domain mixture. Overall, our work demonstrates that constructing and mixing domains provides a valuable complement to quality-based data curation methods, opening new avenues for effective and insightful pre-training data curation.

paragraphs: Web-scale pretraining datasets contain enormous amounts of text, but their unstructured organization makes systematic curation difficult. WebOrganizer addresses this by classifying pages along two complementary dimensions: what they discuss and the format in which they present it. These categories make the composition of a large corpus easier to examine and deliberately adjust.

The framework distills annotations from a large language model into efficient classifiers that automatically label pretraining data. With those labels, the authors study how mixing different domains affects downstream performance. They find that combining insights about useful topics with insights about useful formats produces further gains, making both dimensions relevant to data selection.

Domain mixing also improves existing quality-based selection methods in the reported study. The authors additionally examine how quality filters implicitly alter the mixture of domains, connecting quality judgments to corpus composition. The findings support domain organization as a complement to quality filtering: it provides explicit categories for understanding and adjusting what a model encounters during pretraining.
summary.tldr: WebOrganizer labels web data by topic and format, enabling domain mixtures that improve pretraining and complement quality-based filtering.

title: Organize the Web: Constructing Domains Enhances Pre-Training Data Curation

abstract: Recent advancements in time series forecasting have explored augmenting models with text or vision modalities to improve accuracy. While text provides contextual understanding, it often lacks fine-grained temporal details. Conversely, vision captures intricate temporal patterns but lacks semantic context, limiting the complementary potential of these modalities. To address this, we propose Time-VLM, a novel multimodal framework that leverages pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to bridge temporal, visual, and textual modalities for enhanced forecasting. Our framework comprises three key components: (1) a Retrieval-Augmented Learner, which extracts enriched temporal features through memory bank interactions; (2) a Vision-Augmented Learner, which encodes time series as informative images; and (3) a Text-Augmented Learner, which generates contextual textual descriptions. These components collaborate with frozen pre-trained VLMs to produce multimodal embeddings, which are then fused with temporal features for final prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Time-VLM achieves superior performance, particularly in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios, thereby establishing a new direction for multimodal time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/CityMind-Lab/ICML25-TimeVLM.

Time-VLM combines temporal, visual, and textual information through pretrained vision-language models.

Experiments report superior forecasting performance, particularly in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios. These findings support combining complementary representations while keeping the pretrained vision-language models frozen. The distinctive contribution is the coordinated pipeline: retrieval supplies enriched temporal information, and visual and textual processing contribute additional representations that are brought together at prediction time.
summary.tldr: Time-VLM combines retrieved temporal features, time-series images, and textual descriptions through frozen vision-language models to improve forecasting.

title: Time-VLM: Exploring Multimodal Vision-Language Models for Augmented Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Modern optimizers combine gradients from the current mini-batch with historical optimization state, such as momentum or adaptive moments. While effective, this standard practice can produce parameter updates that actively increase the loss of individual samples. We term this phenomenon per-sample interference and propose redefining the parameter update as an optimization problem that explicitly minimizes it. Because the exact formulation of the problem is computationally prohibitive, we introduce a highly efficient surrogate. By reducing the problem’s dimensionality to the batch size and restricting the optimization to the last linear layer, we overcome memory and speed bottlenecks. This strategy hinges on our unexpected finding that this layer alone can reliably capture core second-order statistics of the full network. The resulting surrogate problem integrates readily into standard optimizers like SGD and AdamW, and can be solved using a small number of GPU-friendly iterations. Crucially, the method exhibits favorable scaling properties, as the relative computational overhead shrinks as the model size or input grows. Experiments on image classification benchmarks confirm reduced per-sample interference and improved generalization.

paragraphs: An optimizer combines current mini-batch gradients with historical information such as momentum or adaptive moments. The resulting update can increase the loss of individual examples even when it is useful overall. This paper calls that effect per-sample interference and proposes selecting parameter updates through an optimization problem that explicitly minimizes it.

Solving the exact problem would be prohibitively expensive, so the authors develop a surrogate whose dimension depends on batch size and whose optimization is restricted to the final linear layer. Image-classification experiments report both lower per-sample interference and better generalization, supporting explicit interference reduction as a useful modification to standard optimization.
summary.tldr: An efficient last-layer surrogate helps standard optimizers reduce updates that hurt individual samples and improves generalization in image-classification experiments.

title: Reducing Per-Sample Interference in Stochastic Optimization

abstract: The layout-to-image (L2I) task enables fine-grained control over image generation via object categories and spatial layouts. However, existing L2I methods yield fragmented and distorted generations under few-shot atypical settings. We term this failure as representation fragmentation, arising from a granularity mismatch that entangles semantic identity with visual details. To address this issue, we propose a representation-driven framework that disentangles semantics from primitives for robust few-shot adaptation. Specifically, Semantic Anchoring aggregates categorical semantics into anchors for stable identity, while Primitive Imbuing models recomposable primitives for robust local detail modeling. Conceptual Steering further regulates optimization with a saliency-aware objective to preserve foreground semantic consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in the 5-shot regime over state-of-the-art L2I methods in both visual fidelity and alignment across diverse atypical domains. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/iCVTEAM/DSP.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation uses object categories and spatial arrangements to control an image. When adapting to unusual domains from only a few examples, existing methods can produce fragmented or distorted results. This paper attributes that failure to representation fragmentation: object identity and visual details become entangled at incompatible levels of granularity.

The proposed framework separates stable semantic identity from reusable visual primitives. Semantic Anchoring aggregates category information into anchors that preserve what an object is. Primitive Imbuing models local visual building blocks that can be recombined. A third component, Conceptual Steering, uses a saliency-aware training objective to maintain semantic consistency in foreground objects.

Experiments in the five-example adaptation setting report consistent improvements over leading layout-to-image methods across diverse atypical domains. The gains concern both visual fidelity and alignment with the requested layout and content. Together, the components address how a model organizes its representation during adaptation: category identity remains stable while local detail can vary and recombine. The stated findings support this separation as a useful approach when examples are scarce and the target domain is unusual.
summary.tldr: Separating object semantics from recomposable visual primitives improves five-shot layout-to-image adaptation across unusual domains.

title: Envisioning Beyond the Few: Disentangled Semantics and Primitives for Few-Shot Atypical Layout-to-Image Generation

abstract: Modern neural networks have shown promise for solving partial differential equations over surfaces, often by discretizing the surface as a mesh and learning with a mesh-aware graph neural network. However, graph neural networks suffer from oversmoothing, where a node’s features become increasingly similar to those of its neighbors. Unitary graph convolutions, which are mathematically constrained to preserve smoothness, have been proposed to address this issue. Despite this, in many physical systems, such as diffusion processes, smoothness naturally increases and unitarity may be overconstraining. In this paper, we systematically study the smoothing effects of different GNNs for dynamics modeling and prove that unitary convolutions hurt performance for such tasks. We propose relaxed unitary convolutions that balance smoothness preservation with the natural smoothing required for physical systems. We also generalize unitary and relaxed unitary convolutions from graphs to meshes. In experiments on PDEs such as the heat and wave equations over complex meshes and on weather forecasting, we find that our method outperforms several strong baselines, including mesh-aware transformers and equivariant neural networks. Our code is available at github.com/EdwardBerman/rayleigh_analysis

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can oversmooth their representations, making neighboring nodes too similar. However, physical dynamics may genuinely become smoother over time, as in diffusion. A model must therefore distinguish unwanted smoothing inside its computation from the smoothing required to describe the physical process.

The paper systematically studies this tension in dynamics models. Unitary graph convolutions preserve smoothness, but that restriction can prevent them from representing the changes in smoothness that a physical system needs. The authors prove performance harm for such tasks and propose relaxed unitary convolutions that balance preservation with permitted smoothing. They also extend both unitary and relaxed unitary operations from graphs to meshes.

Experiments include heat and wave equations on complex meshes and weather forecasting. The proposed method outperforms several strong baselines, including mesh-aware Transformers and equivariant neural networks. These findings show that preserving representation structure must be matched to the dynamics: allowing controlled changes in smoothness can improve prediction when strict preservation overconstrains the model.
summary.tldr: Relaxed unitary convolutions allow physically necessary smoothing while controlling oversmoothing, improving tested PDE and weather-prediction models.

title: Smoothness Errors in Dynamics Models and How to Avoid Them

abstract: We show how an adversarial model trainer can plant backdoors in a large class of deep, feedforward neural networks. These backdoors are statistically undetectable in the white-box setting, meaning that the backdoored and honestly trained models are close in total variation distance, even given the full descriptions of the models (e.g., all of the weights). The backdoor provides access to invariance-based adversarial examples for every input, mapping distant inputs to unusually close outputs. However, without the backdoor, it is provably impossible (under standard cryptographic assumptions) to generate any such adversarial examples in polynomial time. Our theoretical and preliminary empirical findings demonstrate a fundamental power asymmetry between model trainers and model users.

paragraphs: The paper studies a fundamental imbalance between those who train a model and those who receive it. It constructs backdoors for a broad class of deep feedforward networks that are statistically difficult to distinguish from honest training, even when the recipient can inspect the complete model, including all of its weights.

The indistinguishability statement uses total variation distance: the distributions of backdoored and honestly trained models are close in this statistical sense. Possession of the backdoor enables invariance-based adversarial examples for every input. These examples map inputs that are far apart to outputs that are unusually close, exposing a hidden capability available to the trainer.

Without the backdoor, producing any such adversarial examples in polynomial time is provably impossible under standard cryptographic assumptions. This computational claim is distinct from the statistical claim about identifying the altered model. Together, the theory and preliminary empirical findings show how full model access can coexist with a substantial capability advantage for the adversarial trainer in the construction studied.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs neural-network backdoors that remain statistically hidden under full inspection while giving their holder privileged access to adversarial examples.

title: Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Motivated by variational inference methods, we propose a zeroth-order algorithm for solving optimization problems in the space of Gaussian probability measures. The algorithm is based on an interacting system of Gaussian particles that stochastically explore the search space and self-organize around global minima via a consensus-based optimization (CBO) mechanism. Its construction relies on the Linearized Bures–Wasserstein (LBW) space, a novel parametrization of Gaussian measures we introduce for efficient computations. We establish well-posedness and study the convergence properties of the particle dynamics via a mean-field approximation. Numerical experiments on variational inference tasks demonstrate the algorithm’s robustness and superior performance with respect to deterministic gradient-based method in presence of low-dimensional non log-concave targets.

paragraphs: Variational inference motivates optimization problems in which the objects being adjusted are probability distributions. This paper focuses on Gaussian distributions and introduces a zeroth-order method, meaning it does not rely on objective gradients. Rather than following one deterministic optimization path, the method uses an interacting population of Gaussian particles.

The particles explore stochastically and coordinate through a consensus-based optimization mechanism designed to organize them around global minima. To make the calculations efficient, the authors introduce Linearized Bures–Wasserstein space, a new parametrization of Gaussian measures. This representation supplies the computational setting for the interactions and movement of the Gaussian particles.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the dynamics are well posed and studies convergence through a mean-field approximation. Numerical experiments on variational inference show robustness and better performance than a deterministic gradient-based method for low-dimensional targets that are not log-concave. The reported empirical advantage is specific to that setting. Together, the geometry, population search, and analysis provide an alternative way to optimize Gaussian approximations when a deterministic gradient method is less effective.
summary.tldr: A gradient-free population of interacting Gaussian particles offers an effective variational-inference optimizer for the tested low-dimensional, non-log-concave targets.

title: Variational inference via Gaussian interacting particles in the Bures-Wasserstein geometry

abstract: Scaling video generation from seconds to minutes faces a critical bottleneck: while short-video data is abundant and high-fidelity, coherent long-form data is scarce and limited to narrow domains. While multi-resolution image training works because higher resolution is largely an interpolation of the same underlying patch distribution, training across video lengths is fundamentally different: a longer video is an extrapolation that must invent new events and causal structure beyond the short-clip horizon. To address this, we propose a training paradigm where Mode Seeking meets Mean Seeking, decoupling local fidelity from long-term coherence from a unified representation via a Decoupled Diffusion Transformer. Our approach utilizes a global Flow Matching head trained via supervised learning on long videos to capture narrative structure, while simultaneously employing a local Distribution Matching head that aligns sliding windows to a frozen short-video teacher via a mode-seeking reverse-KL divergence. This strategy enables the synthesis of minute-scale videos that learns long-range coherence and motions from limited long videos via supervised flow matching, while inheriting local realism by aligning every sliding-window segment of the student to a frozen short-video teacher.

Our approach utilizes a global Flow Matching head trained via supervised learning on long videos to capture narrative structure, while simultaneously employing a local Distribution Matching head that aligns sliding windows to a frozen short-video teacher via a mode-seeking reverse-KL divergence. paragraphs: Generating a longer video requires extending events and causal structure beyond what appears in short clips. The paper argues that this differs fundamentally from increasing image resolution, where interpolation can preserve the underlying patch distribution. High-quality short videos are abundant, while coherent long videos are scarce and cover narrower domains.

The proposed Decoupled Diffusion Transformer separates local visual fidelity from long-term coherence while using a unified representation. A global Flow Matching head learns narrative structure through supervised training on long videos. Alongside it, a local Distribution Matching head aligns sliding video windows with a frozen short-video teacher using a mode-seeking reverse-KL objective. The two heads assign different learning responsibilities to the available sources of information.

This arrangement enables minute-scale video synthesis by learning long-range coherence and motion from limited long-video data while obtaining local realism from the short-video teacher. Each sliding-window segment is aligned with that teacher, complementing the global training signal. The stated contribution is a training paradigm that combines long-horizon supervision with local distribution matching to address the mismatch between short-video abundance and long-video scarcity.
summary.tldr: A decoupled video transformer learns long-range structure from limited long videos and local realism from a frozen short-video teacher.

title: Mode Seeking meets Mean Seeking for Fast Long Video Generation

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently achieved significant success due to their any-order generation capabilities. However, existing inference methods typically rely on local, immediate-step metrics—such as confidence or entropy—which inherently lack a more reliable perspective, leading to sub-optimal generation quality. To address this, we propose Coherent Contextual Decoding (CCD), a novel inference framework built upon two core innovations. First, CCD bypasses the potential bias of the single context to leverage historical contexts for approximating the marginal distribution of token prediction, leading to better sequence coherence and the early rejection of sub-optimal paths. More importantly, we demonstrate that this mechanism is theoretically equivalent to modeling the consistency of historical steps via the conditional mutual information between contexts and token predictions. Finally, CCD achieves significantly milder performance degradation under highly parallel decoding scenarios compared to baselines. Empirically, our method achieves a simultaneous enhancement in both inference speed and performance across diverse benchmarks on Dream and LLaDA.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate tokens in flexible orders, making the choice of which predictions to accept an important part of inference. Existing decoding methods often judge predictions using confidence or entropy from the current step. The paper argues that this immediate view can favor choices that do not remain coherent as generation develops.

Coherent Contextual Decoding, or CCD, instead uses contexts from earlier decoding steps to approximate the marginal distribution of token predictions. Looking across this history reduces dependence on a single context and helps reject less promising generation paths early. The authors also establish a theoretical equivalence between this mechanism and measuring historical consistency through conditional mutual information between contexts and predictions.

These findings suggest that historical agreement can guide efficient generation more effectively than immediate confidence alone in the evaluated settings, especially when many token decisions are made together.
summary.tldr: CCD uses historical decoding contexts to improve diffusion-language-model coherence, speed, and performance under parallel generation.

title: Beyond Confidence: Adaptive and Coherent Decoding for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: We revisit the central online problem of ski rental in the "algorithms with predictions" framework from the point of view of distributional predictions. If we are given as a prediction a distribution $\hat p$ over the ski days, and the true number of ski days comes from some (unknown) distribution $p$, then we show as our main result that there is an algorithm with expected cost at most $OPT + O\left(\min \left(\max(\eta,1) \cdot \sqrt{b}, b \log b \right) \right)$, where $OPT$ is the expected cost of the optimal policy for the true distribution $p$, $b$ is the cost of buying, and $\eta$ is the Earth Mover’s (Wasserstein-1) distance between $p$ and $\hat p$. An implication of this bound is that our algorithm has consistency $O(\sqrt{b})$ (additive loss when the prediction error is $0$) and robustness $O(b \log b)$ (additive loss when the prediction error is arbitrarily large). Moreover, we do not need to assume that we know (or have any bound on) the prediction error $\eta$, in contrast with previous work in robust optimization which assumes that we know this error. We also complement this upper bound with a variety of lower bounds showing that it is essentially tight: not only can the consistency/robustness tradeoff not be improved, but our particular loss function cannot be meaningfully improved.

paragraphs: The ski-rental problem asks when to stop paying repeated rental costs and buy instead, without knowing how long the service will be needed. This paper studies an algorithm given a predicted distribution over that duration. The true distribution is unknown, as is the accuracy of the prediction.

The algorithm's expected cost is bounded relative to the best policy for the true distribution. Its additive excess cost is O(min(max(η, 1)√b, b log b)), where b is the buying cost and η measures the Wasserstein-1 distance between the predicted and true distributions. Thus the bound responds to prediction quality but also caps the damage from arbitrarily inaccurate predictions.

With perfect predictions, the additive guarantee is O(√b); with unrestricted error, it is O(b log b). The algorithm needs neither the error itself nor an upper bound on it. Lower bounds show that the consistency–robustness tradeoff and the particular error-dependent loss bound are essentially tight. The contribution therefore combines useful distributional advice with protection that does not require knowing how trustworthy that advice is.
summary.tldr: A ski-rental algorithm uses distributional predictions of unknown accuracy with essentially tight guarantees for both accurate and unreliable advice.

title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

abstract: We study the problems of approximate sampling from and distribution testing of mixture models, where the modes satisfy a functional inequality called approximate tensorization of entropy (ATE). While it is known that ATE makes these tasks more efficient in the unimodal setting, mixtures of few distributions satisfying ATE do not necessarily satisfy ATE overall, leading to a lack of theoretical guarantees for multimodal distributions, which are a key challenging case of modern generative models. We show this gap can be overcome by establishing the following pair of results for mixtures of ATE distributions: 1) We show fast mixing of Glauber dynamics from a data-based initialization, with optimal sample complexity, for mixtures of distributions satisfying modified log-Sobolev inequalities, building on similar results in (Koehler et al., 2024, Huang et al., 2024) for mixtures satisfying the weaker Poincaré inequality. 2) Answering an open question from (Blanca et al., 2023), we give efficient identity-testers for mixtures of ATE distributions in the coordinate-conditional sampling access model.

paragraphs: A distribution can be a mixture of individually manageable components while remaining difficult to analyze as a whole. This paper studies mixtures whose components satisfy approximate tensorization of entropy, or ATE. Although ATE helps with sampling and testing for individual distributions, even a mixture of a few such components need not satisfy it globally.

The first result establishes fast mixing of Glauber dynamics from a data-based initialization, with optimal sample complexity, for mixtures of distributions satisfying modified log-Sobolev inequalities. The initialization condition matters: the guarantee uses data to start the sampling process. This extends related work based on the weaker Poincaré inequality.

The second result gives efficient identity testers for mixtures of ATE distributions. These operate with coordinate-conditional sampling access, a specified form of access to the distribution. Together, the results show that useful sampling and testing guarantees can survive even when a mixture loses the global functional property of its components. This addresses a theoretical obstacle associated with multimodal distributions.
summary.tldr: Component-level functional inequalities suffice for new mixture sampling and identity-testing guarantees even when the full mixture lacks ATE.

title: Sampling and Identity-Testing Without Approximate Tensorization of Entropy

abstract: Task-optimized neural networks are the leading in-silico models of sensory cortex, yet the field lacks a unified understanding of which modeling choices drive improved brain alignment. Prior NeuroAI work is fragmented across datasets and modalities, making it difficult to determine robust scaling trends. Here, we systematically investigate the scaling laws of model-to-brain alignment across 8 neural datasets (spanning electrophysiology, fMRI, EEG, and MEG) and over 600 models with diverse architectures and pretraining configurations. We report three scaling trends: (1) Pretraining saturation: Alignment improves with pretraining compute and data scale but saturates across all recording modalities. (2) Complementary fine-tuning: Hybrid task & neural data optimization yields consistent improvements in alignment that generalize across datasets and modalities. (3) Mapping scaling: Increasing the number of neural samples to fit model-to-brain mappings yields log-linear gains with the largest impact on alignment. Finally, we propose a novel subject-shared cross-attention mapping which drastically reduces parameter count and improves alignment. Taken together, these results establish multimodal scaling laws that guide resource allocation for next-generation brain models.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained on tasks are widely used as computational models of sensory cortex, but it is unclear which modeling investments most improve their alignment with brain measurements. This study compares more than 600 models across eight neural datasets spanning electrophysiology, fMRI, EEG, and MEG, bringing several recording modalities into one analysis.

The authors report three trends. Larger pretraining datasets and more computation improve alignment, but those gains saturate across the studied modalities. Combining task optimization with neural-data optimization provides further improvements that generalize across datasets and modalities. Increasing the neural samples used to fit model-to-brain mappings produces log-linear gains and has the largest reported impact on alignment.

The paper also introduces a subject-shared cross-attention mapping that reduces parameter count substantially while improving alignment. Together, these findings distinguish scaling the pretrained model from improving its adaptation and mapping to neural data. Within the study, they provide evidence for allocating resources across those stages instead of treating pretraining scale as the sole driver of better brain models.
summary.tldr: A broad study finds saturating pretraining gains and substantial benefits from neural-data fine-tuning and larger model-to-brain mapping datasets.

title: Multimodal Scaling Laws for Task & Data-Optimized Models of Visual Cortex

abstract: We propose a new paradigm for long video understanding by treating a long video as a Neural Knowledge Representation (NKR). NKR represents video contents neither as a stream of tokens nor pre-organized databases, but as an individual small portion of network weights attached to the VLM backbone. The NKR weights are optimized to encapsulate the video’s semantic content via a novel Agentic Knowledge Distillation (AKD) process, where an agent automatically synthesizes dense descriptions and question-answer pairs to distill the video’s knowledge into the NKR. While AKD serves as a comprehensive, one-time encoding phase, the resulting NKR transforms the video into a portable, reusable asset. At inference, the lightweight NKR is mounted onto a frozen Vision-Language Model (VLM), enabling direct, query-based understanding without reloading or re-encoding the original video. This approach decouples video length from inference cost, offering high amortized efficiency for multi-turn video understanding. Experiments on the LVBench benchmark show our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches while reducing end-to-end latency by over two orders of magnitude, opening new possibilities for interactive long-video understanding.

paragraphs: This paper represents a long video's semantic content in a small set of network weights attached to a vision-language model. The resulting Neural Knowledge Representation becomes a reusable asset for answering questions about that video. Its purpose is to avoid repeatedly loading or encoding the original video when users ask multiple questions.

Creating this representation requires a one-time Agentic Knowledge Distillation phase. An agent synthesizes detailed descriptions and question-answer pairs, which are used to optimize the video-specific weights. At inference, those weights are attached to a frozen vision-language model, allowing it to answer queries using the distilled content.

The approach separates the cost of preparing video knowledge from the cost of later interactions. Its efficiency advantage is therefore especially relevant when the representation is reused across turns. On LVBench, the authors report performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and an end-to-end latency reduction exceeding two orders of magnitude. The findings support storing reusable semantic knowledge in model weights for interactive long-video understanding.
summary.tldr: A one-time distillation process stores video knowledge in small reusable network weights, enabling fast follow-up queries without re-encoding the video.

title: From Content to Knowledge: Lightning Fast Long-Video Understanding with Neural Knowledge Representations

abstract: In this paper, we propose AlphaGRPO, a novel framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to AR-Diffusion Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) to enhance multimodal generation capabilities without relying on external knowledge injection. Our approach unlocks the model’s intrinsic potential to perform advanced reasoning tasks: Reasoning Text-to-Image Generation, where the model actively infers implicit user intents, and Self-Reflective Refinement, where it autonomously diagnoses and corrects misalignments in generated outputs. To address the challenge of providing stable supervision for real-world multimodal generation, we introduce the Decompositional Verifiable Reward (DVReward). Unlike holistic scalar rewards, DVReward utilizes an LLM to decompose complex user requests into atomic, verifiable semantic and quality questions, which are then evaluated by a general MLLM to provide reliable and interpretable feedback. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AlphaGRPO yields robust improvements across multimodal generation benchmarks, including GenEval, TIIF-Bench, DPG-Bench and WISE, while also achieving significant gains in editing tasks on GEdit without training on editing tasks. These results validate that our self-reflective reinforcement approach effectively leverages inherent understanding to guide high-fidelity generation.

paragraphs: AlphaGRPO aims to help a unified multimodal model use its existing understanding more effectively during generation. It applies Group Relative Policy Optimization to models combining autoregressive and diffusion components. The targeted capabilities include inferring implicit user intentions when generating images and diagnosing and correcting mismatches in outputs through self-reflective refinement.

A central component is DVReward, which turns a complex request into smaller questions that can be checked individually. An LLM produces questions about semantic requirements and output quality, and a multimodal LLM evaluates them. This decomposition gives the reinforcement-learning process more interpretable feedback than a single holistic judgment and is intended to provide stable supervision for complex generation requests.

The authors report robust improvements on GenEval, TIIF-Bench, DPG-Bench, and WISE. They also report significant improvements on GEdit despite not training on editing tasks. These results suggest that the approach can transfer some gains beyond its training tasks. The stated contribution is to activate and coordinate capabilities already present in the model, without relying on external knowledge injection.
summary.tldr: AlphaGRPO uses decomposed, verifiable feedback to improve multimodal generation and self-correction, with reported editing gains even without editing-task training.

title: AlphaGRPO: Unlocking Self-Reflective Multimodal Generation in Unified Multimodal Models via Decompositional Verifiable Reward

abstract: Understanding how anatomical shapes evolve in response to developmental covariates—and quantifying their spatially varying uncertainties—is critical in healthcare research. Existing approaches typically rely on global time-warping formulations that ignore spatially heterogeneous dynamics. We introduce PRISM, a novel framework that bridges implicit neural representations with uncertainty-aware statistical shape analysis. PRISM models the conditional distribution of shapes given covariates, providing spatially continuous estimates of both the population mean and covariate-dependent uncertainty at arbitrary locations. A key theoretical contribution is a closed-form Fisher Information metric that enables efficient, analytically tractable local temporal uncertainty quantification via automatic differentiation. Experiments on three synthetic datasets and one clinical dataset demonstrate PRISM’s strong performance across diverse tasks—from modeling shape evolution to anomaly detection—within a unified framework, while providing interpretable and clinically meaningful uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Anatomical shapes can change differently across regions, and uncertainty about those changes can vary spatially as well. PRISM addresses this heterogeneity by combining implicit neural representations with probabilistic shape analysis. Instead of relying on a global time-warping description, it models a distribution of shapes conditioned on developmental covariates.

The model supplies spatially continuous estimates of both the population mean and covariate-dependent uncertainty at arbitrary locations. This allows the representation to describe how expected anatomy and its variability differ across space. A closed-form Fisher Information metric provides an analytically tractable way to quantify local temporal uncertainty efficiently using automatic differentiation.

Experiments on three synthetic datasets and one clinical dataset demonstrate strong performance on tasks including shape evolution and anomaly detection. The authors also report interpretable, clinically meaningful uncertainty estimates. The contribution brings those tasks into one framework, connecting a flexible representation of three-dimensional shape with statistical quantities that describe where and how confidently developmental variation can be characterized.
summary.tldr: PRISM models anatomical shape distributions with spatially varying means and uncertainties, supporting shape evolution analysis and anomaly detection.

title: $\textttPRISM$:A 3D Probabilistic Neural Representation for Interpretable Shape Modeling

abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) serves as an indispensable diagnostic tool in clinical practice, yet existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain unreliable for ECG interpretation, often producing plausible but clinically incorrect analyses. To address this, we propose ECG-R1, the first reasoning ECG MLLM designed for reliable ECG interpretation via three innovations. First, we construct the interpretation corpus using Protocol-Guided Instruction Data Generation, grounding interpretation in measurable ECG features and monograph-defined quantitative thresholds and diagnostic logic. Second, we present a modality-decoupled architecture with Interleaved Modality Dropout to improve robustness and cross-modal consistency when either the ECG signal or ECG image is missing. Third, we present Reinforcement Learning with ECG Diagnostic Evidence Rewards to strengthen evidence-grounded ECG interpretation. Additionally, we systematically evaluate the ECG interpretation capabilities of proprietary, open-source, and medical MLLMs, and provide the first quantitative evidence that severe hallucinations are widespread, suggesting that the public should not directly trust these outputs without independent verification. Code is available at https://github.com/PKUDigitalHealth/ECG-R1.

paragraphs: ECG interpretations generated by multimodal language models can sound plausible while being clinically incorrect. ECG-R1 addresses this problem by grounding interpretation in measurable evidence and explicit diagnostic procedures. Its training corpus is generated using protocols that connect ECG features to quantitative thresholds and diagnostic logic defined in monographs.

The architecture separates modalities and uses Interleaved Modality Dropout to improve consistency when either a signal or an ECG image is unavailable. This targets a different source of unreliability: dependence on receiving both forms of input. Reinforcement learning with diagnostic evidence rewards further encourages the model to support its interpretations with ECG evidence.

The paper also evaluates proprietary, open-source, and medical multimodal models, reporting quantitative evidence that severe hallucinations are widespread. That finding gives the proposed evidence-grounding mechanisms their practical motivation. The authors explicitly caution against directly trusting such outputs without independent verification. The abstract presents ECG-R1’s training and architectural strategy alongside this diagnostic evaluation, making reliability of the reasoning process central to the contribution.
summary.tldr: ECG-R1 combines protocol-based data, missing-modality training, and evidence rewards to target unreliable ECG interpretation.

title: ECG-R1: Protocol-Guided and Modality-Agnostic MLLM for Reliable ECG Interpretation

abstract: The quadratic complexity of attention remains the central bottleneck in long-context inference for large language models. Prior acceleration methods either sparsify the attention map with structured patterns or permanently evict tokens at specific layers, which can retain irrelevant tokens or rely on irreversible early decisions despite the layer-/head-wise dynamics of token importance. In this paper, we propose Token Sparse Attention, a lightweight and dynamic token-level sparsification mechanism that compresses per-head $Q, K, V$ to a reduced token set during attention and then decompresses the output back to the original sequence, enabling token information to be reconsidered in subsequent layers. Furthermore, Token Sparse Attention exposes a new design point at the intersection of token selection and sparse attention. Our approach is fully compatible with dense attention implementations, including Flash Attention, and can be seamlessly composed with existing sparse attention kernels. Experimental results show that Token Sparse Attention consistently improves accuracy–latency trade-off, achieving up to $\times$3.23 attention speedup at 128K context with less than 1% accuracy degradation. These results demonstrate that dynamic and interleaved token-level sparsification is a complementary and effective strategy for scalable long-context inference.

paragraphs: Long-context attention is expensive because its computation grows quadratically with sequence length. Reducing the number of participating tokens can help, but a token’s importance varies across layers and attention heads. Permanently removing tokens early can therefore lock the model into decisions that later processing would have changed.

Token Sparse Attention selects a reduced token set separately for each head’s query, key, and value representations during attention. It then expands the attention output back to the original sequence structure. This allows token information to be reconsidered in subsequent layers, making sparsification an interleaved operation instead of an irreversible deletion.

The method works with dense attention implementations, including Flash Attention, and can also combine with existing sparse attention kernels. Experiments report an improved accuracy–latency trade-off, including up to 3.23 times attention speedup at a 128K context length with less than 1% accuracy degradation. The speed figure concerns attention specifically. The findings support dynamic token selection as a complementary mechanism for making long-context inference more efficient.
summary.tldr: Token Sparse Attention dynamically selects tokens within attention while preserving later reconsideration, achieving up to 3.23 times attention speedup at 128K context.

title: Token Sparse Attention: Efficient Long-Context Inference with Interleaved Token Selection

abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their global, non-causal generation process, but their continuous latent dynamics make discrete constraints—e.g., the output should be a JSON file that matches a given schema—difficult to impose. We introduce a training-free guidance method for steering continuous diffusion language models to satisfy formal syntactic constraints expressed using regular expressions. Our approach constructs an analytic score estimating the probability that a latent state decodes to a valid string accepted by a given regular expression, and uses its gradient to guide sampling, without training auxiliary classifiers. The denoising process targets the base model conditioned on syntactic validity. We implement our method in Diffinity on top of the PLAID diffusion model and evaluate it on 180 regular-expression constraints over JSON and natural-language benchmarks. Diffinity achieves 68-96% constraint satisfaction while incurring only a small perplexity cost relative to unconstrained sampling, outperforming autoregressive constrained decoding in both constraint satisfaction and output quality. Diffinity is open-sourced at github.com/large-loris-models/Diffinity.

paragraphs: Continuous diffusion language models generate through evolving latent representations, which makes discrete formatting rules difficult to enforce. This paper introduces a way to guide that process toward strings satisfying constraints expressed as regular expressions. It requires neither additional model training nor a separately trained classifier.

The method constructs an analytic score estimating how likely a latent state is to decode into a string accepted by the expression. The score's gradient then steers sampling toward syntactic validity. The intended target is the original model conditioned on producing valid syntax, connecting a discrete acceptance rule to the continuous denoising process.

Implemented as Diffinity on the PLAID model, the approach is evaluated on 180 constraints covering JSON and natural-language benchmarks. It achieves 68–96% constraint satisfaction with a small perplexity cost compared with unconstrained generation. It also outperforms the evaluated autoregressive constrained decoding approach on satisfaction and output quality. These results demonstrate useful control over continuous generation, while the reported satisfaction rates show that validity is not guaranteed for every sample.
summary.tldr: Diffinity guides continuous diffusion language models toward regular-expression constraints without training, achieving 68–96% satisfaction in the reported evaluation.

title: Continuous Diffusion Models Can Obey Formal Syntax

abstract: Inference-time steering adapts pretrained diffusion and flow models to new tasks without retraining, often utilizing ratio-of-densities constructions that reweight time-indexed marginals with fixed exponents. We identify Marginal Path Collapse, a failure mode in which the intermediate density defined by such compositions becomes non-normalizable despite valid endpoints. This collapse can arise when composing heterogeneous experts trained with mismatched noise schedules (and/or negative exponents / partial supports). To address this, we provide (i) a sharp sufficient Path Existence Criterion that characterizes when the composed intermediate densities are mathematically well-defined, and (ii) Adaptive Path Correction with Exponents (ACE), which generalizes Feynman–Kac steering to support time-varying exponents. Our analysis reveals that ACE controls the quantile radius of the intermediate distributions, providing a theoretical mechanism for path stabilization observed in experiments. On flexible-pose scaffold decoration, a drug design task composed of de-novo, conformer, and protein-conditioned experts, ACE prevents collapse and significantly outperforms constant-exponent baselines. Furthermore, ACE improves attribute success rates in compositional image generation, establishing it as a general framework for compositional sampling.

title: On the Collapse of Generative Paths: A Criterion and Correction for Diffusion Steering

abstract: Graph anomaly detection methods aim to distinguish anomalous nodes. While prior methods characterize anomalies through increased variation in the spectral energy distributions, they overlook those that result in decreased variation, i.e., camouflaged anomalies that appear normal. We show that this type of anomaly persists across multiple datasets and remains undetectable by existing spectral approaches. To address this limitation, we propose a node-level spectral energy formulation that is fully compatible with message passing and enables the detection of camouflaged anomalies. Building on this formulation, we introduce an energy-aware graph learning framework that models spectral shifts through energy-driven message passing in both static and time-series graphs. Besides, our unified architecture extends to temporal settings without introducing specialized sequence modules, enabling efficient learning under long sliding windows. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/AICPS-Lab/Spectral-Energy-Shifts-in-GAD.

paragraphs: Graph anomaly detection aims to identify unusual nodes through their relationships and attributes. Existing spectral methods look for increased variation in energy distributions, but the paper identifies another pattern: anomalies can reduce variation and appear deceptively normal. The authors find these camouflaged anomalies across multiple datasets and show that existing spectral approaches miss them.

To detect this pattern, they formulate spectral energy at the node level in a way that works directly with message passing. Their energy-aware graph learning framework then models shifts in energy through the messages exchanged among nodes. This allows the learning process to address the overlooked direction of spectral change.

The same architecture handles static graphs and graphs observed over time, without adding specialized sequence modules for temporal processing. The authors report efficient learning with long sliding windows and effective, scalable performance on large benchmarks. The contribution broadens the spectral patterns that anomaly detectors can use while retaining a unified graph-learning approach across static and temporal settings.
summary.tldr: The method detects camouflaged graph anomalies by modeling spectral energy shifts that existing increased-variation approaches overlook.

title: Modeling Spectral Energy Shifts in Spatio-Temporal Graph Anomaly Detection

abstract: Imbalanced Unreliable Partial Label Learning (I-UPLL) is a challenging weakly supervised learning setting in which severe class imbalance and unreliable candidate labels jointly degrade model performance. By revisiting existing approaches for imbalanced learning, we observe that most of them fundamentally rely on estimating the class prior to guide balancing operations, such as re-sampling, pseudo-label generation, or logit adjustment. However, under I-UPLL, obtaining stable and accurate prior estimates at the early stage of training is often unrealistic due to the ambiguity and unreliability of partial labels, thereby leading the model to rapidly converge to a suboptimal solution. To address this issue, we propose CLAPOR, a novel CLAss-PriOr perturbation-Robust regularization framework that fundamentally avoids dependence on accurate prior estimation. Specifically, the proposed regularization trains the model under deliberately perturbed class priors, sampled from a Dirichlet distribution that deviates from the current estimated prior. This design encourages consistent performance under prior uncertainty and naturally preserves attention to minority classes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CLAPOR across various settings of I-UPLL.

paragraphs: Learning becomes especially difficult when some classes are rare and each example comes with an uncertain, potentially unreliable set of candidate labels. Many techniques for class imbalance depend on estimating class frequencies, also called class priors. Those estimates then guide decisions such as resampling examples or adjusting predictions.

The paper identifies a problem with relying on these estimates early in training: ambiguous labels can make them unstable or inaccurate, sending the model toward a poor solution. CLAPOR addresses this by training under deliberately varied class priors. It samples these alternatives from a Dirichlet distribution that departs from the current estimate, encouraging performance to remain consistent despite uncertainty about the true class proportions.

The method still uses a current estimate to construct perturbations, but its design avoids requiring that estimate to be accurate. Training across plausible disturbances also helps preserve attention to minority classes. Experiments on benchmark datasets report effectiveness across multiple imbalanced, unreliable partial-label settings. The main idea is to make balancing robust to uncertain class frequencies instead of letting an early estimate dictate learning.
summary.tldr: CLAPOR improves learning with imbalanced, unreliable candidate labels by making training robust to deliberately perturbed class-frequency estimates.

title: Class-Prior Perturbation-Robust Regularization for Imbalanced Unreliable Partial Label Learning

abstract: We introduce Unsupervised Partner Design (UPD), a population-free multi-agent reinforcement learning method for robust ad-hoc teamwork. UPD generates training partners on-the-fly and selects them adaptively based on a learnability criterion, removing the need for pre-trained partner populations or manual parameter tuning. We show that this simple mechanism enables effective partner diversity and can be extended to joint partner-environment selection when a procedural level generator is available. Across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked-AI, and the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge, UPD consistently achieves strong performance compared to both population-based and population-free baselines. In a human-AI user study, agents trained with UPD achieve higher returns and are rated as more adaptive, more human-like, and less frustrating than all evaluated baseline methods.
