paragraphs: Ad-hoc teamwork requires an agent to cooperate effectively with partners it was not specifically trained alongside. Unsupervised Partner Design, or UPD, prepares agents for that challenge by generating training partners as learning proceeds. It avoids maintaining a pretrained partner population or manually tuning partner parameters.

UPD adaptively chooses partners using a learnability criterion, directing training toward partners selected for their learning value. The authors find that this mechanism produces effective partner diversity. When a procedural level generator is available, the same idea can extend to selecting both a partner and an environment, coordinating these two aspects of training.

Across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked-AI, and the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge, UPD consistently performs strongly against both population-based and population-free baselines. In a human–AI study, its agents earn higher returns and receive better ratings for adaptability, human-likeness, and reduced frustration than every evaluated baseline. These findings connect the training mechanism to both benchmark teamwork and human experience, supporting adaptive partner generation as a practical route to more flexible cooperation.
summary.tldr: UPD generates and adaptively selects training partners, producing strong teamwork results and better human-partner ratings than evaluated baselines.

title: Unsupervised Partner Design Enables Robust Ad-hoc Teamwork

abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis aims to infer human emotions by integrating signals from diverse modalities. However, missing modalities are common in real-world applications due to sensor failure, data corruption, or privacy concerns. Existing approaches typically follow two main paradigms: recovery-based and non-recovery-based methods. This dichotomy results in two critical limitations: I) computational inefficiency and semantic inconsistency (recovery-based methods rely on heavy generators that incur prohibitive inference latency and risk semantic drift due to lack of class-level priors); II) lack of instance specificity (non-recovery-based methods rely on static global mappings that fail to capture sample-specific affective cues). To address these gaps, we propose Adaptive Prototype Imputation (API). To mitigate I), we introduce Semantic-anchored Class-Temporal Prototype Estimation (SCOPE) to construct non-trainable prototypes as stable semantic anchors, promoting semantic reliability. To resolve II), we design Directional Instance-Adaptive Affine Modulation (DIAM) to dynamically modulate these anchors via direction-specific affine transformations, capturing instance-unique affective characteristics without generative overhead. Experimental results on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI demonstrate that API outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, establishing a robust and lightweight prototype-centric paradigm for multimodal sentiment analysis. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/KX-yolo/API.

paragraphs: Multimodal sentiment analysis combines different signals to infer emotion, but some signals may be missing because of sensor failures, corrupted data, or privacy concerns. Existing recovery methods can require expensive generators and introduce semantic drift. Methods that avoid recovery can instead rely on static mappings that miss the emotional details of individual samples.

Adaptive Prototype Imputation addresses both problems with reference representations that can be adjusted for each instance. Its SCOPE component constructs non-trainable class-temporal prototypes to provide stable semantic anchors. These anchors supply class-level structure, helping the missing-modality representation remain connected to the sentiment information the model needs.

The DIAM component then adapts those anchors using direction-specific affine transformations. This allows the representation to reflect the particular sample without introducing a heavy generative recovery process. Experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support combining stable prototypes with instance-dependent adjustments as a lightweight approach to sentiment analysis when some modalities are unavailable.
summary.tldr: API adapts stable sentiment prototypes to individual samples, handling missing modalities without heavy generative reconstruction.

title: API: Adaptive Prototype Imputation for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis

abstract: Prevailing autonomous agents are often constrained by a single, predefined action space, which limits their generalization capabilities across diverse tasks and can introduce compounding errors through decoupled policy execution. To address these limitations, we introduce the Deep Hierarchical Agent (DeepHA), a unified architecture that operates across a mixture of heterogeneous action spaces, flexibly generating actions ranging from high-level semantic skills to low-level motor controls. We further propose a Chain-of-Action (CoA) reasoning framework, which enables the agent to use higher-level abstract actions as structured ‘thoughts’ to guide the generation of more granular, subsequent actions. To manage the computational demands of this deep reasoning in long-horizon tasks, we develop a memory-efficient mechanism that dynamically compresses historical context and leverages Key-Value (KV) caching, reducing context length by approximately 75% without sacrificing performance. We conduct extensive evaluations on a new, large-scale benchmark of over 800 diverse Minecraft tasks. Results show that DHA significantly outperforms prior methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art and demonstrating superior generalization, particularly in complex, multi-step planning tasks. Our work presents a novel, unified framework for building more capable and efficient autonomous agents.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent can act through broad semantic skills or detailed motor controls. Restricting it to one predefined action space can limit the tasks it handles, while separating planning from execution can introduce accumulating errors. DeepHA brings heterogeneous action spaces into one architecture so that a single agent can generate actions at different levels of abstraction.

Its Chain-of-Action framework uses higher-level actions as structured reasoning steps that guide more detailed actions. This creates a progression from abstract intent toward executable behavior within the unified model. To manage the context required for long tasks, the system dynamically compresses its history and uses key-value caching. The authors report roughly a 75% reduction in context length without sacrificing performance.

Evaluation uses a new Minecraft benchmark containing more than 800 diverse tasks. DeepHA significantly outperforms prior methods and achieves state-of-the-art results, with particularly strong generalization on complex tasks requiring multiple planning steps. The reported findings connect hierarchical action generation with both broader task capability and a more manageable context cost for sustained reasoning.
summary.tldr: DeepHA chains abstract skills into detailed actions within one agent, improving Minecraft task performance while reducing historical context length by about 75%.

title: DeepHA: Scaling Action Chains Elicits Deep Hierarchical Agents

abstract: Federated Incremental Learning (FIL) aims to learn streaming tasks across distributed clients without catastrophic forgetting while preserving privacy. Most existing methods mitigate forgetting by replaying historical samples, but it can pose privacy risks and incur high resource overhead, limiting deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Lightweight Federated Incremental Learning framework called Li-FIL that leverages dense features synthesized by a server-side secure generator to enable efficient feature-based decoupled replay. More specifically, each client extracts high-confidence features from new tasks, enrich them via mixup, and privatize them before uploading to the server, which reduces both storage and communication overhead. A generator is deployed on the server to learn the distributions of clients and generate global features for replay. Moreover, to enable clients to better learn from these dense features, we decouple local training into classifier stabilization and encoder regularization. This design allows feature replay and alignment between new and previous features to be conducted separately and more effectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Li-FIL outperforms other state-of-the-art methods by up to 10.14% in terms of accuracy on both old and new tasks with superior resource efficiency.

paragraphs: Federated incremental learning asks distributed clients to learn new tasks without forgetting previous ones. Replaying old examples can help, but storing and communicating historical samples creates resource costs and privacy risks. Li-FIL replaces sample replay with dense feature replay generated on a server, aiming to make continued learning more practical on constrained devices.

Clients extract high-confidence features from new tasks, enrich those features through mixup, and privatize them before upload. A server-side generator learns the clients’ feature distributions and synthesizes global features for replay. This arrangement reduces storage and communication overhead while supplying representations that carry information useful for retaining earlier knowledge.

The split allows learning from replayed features and aligning old and new feature representations to be handled separately. Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 10.14% over other state-of-the-art methods across old and new tasks, along with better resource efficiency. The findings support combining feature-level replay with decoupled training to address forgetting and device resource demands together.
summary.tldr: Li-FIL combines server-generated feature replay with separated classifier and encoder training, improving federated incremental learning accuracy and resource efficiency.

title: Lightweight Federated Incremental Learning via Decoupled Replay

abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) deliver strong cross-domain generalization, but their scale makes deployment costly. Knowledge distillation is a natural compression route, yet prior TSFM distillation typically imitates teacher outputs, features, or pairwise relations, and therefore remains tightly coupled to teacher-specific training trajectories while underutilizing two empirical properties: (i) high-level representations across model scales tend to converge toward a shared, approximately low-rank geometry, and (ii) layer-wise utility follows a long-tail pattern. We propose consensus subspace distillation, which reframes distillation as aligning a student to a model-agnostic geometric object: a scale-invariant low-rank consensus subspace together with its center statistics. Offline, we screen high-contribution layers via drop-layer marginal loss, estimate a shrinkage-stabilized covariance from their embeddings, and derive a truncated eigensubspace that defines a consensus projector. Online, we project student embeddings into this subspace and match the teacher’s projected mean and covariance using a lightweight mean–covariance objective, enabling stable optimization without rigid pointwise feature binding. To mitigate subset-induced bias, we further introduce a frequency-domain uncertainty injection mechanism that inflates spectral density based on characteristic-function discrepancies and injects dispersion only within the consensus directions. Across forecasting and imputation, the distilled student matches or slightly improves upon the teacher, while exhibiting a predictable trade-off under strict zero-shot classification. With MOMENT-Large as teacher, we achieve about 90% parameter reduction and substantial distillation-time savings while retaining comparable performance across multiple time-series tasks. Code and compressed weights are available at anonymous.4open.science/r/CSD-13C3/.

paragraphs: Compressing a time-series foundation model by copying its individual features can tie the smaller model closely to the teacher’s particular training history. This paper instead distills a shared geometric structure, motivated by observations that high-level representations across model sizes tend toward an approximately low-rank geometry and that layer usefulness is unevenly distributed.

The method selects influential teacher layers, estimates a stabilized covariance of their embeddings, and extracts a low-dimensional consensus subspace. During student training, it matches the mean and covariance of representations projected into that subspace. This provides statistical alignment without requiring point-by-point feature imitation. A further frequency-domain mechanism injects uncertainty within the consensus directions to mitigate bias introduced by selecting only a subset of layers.

The student matches or slightly improves on its teacher in forecasting and imputation, while showing a trade-off in strict zero-shot classification. With MOMENT-Large as teacher, the authors report about 90% fewer parameters and substantial distillation-time savings. The findings support transferring shared representation geometry as a practical compression target, with results differing across task types.
summary.tldr: Consensus subspace distillation compresses time-series models by matching shared representation statistics, achieving about 90% parameter reduction with MOMENT-Large.

title: From Teacher Pathways to Invariant Manifolds: Consensus Subspace Distillation for TSFMs

abstract: Are two distributions close to each other with statistical significance? Distribution closeness testing (DCT) formalizes this question by testing whether the distance between a distribution pair is at least $\epsilon$-far. Existing DCT methods mainly measure discrepancies between a distribution pair defined on discrete spaces (e.g., using total variation), which limits their applications to complex data (e.g., images). To extend DCT to more types of data, a natural idea is to introduce maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a powerful measurement of the distributional discrepancy between two complex distributions, into DCT scenarios. However, the empirical results indicate that many distribution pairs can have the same MMD value despite having different norms in the same reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and these pairs may exhibit different finite-sample distinguishability and reflect different practical closeness levels, making MMD less informative in DCT. To mitigate the issue, we design a new measurement of distributional discrepancy, norm-adaptive MMD (NAMMD), which scales MMD’s value using the RKHS norms of distributions. Based on the asymptotic distribution of NAMMD, we finally propose the NAMMD-based DCT to assess the closeness level of a distribution pair. Theoretically, we prove that NAMMD-based DCT has higher test power compared to MMD-based DCT, with bounded type-I error, which is also validated by extensive experiments on many types of data (e.g., synthetic noise, real images). Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhijianzhouml/NAMMD.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to establish statistically that two data distributions are sufficiently close. Distribution closeness testing frames this around a distance threshold: whether the distributions are at least epsilon apart. Existing approaches largely target discrete data, motivating a kernel-based method that can also handle more complex observations such as images.

A natural distance measure is maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. The authors observe that pairs of distributions can have identical MMD values while having different norms in the same kernel representation space. Such pairs may differ in how distinguishable they are from finite samples and in their practical closeness. Their proposed norm-adaptive MMD rescales the discrepancy using those norms to retain this additional information.

The authors derive the measure’s asymptotic distribution and use it to build a closeness test. They prove higher test power than the MMD-based alternative while keeping type-I error bounded, and report supporting experiments with synthetic noise and real images. The contribution connects a more informative discrepancy measure with stronger statistical evidence for assessing closeness.
summary.tldr: Norm-adaptive MMD uses distribution norms to strengthen kernel-based closeness testing while bounding type-I error.

abstract: Many NLP tasks rely on accurately estimating word dependency probabilities P(w1|w2), where the words w1 and w2 have a particular relationship (such as verb-object). Because of the sparseness of counts of such dependencies, smoothing and the ability to use multiple sources of knowledge are important challenges. For example, if the probability P(N|V) of noun N being the subject of verb V is high, and V takes similar objects to V', and V' is synonymous to V'', then we want to conclude that P(N|V'') should also be reasonably high---even when those words did notcooccur in the training data. To capture these higher order relationships, we propose a Markov chain model, whose stationary distribution is used to give word probability estimates. Unlike the manually defined random walks used in some link analysis algorithms, we show how to automatically learn a rich set of parameters for the Markov chain's transition probabilities. We apply this model to the task of prepositional phrase attachment, obtaining an accuracy of 87.54%.

We apply this model to the task of prepositional phrase attachment, obtaining an accuracy of 87.54%.

paragraphs: Many language tasks need probabilities describing relationships between words, such as which nouns occur with a verb. Direct counts are often sparse, so observed word pairs provide incomplete evidence. The paper addresses how to combine several sources of linguistic knowledge and use relationships that connect words indirectly.

The proposed model is a Markov chain whose stationary distribution supplies word-probability estimates. Its motivation is that evidence can pass through multiple relationships: a noun associated with one verb may also be plausible with another verb connected through shared objects and synonymy. The authors learn a rich set of transition parameters automatically, rather than manually specifying the random walk.

This makes the chain's movement through relationships part of the learned model, providing a way to estimate dependencies even when particular words did not occur together in training. Applied to prepositional phrase attachment, the method achieves 87.54% accuracy. That result demonstrates its use in a concrete language task, while the broader contribution is the learned random-walk formulation for dependency probabilities.
summary.tldr: Learned Markov-chain transitions combine indirect word relationships to estimate dependency probabilities, achieving 87.54% accuracy on prepositional phrase attachment.

title: Learning random walk models for inducing word dependency distributions

abstract: We describe a manifold learning framework that naturally accommodates supervised learning manifold learning, partially supervised learning and unsupervised clustering as particular cases. Our method chooses a function by minimizing loss subject to a manifold regularization penalty. This augmented cost is minimized using a greedy stagewise functional minimization procedure, as in Gradientboost. Each stage of boosting is fast and efficient. We demonstrate our approach using both radial basis function approximations and classification trees. The performance of our method is at the state of the art on standard problems.

We demonstrate our approach using both radial basis function approximations and classification trees. The performance of our method is at the state of the art on standard problems.

paragraphs: ManifoldBoost provides a manifold learning framework that accommodates supervised learning, partially supervised learning, and unsupervised clustering. These settings become particular cases of a shared method. The paper's organizing idea is to choose a function using an objective that combines a loss with a manifold regularization penalty.

The augmented objective is optimized through greedy, stagewise functional minimization, following the approach used in gradient boosting. Rather than completing the entire optimization in one step, the procedure advances through successive stages. The authors report that each boosting stage is fast and efficient, making the optimization strategy an important part of the framework.

The paper demonstrates the method with both radial basis function approximations and classification trees. These examples show that the framework supports different kinds of function representations. Its reported performance reaches the state of the art on standard problems. The contribution combines a common objective across supervision settings with an efficient stagewise procedure and demonstrations using two distinct approximation families.
summary.tldr: ManifoldBoost uses efficient boosting stages to optimize manifold-regularized objectives across supervised, partially supervised, and unsupervised learning.

title: ManifoldBoost: stagewise function approximation for fully-, semi- and un-supervised learning

abstract: We are interested in learning programs for multiple related tasks given only a few training examples per task. Since the program for a single task is underdetermined by its data, we introduce a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian prior over programs which shares statistical strength across multiple tasks. The key challenge is to parametrize this multi-task sharing. For this, we introduce a new representation of programs based on combinatory logic and provide an MCMC algorithm that can perform safe program transformations on this representation to reveal shared inter-program substructures.

For this, we introduce a new representation of programs based on combinatory logic and provide an MCMC algorithm that can perform safe program transformations on this representation to reveal shared inter-program substructures.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning programs for several related tasks when each task provides only a few examples. Such limited evidence leaves the program for an individual task underdetermined: its examples do not settle which program should be learned. The authors address this by allowing information to be shared across tasks.

They introduce a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian prior over programs. Its purpose is to express common structure among the programs so that learning one task can inform learning another. The central modeling challenge is specifying what is shared, rather than treating related programs as completely separate objects.

To make that sharing possible, the authors develop a program representation based on combinatory logic. They also provide a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that performs safe transformations of programs in this representation to reveal shared substructures. The contribution joins a statistical model of related tasks with a representation and inference procedure that can expose their common program components. This directly addresses the ambiguity created by scarce examples.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian program learner shares information across tasks by uncovering common substructures through safe program transformations.

title: Learning Programs: A Hierarchical Bayesian Approach

abstract: The Nystrom method is an efficient technique for the eigen value decomposition of large kernel matrices. However, in order to ensure an accurate approximation, a sufficiently large number of columns have to be sampled. On very large data sets, the SVD step on the resultant data sub matrix will soon dominate the computations and become prohibitive. In this paper, we propose an accurate and scalable Nystrom scheme that first samples a large column subset from the input matrix, but then only performs an approximate SVD on the inner sub matrix by using the recent randomized low-rank matrix approximation algorithms. Theoretical analysis shows that the proposed algorithm is as accurate as the standard Nystrom method that directly performs a large SVD on the inner sub matrix On the other hand, its time complexity is only as low as performing a small SVD. Experiments are performed on a number of large-scale data sets for low-rank approximation and spectral embedding. In particular, spectral embedding of a MNIST data set with 3.3 million examples takes less than an hour on a standard PC with 4G memory.

paragraphs: The Nyström method approximates the eigendecomposition of a large kernel matrix by sampling columns. Accuracy can require many columns, but that creates another computational problem: the singular value decomposition of the resulting inner submatrix becomes expensive. This paper targets that bottleneck while retaining the benefit of a large column sample.

The proposed method first samples a large subset of columns, then uses randomized low-rank approximation algorithms to compute an approximate SVD of the inner submatrix. Its theoretical analysis establishes accuracy comparable to standard Nyström with a large SVD, while giving time complexity as low as performing a small SVD. The computational saving comes from changing the inner decomposition.

Experiments evaluate low-rank approximation and spectral embedding on several large datasets. A reported example embeds 3.3 million MNIST examples in under an hour on a standard computer with 4 GB of memory. This demonstrates the practical scale reached in that experiment, complementing the theoretical account of the method's accuracy and computational cost.
summary.tldr: Randomized approximate SVD makes large-column Nyström approximation scalable while retaining the accuracy established for the standard method.

title: Making Large-Scale Nyström Approximation Possible

abstract: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference in graphical models requires that we maximize the sum of two terms: a data-dependent term, encoding the conditional likelihood of a certain labeling given an observation, and a data-independent term, encoding some prior on labelings. Often, data-dependent factors contain fewer latent variables than data-independent factors -- for instance, many grid and tree-structured models contain only first-order conditionals despite having pair wise priors. In this paper, we note that MAP-inference in such models can be made substantially faster by appropriately preprocessing their data-independent terms. Our main result is to show that message-passing in any such pair wise model has an expected-case exponent of only 1.5 on the number of states per node, leading to significant improvements over existing quadratic-time solutions.
originalAbstract: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference in graphical models requires that we maximize the sum of two terms: a data-dependent term, encoding the conditional likelihood of a certain labeling given an observation, and a data-independent term, encoding some prior on labelings. Often, data-dependent factors contain fewer latent variables than data-independent factors -- for instance, many grid and tree-structured models contain only first-order conditionals despite having pair wise priors. In this paper, we note that MAP-inference in such models can be made substantially faster by appropriately preprocessing their data-independent terms. Our main result is to show that message-passing in any such pair wise model has an expected-case exponent of only 1.5 on the number of states per node, leading to significant improvements over existing quadratic-time solutions.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable labeling in a graphical model involves combining evidence from an observation with prior preferences over labelings. This paper exploits the fact that the prior-related terms do not change with the observed data. Preparing those terms in advance can reduce the work required during inference.

The relevant structure is that observation-dependent factors often involve fewer hidden variables than the prior factors. For example, an observation may contribute a separate term for each variable while the prior connects pairs of variables. The authors show how preprocessing the data-independent terms can make message passing substantially faster in models with this structure.

Their main result gives an expected-case dependence proportional to the number of states per node raised to the power 1.5 for message passing in such pairwise models, improving on quadratic dependence. This is an expected-case result tied to the stated model setting. It shows that separating reusable prior computation from observation-specific computation can materially change inference costs.
summary.tldr: Preprocessing data-independent terms reduces the expected-case state-count exponent of message passing from two to 1.5 in the studied pairwise models.

title: Exploiting Data-Independence for Fast Belief-Propagation
On the Use of Variational Inference for Learning Discrete Graphical Model

abstract: Recently, there has been much interest in spectral approaches to learning manifolds—so-called kernel eigenmap methods. These methods have had some successes, but their applicability is limited because they are not robust to noise. To address this limitation, we look at two-manifold problems, in which we simultaneously reconstruct two related manifolds, each representing a different view of the same data. By solving these interconnected learning problems together, two-manifold algorithms are able to succeed where a non-integrated approach would fail: each view allows us to suppress noise in the other, reducing bias. We propose a class of algorithms for two-manifold problems, based on spectral decomposition of cross-covariance operators in Hilbert space and discuss when two-manifold problems are useful. Finally, we demonstrate that solving a two-manifold problem can aid in learning a nonlinear dynamical system from limited data.

By solving these interconnected learning problems together, two-manifold algorithms are able to succeed where a non-integrated approach would fail: each view allows us to suppress noise in the other, reducing bias. We propose a class of algorithms for two-manifold problems, based on spectral decomposition of cross-covariance operators in Hilbert space and discuss when two-manifold problems are useful. Finally, we demonstrate that solving a two-manifold problem can aid in learning a nonlinear dynamical system from limited data.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks an underlying geometric representation of data, but spectral kernel eigenmap methods can be sensitive to noise. This paper addresses that difficulty when the same data have two related views. Instead of reconstructing each view separately, it treats the two manifold-learning problems as interconnected.

The proposed algorithms use spectral decomposition of cross-covariance operators in Hilbert space. In plain language, they extract structure from the relationship between the two views. Each view can help suppress noise in the other, reducing bias and allowing the joint approach to succeed in situations where a non-integrated approach would fail. The usefulness of the connection between views is central to this argument.

The authors discuss when two-manifold problems are useful and demonstrate an application to learning a nonlinear dynamical system from limited data. This shows a role for joint geometric reconstruction beyond representing a static dataset. The contribution is a class of algorithms that uses related views as mutual sources of information for recovering structure in noisy observations.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning two related manifolds lets each view suppress noise in the other and can aid nonlinear system identification.

title: Two Manifold Problems with Applications to Nonlinear System Identification

abstract: The statistical leverage scores of a matrix A are the squared row-norms of the matrix containing its (top) left singular vectors and the coherence is the largest leverage score. These quantities have been of interest in recently-popular problems such as matrix completion and Nystrom-based low-rank matrix approximation; in large-scale statistical data analysis applications more generally; and since they define the key structural nonuniformity that must be dealt with in developing fast randomized matrix algorithms. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that takes as input an arbitrary n × d matrix A, with n >> d, and that returns as output relative-error approximations to all n of the statistical leverage scores. The proposed algorithm runs in O(nd log n) time, as opposed to the O(nd2) time required by the naıve algorithm that involves computing an orthogonal basis for the range of A. This resolves an open question from (Drineas et al., 2006b) and (Mohri & Talwalkar, 2011); and our result leads to immediate improvements in coreset-based L2-regression, the estimation of the coherence of a matrix, and several related low-rank matrix problems. Interestingly, to achieve our result we judiciously apply random projections on both sides of A.

paragraphs: Statistical leverage scores describe structural nonuniformity among a matrix's rows, and coherence is the largest of these scores. They are defined using squared row lengths in a matrix of left singular vectors. These quantities matter in matrix completion, low-rank approximation, and randomized matrix algorithms, where uneven row contributions affect how computation should be organized.

The paper gives a randomized algorithm that approximates every leverage score with relative error for an arbitrary n-by-d matrix with many more rows than columns. Its running time is O(nd log n), compared with O(nd²) for the straightforward method based on computing an orthogonal basis for the matrix's range.

The construction carefully applies random projections on both sides of the input matrix. The result resolves a previously open question and immediately improves methods for coreset-based least-squares regression, coherence estimation, and related low-rank matrix problems. Its significance is that useful structural information about a large matrix can be approximated without paying the full cost of the direct basis computation.
summary.tldr: A randomized algorithm approximates all leverage scores of a tall matrix in O(nd log n) time instead of the naive O(nd²).

title: Fast approximation of matrix coherence and statistical leverage
Linear Separability and Concept Naturalness
